just breathe.text_pt:
'Just Breathe' é a quinta faixa de Backspacer (2009) e a música mais bem sucedida comercialmente do Pearl Jam desde 'Last Kiss'. Vedder escreveu tanto a música quanto a letra. A canção foi lançada como segundo single do álbum em outubro de 2009 e chegou ao top quarenta da Billboard Hot 100, a posição mais alta da banda em uma composição original desde 'Better Man' ter entrado no rádio rock quinze anos antes. A canção é uma declaração de amor escrita por um homem que está mais consciente de quanto pode perder do que de quanto tem.

A letra é uma das peças mais domésticas de escrita de Vedder. O narrador está refletindo sobre seu relacionamento com uma parceira, sobre o fato de ter sorte de tê-la, sobre a sombra da mortalidade que paira sobre a vida em comum de qualquer casal. A canção foi escrita durante as sessões de Backspacer em 2008 e 2009, em um período em que Vedder havia se tornado pai recentemente (sua filha Olivia nasceu em 2004; sua filha Harper nasceu em 2008) e em que ele estava enquadrando abertamente a própria escrita como tendo se deslocado pra a gratidão e pra longe da raiva. 'Just Breathe' é a impressão digital mais direta dessa virada no catálogo.

A melodia e a progressão de acordes são fortemente devedoras da trilha de Vedder pra Into the Wild de 2007, particularmente de 'Tuolumne' e 'Society'. Vedder discutiu em entrevistas do período Backspacer (uma conversa de 2009 com a Rolling Stone é a mais citada) que vinha escrevendo mais no violão desde Into the Wild, e que 'Just Breathe' foi uma das músicas que sobreviveu à transição de material solo pra material de banda. Glen Hansard, que colaborou com Vedder em Into the Wild, contribuiu com vocais de fundo na gravação de estúdio.

O arranjo é um dos mais despojados de Backspacer. O verso é construído sobre uma figura de violão dedilhado; a banda entra sob o segundo verso mas permanece contida. Matt Cameron toca vassourinhas em vez de baquetas na maior parte da música. Mike McCready não toca solo. A contribuição de Stone Gossard é uma única camada de guitarra estilo pedal steel que flutua sob o refrão. O arranjo honra a intimidade da letra ao se recusar a escalar pra uma liberação tamanho estádio.

got some.text:
'Got Some' is the second track on Backspacer (2009), the album's most aggressive immediate burst, and the song that most cleanly bridges Vedder's late-2000s political concerns and the band's instinct toward direct three-minute rock writing. The music is credited collectively to Pearl Jam; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was Backspacer's lead-off statement after the opener 'Gonna See My Friend' and is a sustained appeal for relief from the cumulative exhaustion of the post-9/11 American decade.

The lyric works as a list. The narrator is asking, in compressed punk-style address, for a specific kind of mercy: an honest answer, a relief from cynicism, a remedy for the cumulative spiritual erosion that the Bush years and the financial crisis of 2008 had imposed on the American public. The song was written during the Backspacer sessions in late 2008 and early 2009, in the immediate aftermath of the Obama election; the song's relief is the relief of someone who has not yet fully believed that the bad period is over and is asking for confirmation that it is.

Musically, 'Got Some' is one of the shortest songs on Backspacer (under three minutes) and one of the fastest. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging. McCready's solo is a controlled six-bar burst rather than an extended melodic statement. The song was produced by Brendan O'Brien, who has produced the majority of Pearl Jam's albums since Vs., and his preference for tight rhythm-section recording is audible across the track.

The song was released as a 7-inch vinyl single accompanying Target Stores copies of Backspacer in September 2009 (Pearl Jam's distribution deal for that album was an exclusive arrangement with Target, the band's first major-retailer-exclusive release). The song was therefore harder to find on conventional vinyl than other Backspacer material, which gave it an unusual collectible status among Pearl Jam fans for several years.

byShow.pj-2011-11-03: On 3 November 2011 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Got Some' arrived in the show's sixth slot as one of the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour's most consistent deployments of Backspacer-era material. Cameron's snare-pushed verse pattern landed at the slot's pacing function: a high-velocity peak in the show's first third. The Morumbi crowd's energy through this slot, captured on the bootleg, sustained the volume that the four-song Vs.-era opening sequence had built.

got some.text_pt:
'Got Some' é a segunda faixa de Backspacer (2009), a explosão imediata mais agressiva do álbum, e a música que faz a ponte mais limpa entre as preocupações políticas de Vedder do fim dos anos 2000 e o instinto da banda em direção à escrita de rock direto de três minutos. A música é creditada coletivamente ao Pearl Jam; a letra é de Vedder. A canção foi a declaração de início de Backspacer depois da abridora 'Gonna See My Friend' e é um apelo sustentado por alívio da exaustão acumulada da década americana pós-11 de setembro.

A letra funciona como uma lista. O narrador está pedindo, em endereçamento comprimido em estilo punk, por um tipo específico de misericórdia: uma resposta honesta, um alívio do cinismo, um remédio pra a erosão espiritual acumulada que os anos Bush e a crise financeira de 2008 tinham imposto ao público americano. A canção foi escrita durante as sessões de Backspacer no fim de 2008 e início de 2009, no rescaldo imediato da eleição de Obama; o alívio da canção é o alívio de alguém que ainda não acreditou totalmente que o período ruim acabou e está pedindo confirmação de que acabou.

Musicalmente, 'Got Some' é uma das músicas mais curtas de Backspacer (menos de três minutos) e uma das mais rápidas. O verso é construído sobre um riff em andamento de punk que não varia; o refrão se abre em um movimento harmônico mais largo que se resolve imediatamente de volta no verso. A bateria de Matt Cameron empurra o tempo pra frente sem cair. O solo de McCready é uma rajada controlada de seis compassos em vez de uma declaração melódica estendida. A música foi produzida por Brendan O'Brien, que produziu a maioria dos álbuns do Pearl Jam desde Vs., e a preferência dele por gravação densa de cozinha rítmica é audível em toda a faixa.

A canção foi lançada como single de vinil 7-polegadas acompanhando cópias de Backspacer da Target Stores em setembro de 2009 (o acordo de distribuição do Pearl Jam pra aquele álbum foi um arranjo exclusivo com a Target, o primeiro lançamento exclusivo de major retailer da banda). A música foi portanto mais difícil de achar em vinil convencional do que outro material de Backspacer, o que lhe deu um status colecionável incomum entre fãs do Pearl Jam por vários anos.

byShow_pt.pj-2011-11-03: Em 3 de novembro de 2011 no Estádio do Morumbi, 'Got Some' chegou no slot 6 do show como um dos empregos mais consistentes da Pearl Jam Twenty Tour de material da era Backspacer. A faixa de 2009, do então álbum de estúdio mais recente da banda, deu ao slot uma âncora contemporânea em um setlist que de resto se apoiava muito em Ten e Vs. O padrão de verso empurrado pela caixa de Cameron aterrissou na função de andamento do slot: um pico de alta velocidade no primeiro terço do show. wma.text:
'W.M.A.' is the eighth track on Vs. (1993). The acronym in the title is the song's argument: White Male American. The music is credited to Jeff Ament and Dave Abbruzzese; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written in direct response to a real incident: Vedder and a Black friend were standing outside the Pearl Jam offices in Seattle when a police officer approached the two of them and singled out the friend for questioning while ignoring Vedder. The song is the thought experiment the moment generated. Vedder describes, in third-person address, a man who moves through the world without friction because of his racial demographic, and the song is the indictment of that frictionless movement.

The arrangement is the most rhythmically aggressive thing on Vs. Jeff Ament's bass line is the structural engine, and Dave Abbruzzese's drumming (this is one of two songs on Vs. where Abbruzzese receives co-writing credit, an unusual designation for a Pearl Jam record) builds a tribal-pulse texture that Vedder has compared, in interviews from the 1993 Vs. promotional cycle, to the rhythm vocabulary of Public Enemy's late-80s work. The song is therefore Pearl Jam's most explicit attempt to engage with hip-hop rhythmic priorities, and the result is unlike anything else in the band's catalog.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct political statements. The narrator names the demographic, names the privilege, and refuses to soften the indictment with personal mitigation. Vedder discussed the song's argument extensively during the Vitalogy tour of 1995 in stage introductions and in select interviews, framing the song as an attempt to make audible to white American audiences the racial weather they were inhabiting without noticing. The song does not offer redemption. It diagnoses.

Live, 'W.M.A.' has been a rare song. It appears in fewer than 200 shows in three decades of touring, partly because the rhythmic arrangement is difficult to land outside the studio environment and partly because the band has historically reserved the song for moments when its argument feels particularly necessary. The song is more often deployed as a tag during 'Daughter' than as a standalone performance, which lets the band fold the W.M.A. argument into the W.M.A.-adjacent argument of 'Daughter' (a song about another kind of demographic vulnerability).

byShow.pj-2011-11-03: On 3 November 2011 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'W.M.A.' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as the night's deepest pull into the Vs.-era material's political layer. The song (whose title is the band's compressed name for 'White Male American') had been written in 1993 in response to a specific incident at Pearl Jam's Seattle rehearsal space involving police treatment of bandmate Eddie's Black friend, and the song's argument has remained legible across the touring decades. The slot's pacing function, after the emotional weight of 'Daughter' had been discharged, was to maintain the show's mid-section weight while pushing the political argument back into the room. The Morumbi crowd's response sustained the kind of attentive engagement that the song's accusatory verse structure requires.
byShow.pj-2018-03-21: On 21 March 2018 at Maracanã, 'W.M.A.' arrived as the second half of the twenty-first slot's medley with 'Daughter'. The 1993 Vs.-era song's documentation of racial-disparate police treatment retained specific legibility in 2018 (the Black Lives Matter movement had now been operating for five years, and the Movement for Black Lives' policy framework had been published in 2016). The Brazilian audience's response sustained the song's accusatory weight.
byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome, 'W.M.A.' arrived in the show's fifth slot as the Vs.-era track on racial-disparate police treatment. The 2022 deployment in Amsterdam (a city with its own complex policing history around drug-tourism and immigration) carried specific contextual weight.

ole.text:
'Olé' is one of the few standalone single releases in the Pearl Jam catalog, distributed for free to members of the band's Ten Club fan organization in March 2011 ahead of the PJ20 Anniversary Tour. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was recorded in Henry Rollins's home studio in Los Angeles in early 2011 with the band on a quick session that did not produce a full album. 'Olé' was therefore a one-off release rather than a track from a larger record, which gives it a particular standing in the catalog.

The song's title and its central refrain reference the Spanish-language exclamation 'Olé,' which originated in flamenco performance traditions and which entered global stadium culture through bullfighting and football crowds. The song is, at the simplest level, a celebration song, written in 2011 when the band was preparing to celebrate its twentieth anniversary as a touring entity. The lyric is unusually optimistic for Vedder. The narrator is honoring a partner, honoring the persistence of a relationship across decades, honoring the kind of shared survival that becomes its own celebration.

The arrangement is one of the most pop-leaning things the band recorded in the 2010s. The chord progression is a clean four-bar pattern that does not deviate; the chorus opens into the wordless 'Olé' refrain that is designed to be carried by stadium audiences. Matt Cameron's drumming is a straight 4/4 with brushed accents. The song's accessibility is intentional. The band wanted a song that could function as a mid-show audience moment on the PJ20 tour, and 'Olé' was built for exactly that role.

Live, the song was a fixture of the 2011 PJ20 cycle and has appeared sporadically on subsequent tours. Its status as a free-download single rather than an album track gives it an unusual lifespan: it is well-known enough among fans that audiences sing the refrain, but is rarely heard on radio, and most casual Pearl Jam listeners have never heard it. This makes the song's live performance a kind of fan-club handshake: if you sing along, you announce yourself as a Ten Club member.

the fixer.text:
'The Fixer' is the third track on Backspacer (2009) and the album's lead single, released in August 2009 ahead of the September album release. The music is credited collectively to the band; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was the most commercially successful Pearl Jam single since 'Just Breathe' would land later in the same album cycle, and it reached number one on the Billboard Alternative Songs chart, the band's first chart-topper in that category since 'World Wide Suicide' in 2006.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most simple optimistic declarations. The narrator describes himself as someone who repairs what is broken, who restores what has been damaged, who restores what has gone missing. The song is, in deliberate contrast to almost every Pearl Jam track from the 2002 to 2006 period, a refusal of pessimism. Vedder discussed the song in a 2009 Rolling Stone interview around the Backspacer release as a song he had been wanting to write for years and had only been able to write after the Bush administration ended; the song's optimism is the optimism of someone who has been holding it back for half a decade.

The arrangement is the brightest thing on Backspacer. The verse is built on a major-key chord progression that climbs rather than descends; the chorus opens into a wider arrangement that includes glockenspiel and tambourine, instruments that almost never appear in the Pearl Jam catalog. The song is closer in spirit to The Who's 'Substitute' or to early 70s power-pop than to anything Pearl Jam had recorded before. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the song forward at a tempo that the band has only rarely sustained on a recording.

The song was produced by Brendan O'Brien, and his fingerprint is unusually visible on the recording. O'Brien has discussed in interviews from the 2009 Backspacer cycle that 'The Fixer' was the first song from the sessions to be finished, and that the band's enthusiasm for the recording set the tone for the rest of the album. The song therefore functions, structurally, as the album's emotional thesis: the entire Backspacer record is built around the optimistic posture that 'The Fixer' establishes.

down.text:
'Down' is one of two songs (with 'Yellow Ledbetter' the other) released as B-sides during the Riot Act period that became, retroactively, more important to the band's catalog than most of the album they were supporting. The song was recorded during the Riot Act sessions in 2002 and was issued in November 2002 as the B-side to the 'I Am Mine' single. It was eventually collected on Lost Dogs (2003), the rarities compilation. The music is credited to Mike McCready; the lyric is Vedder's.

The lyric is one of the most direct political tracks Pearl Jam wrote during the Bush administration, and one of the most temporally specific. The song addresses someone (the second person 'you' is the political figure being indicted) who is dragging the country down, who is taking the worst available path, who is making the moment worse than it had to be. Vedder confirmed in a 2003 interview during the Riot Act tour that the song was about the Bush administration's response to 9/11 and the rush to war in Iraq. The song was written after the studio sessions for 'Bu$hleaguer' (also on Riot Act) and was not included on the album because the band felt the political content of Riot Act was already at saturation.

The arrangement is one of McCready's most economical pieces of writing. The verse is built on a tight, almost punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. The song is structured for velocity rather than for argument, and the lyric's anger is therefore delivered through the music's pace rather than through extended rhetorical development. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is among the most aggressive of the Riot Act sessions.

Live, 'Down' has been a regular but not heavy presence in setlists since 2003. The song's specific political target makes it most useful during American electoral cycles or during periods when the political climate the song was written about feels current again. The band has historically reserved 'Down' for shows where the lyric will resonate, which is unusual for a B-side that the band could have allowed to fade from the live catalog.

byShow.pj-2011-11-03: On 3 November 2011 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Down' arrived in the show's thirteenth slot as a Lost Dogs deep cut that the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour rotated into circulation as part of the catalog-wide retrospective the tour was performing. The song (a 2003 Riot Act-era track originally released as a B-side and later collected on Lost Dogs in 2003) is a relatively rare live appearance, and the Morumbi placement reflected the tour's commitment to surfacing material from the 'Lost Dogs' compilation. The slot's pacing function was to maintain the show's mid-section forward motion while pulling the audience into a piece whose familiarity ran shallower than the surrounding material.

severed hand.text:
'Severed Hand' is the fourth track on Pearl Jam (2006), the self-titled album often called Avocado for its cover image. The music is Mike McCready's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most stylistically unusual things on the album, a sustained psychedelic burst that draws openly from late-60s rock vocabulary (the Doors and the Jefferson Airplane are the two most-cited reference points) and applies that vocabulary to a lyric about a transformative drug experience. Pearl Jam had not previously recorded a song this explicitly about psychedelics, and they have not recorded one since.

The lyric describes a vision the narrator receives during an altered state. The vision is not described in detail; the song is more interested in the emotional aftermath than in the specifics of the experience. The narrator emerges from the vision changed, with a clarity about something that the song refuses to name. Vedder discussed the song in a 2006 Spin interview during the Avocado promotional cycle as 'a song about realizing something' but declined to specify what was realized. This refusal to specify is consistent with how psychedelic literature has historically described peak experiences: the experience cannot be communicated in the language available to non-experiencers, so the song chooses not to try.

The arrangement is one of McCready's most ambitious solo features. The intro is built on a wah-wah guitar figure that explicitly references Hendrix's 'Voodoo Chile (Slight Return),' and the closing solo extends McCready's Hendrix vocabulary into territory the band rarely allows him to explore in studio recordings. The song's psychedelic arrangement is therefore not just thematic decoration; it is the music doing the same work the lyric is doing, attempting to render in sound what the lyric refuses to render in language.

The song was produced by Adam Kasper rather than by Brendan O'Brien. Avocado is the only Pearl Jam album of the 2000s that O'Brien did not produce, and Kasper's production is audibly different: the recording is rawer, the rhythm section is more present, and McCready's guitar is mixed louder than O'Brien typically allows. 'Severed Hand' is the song where Kasper's production approach is most visible, and the result is one of the most distinctive-sounding tracks in the post-2000 Pearl Jam catalog.

not for you.text:
'Not for You' is the third track on Vitalogy (1994) and one of the most direct anti-music-industry statements in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is credited to all five band members; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was the most public artifact of Pearl Jam's protracted feud with Ticketmaster, the ticketing monopoly that the band fought between 1994 and 1995 in a Justice Department antitrust complaint that ultimately failed but that defined the band's relationship to commercial infrastructure for the rest of the decade.

The lyric is, in the most direct reading, a message to people in their twenties about who their music belongs to and who is allowed to monetize it. The narrator addresses an unnamed older figure (a music executive, a venue owner, a corporate gatekeeper) and refuses to let that figure claim ownership over the music being made by the speaker's generation. Vedder discussed the song's argument extensively during the Vitalogy promotional cycle in 1994 and during the Ticketmaster-related congressional testimony the band gave in 1994. The song is a thesis statement for a position the band would defend in court for two years.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most muscular pieces of writing. The verse is built on a tight, mid-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a McCready solo. The song's structure is designed for sustained anger rather than for cathartic release; the music does not allow the listener relief, which is consistent with the lyric's refusal to let the addressee off the hook.

The Morumbi crowd's response sustained the political weight the song carries, which by 2011 the band had been carrying on every continent for seventeen years.

not for you.text_pt:
'Not for You' é a terceira faixa de Vitalogy (1994) e uma das declarações mais diretas anti-indústria-musical no catálogo do Pearl Jam. A música é creditada aos cinco membros da banda; a letra é de Vedder. A canção foi o artefato público mais importante da rixa prolongada do Pearl Jam com a Ticketmaster, o monopólio de venda de ingressos contra o qual a banda lutou entre 1994 e 1995 em uma denúncia antitruste do Departamento de Justiça que acabou falhando mas que definiu a relação da banda com a infraestrutura comercial pelo resto da década.

A letra é, na leitura mais direta, uma mensagem a pessoas na casa dos vinte sobre a quem a música delas pertence e a quem é permitido monetizá-la. O narrador se dirige a uma figura mais velha não nomeada (um executivo da indústria, um dono de casa de show, um porteiro corporativo) e se recusa a deixar essa figura reivindicar posse sobre a música feita pela geração do falante. Vedder discutiu o argumento da canção extensivamente durante o ciclo promocional de Vitalogy em 1994 e durante o testemunho ao congresso relacionado à Ticketmaster que a banda deu em 1994. A música é uma declaração de tese pra uma posição que a banda defenderia em juízo por dois anos.

O arranjo é uma das peças de escrita mais musculosas de Stone Gossard. O verso é construído sobre um riff denso, mid-tempo, que não varia; o refrão se abre em um movimento harmônico mais largo que se resolve pela ponte em um solo de McCready. A estrutura da canção é projetada pra raiva sustentada em vez de pra liberação catártica; a música não permite alívio ao ouvinte, o que é consistente com a recusa da letra em soltar o destinatário do gancho.

A colocação da canção no slot 12 seguiu o emprego típico de meio de show de material de Vitalogy da Pearl Jam Twenty Tour: profunda o bastante no show pra que a banda tivesse ganhado a atenção do público, estruturada o bastante pra dar ao show uma continuidade Vs.-Vitalogy sustentada. spin the black circle.text:
'Spin the Black Circle' is the second track on Vitalogy (1994) and one of the most musically aggressive things Pearl Jam has ever recorded. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is a love letter to vinyl records as a physical medium, written at exactly the moment when the music industry was completing its transition from vinyl to compact disc and when vinyl as a consumer format was at its lowest commercial ebb in fifty years. The song is therefore a declaration of attachment to a medium that the industry was actively trying to retire.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most economical pieces of writing. The narrator describes the physical ritual of putting a record on a turntable, the anticipation of the needle dropping, the sound of the run-in groove, the moment the music starts. The song does not editorialize; it documents the ritual and lets the listener observe how much the narrator loves what he is doing. The song's argument is implicit: this ritual is worth preserving, and the medium that allows it deserves to survive.

The arrangement is the punkest thing on Vitalogy. The verse is built on a thrash-tempo riff that almost never varies; the chorus releases the verse's tension through a controlled scream rather than through a melodic lift. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording is the most punishing of his Pearl Jam tenure (Vitalogy was his last album with the band; he was fired during the Vitalogy tour in 1994). McCready's solo at the song's center is short and aggressive.

The song won the Grammy for Best Hard Rock Performance at the 1996 ceremony. Vedder accepted the award in person, which is one of the few times he has attended a Grammy ceremony. His acceptance speech was brief and ironic: he held the award and noted that the band did not know what the award meant. The moment is one of the more public Pearl Jam-and-Grammy interactions in the catalog and is consistent with the band's general posture toward the awards infrastructure.

byShow.pj-2011-11-04: On 4 November 2011 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Spin the Black Circle' arrived in the show's twenty-ninth slot as the Vitalogy-era hardcore-adjacent track whose 1994 release had won the band a Grammy for Best Hard Rock Performance in 1996. The song's role in late-set sequences is specifically about velocity: the compressed under-three-minute structure and the verse's punk-tempo riff give the slot the kind of unmediated forward motion the show's pre-final-anthem energy curve demands. The Morumbi audience's response sustained the volume that the previous two covers had built.
byShow.pj-2015-11-11: On 11 November 2015 at Arena do Grêmio, 'Spin the Black Circle' arrived in the show's seventeenth slot, deploying the Vitalogy-era Grammy winner (Best Hard Rock Performance, 1996) for vinyl culture. The placement after 'Let the Records Play' created an unusual back-to-back vinyl-themed sequence, two songs about the materiality of music in a streaming-dominated era.
byShow.pj-2015-11-22: On 22 November 2015 at Maracanã, 'Spin the Black Circle' arrived in the show's twenty-ninth slot, deploying the Vitalogy-era Grammy winner for vinyl culture in a compressed under-three-minute burst.

state of love and trust.text:
'State of Love and Trust' is one of the songs Pearl Jam recorded for the Singles soundtrack (1992), the Cameron Crowe film about Seattle musicians and their romantic lives that featured several Pearl Jam members in cameo roles. The song was recorded during the band's earliest studio sessions in 1991 and 1992, alongside the Ten material, but was held off the album for the Singles project. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about disillusion. The narrator addresses someone (the second-person 'you' is deliberately ambiguous; it could be a partner, a parent, a politician, or the listener) who has broken trust in a way the speaker is still processing. The song is not an indictment; it is a description. The narrator is observing the wreckage of a relationship of trust without yet knowing what to do about the wreckage. This kind of observational lyric is rare in Vedder's early catalog and is part of why the song has aged better than some of the more declarative material from the Ten era.

The arrangement is one of the most economical Pearl Jam recordings from the early 90s. The verse is built on a single chord with passing tones; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge. The song is under four minutes and has only one McCready solo, which is uncharacteristically short for the period. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming is restrained throughout, which is consistent with the lyric's posture of observation rather than confrontation.

The Singles soundtrack was a commercial success that surprised the bands involved. The album reached the Billboard top ten in 1992 and brought Pearl Jam a first wave of mainstream attention separate from their own debut. 'State of Love and Trust' became a regular live song almost immediately after the soundtrack's release and has remained in setlists since.

byShow.pj-2011-11-04: On 4 November 2011 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'State of Love and Trust' arrived in the show's twenty-first slot as the Singles soundtrack track whose 1992 release had positioned it as one of the band's earliest non-album hits. The song's high-velocity verse riff and Cameron's straight drumming gave the slot the kind of sustained-attack pattern the show's late-middle section demanded. The Morumbi audience's energy through this slot was sustained at the kind of full volume that the song's compact under-four-minute structure invites.

habit.text:
'Habit' is the seventh track on No Code (1996), the album where Pearl Jam concluded its retreat from mainstream visibility, and one of the most directly addressed songs in the catalog. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is a second-person address to an unnamed friend (widely understood, though Vedder has refused to confirm, to be Mike McCready) who has been struggling with substance dependency. The song is not a song of judgment; it is a song of worry and of the narrator's frustration with his own inability to help.

Mike McCready had publicly entered treatment for cocaine and alcohol addiction in 1994, between the Vs. and Vitalogy tours, and his recovery was one of the structuring stories of the No Code period. The band was protective of McCready's recovery in interviews and refused to discuss the specifics. 'Habit' is therefore best understood as an artifact of that protection: a song that names the situation in detail without naming the person, and that lets the situation be public knowledge without forcing the friend to become public himself.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most aggressive No Code pieces. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that pushes against Jack Irons's drumming (Irons was the band's drummer during No Code, after Abbruzzese was fired and before Matt Cameron joined). The chorus releases the verse's tension into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a short, controlled solo. The song is structured for forward momentum rather than for cathartic release, which suits the lyric's refusal to deliver advice the song knows the addressee cannot use.

No Code as a whole was an album that confused the band's audience in 1996. After Vitalogy's commercial success, fans expected another sustained rock record, and got instead an album of stylistic experiments that included 'Sometimes' (a folk meditation), 'Who You Are' (an Eastern-tinged single), and 'I'm Open' (spoken word). 'Habit' was the most conventional rock song on the record and was therefore one of the few No Code tracks that received significant rock-radio play.

The Rio crowd's response sustained the volume the previous slot had built.

off he goes.text:
'Off He Goes' is the sixth track on No Code (1996) and one of the gentlest things Pearl Jam has ever recorded. The music is Vedder's (a rare solo Vedder music credit on a Pearl Jam album); the lyric is also Vedder's. The song is a third-person portrait of a friend whose pattern of behavior the narrator has learned to predict. The friend appears, makes himself the center of attention, and then disappears for months at a time, leaving the people around him to fill in the absence.

Vedder has discussed the song in interviews from the No Code promotional cycle of 1996 and 1997. He has framed the song as self-examination rather than as criticism: the friend in the lyric is, by Vedder's own occasional admission in interviews, a version of Vedder himself, observed from outside. The third-person framing is a literary device that lets the narrator describe his own behavior with the kind of clarity that first-person address would not allow. This technique is rare in the Pearl Jam catalog and is part of why 'Off He Goes' has remained a critical favorite even though it was never a single.

The arrangement is the most country-inflected thing on No Code. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure; the band enters under the second verse but stays restrained. Stone Gossard plays a pedal steel-style line under the chorus that gives the song a feel closer to a Gram Parsons recording than to anything Pearl Jam had done before. Jack Irons's drumming on the recording is brushed rather than sticked, which is the only time he played the song that way on a recording.

last exit.text:
'Last Exit' is the opening track of Vitalogy (1994), the first thing the listener encounters on a record that is, structurally, the band's most adventurous album of the 1990s. The music is credited to Vedder and Stone Gossard; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is short, fast, and structurally compressed: under three minutes, with a punk-tempo verse and a chorus that does not pretend to lift in any conventional sense. The choice to open Vitalogy with this song was deliberate. After the slow-build opening of Ten ('Once') and the medium-tempo opening of Vs. ('Go'), 'Last Exit' was the band announcing that Vitalogy would be a faster, harder, less melodic record than its predecessors.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most existential pieces of writing. The narrator is contemplating the moment of death and the kind of clarity that some people report arriving in the final seconds of a life. The song does not editorialize about whether this clarity is real or illusory; it documents the narrator's interest in the question and lets the listener observe the curiosity. This is Vedder writing in a register he rarely visited later in his career, where the question itself is the song's argument and the song refuses to provide an answer.

The arrangement is the most punk-inflected thing on Vitalogy's first half. The verse is built on a tight, palm-muted riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording (this is one of his last Pearl Jam tracks; he was fired during the Vitalogy tour in 1994) is among the most aggressive on the album. McCready's solo at the song's center is a controlled six-bar burst rather than an extended melodic statement.

Vitalogy itself was an album the band recorded under unusual constraints. The sessions ran from late 1993 through April 1994, in studios in Atlanta, New Orleans, and Seattle, and the band was famously fighting with each other and with Epic Records throughout. Vedder was insisting on releasing the album on vinyl two weeks before the CD release, which he eventually won. 'Last Exit' was the song the band recorded most quickly during the Vitalogy sessions, by Vedder's own description in PJ20: he wrote the lyric in one sitting and the band tracked the song in fewer than three takes.

The slot placement was unusual: 'Last Exit' is more often found early in opening sequences as a propulsive opener itself, and the band's choice to deploy it at slot 2 after a slow opener reflected the Rio show's structurally distinctive running order. The compressed under-three-minute structure suited the slot's pacing function: a sharp acceleration after the room had settled into the venue's open-air acoustics.

blood.text:
'Blood' is the eleventh track on Vs. (1993) and one of the most direct songs in the Pearl Jam catalog about being a public figure under press scrutiny. The music is credited to all five members of Pearl Jam; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is the most concentrated burst of the Vs. album's anti-fame argument. Where 'Animal' addresses the music industry collectively and 'Glorified G' addresses the gun-collecting friend, 'Blood' addresses the press itself, the cameras, the magazine covers, the late-night radio voices that had been treating Vedder's interior life as raw material since Ten broke.

The lyric works as an indictment delivered at velocity. The narrator describes himself as material being consumed: a body whose blood the press wants in print, a face whose suffering is more saleable than its joy, a person whose privacy has been determined to be a commodity rather than a right. Vedder's specific reference is, as he confirmed in a 1993 Rolling Stone interview, the magazine cover that put him on the front page of Time in October 1993 with the headline 'All The Rage' and the kicker 'Angry Young Rockers Like Pearl Jam Give Voice to the Passions and Fears of a Generation.' Vedder did not want to be on the cover, did not give Time an interview, and was furious that the magazine ran the cover anyway. 'Blood' is one of the songs that anger produced.

The arrangement is the most formally aggressive thing on Vs. The verse is built on a single chord that is hammered at thrash-tempo; the chorus releases the verse's tension into a sustained scream rather than a melodic lift. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording is the most brutal of his Pearl Jam tenure. McCready's solo at the song's center is short, fast, and harmonically destabilizing, which suits the lyric's posture of refusing to allow the listener any relief from what is being said.

The song was recorded in fewer than five takes during the Vs. sessions at The Site in early 1993, and the band has discussed in PJ20 that 'Blood' was the song they tracked when they wanted to externalize whatever frustration the day had built up. The recording captures the kind of band performance that depends on simultaneous physical exhaustion: nobody is playing carefully because nobody has the spare attention required to play carefully.

The song's specific lyrical engagement with the press's treatment of Vedder during the Vs. period (the 'Stone' figure in the song is widely read as representing a journalist or critic) had remained legible in the band's live readings since 1993. The Rio crowd's response sustained the kind of full-volume engagement the Sambadrome's open-air structure encouraged, and the slot continued the night's high-velocity opening sequence.

nothingman.text:
'Nothingman' is the fifth track on Vitalogy (1994) and the most accessible ballad on an album that otherwise makes accessibility difficult. The music is Jeff Ament's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is the second-most commercially successful single from Vitalogy (after 'Better Man') and the song from that album that has remained most reliably in setlists. The lyric is a third-person portrait of a man who has lost a partner through indifference, accumulated regret over the loss, and arrived at a permanent state of having missed his life.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most patient pieces of writing. The narrator does not editorialize about the figure described; the song documents the figure's interior reasoning and lets the listener observe both the regret and the way the regret has hardened into a posture rather than dissolving over time. Vedder has discussed the song in interviews from the Vitalogy promotional cycle (a 1994 Spin conversation is the most cited) as a song about the kind of inattention that destroys a partnership without anyone in the partnership noticing it has happened. The song's argument is implicit: the worst kind of loss is the loss you did not see coming because you were not paying attention.

The arrangement is one of Jeff Ament's most economical pieces of writing. The verse is built on a slow-rolling bass line that resolves through a chorus that opens into a wider chord. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic, more in the Mark Knopfler vein than the Hendrix one. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming is brushed rather than sticked, which is unusual for him and which suits the song's emotional architecture. The arrangement is therefore a deliberate inversion of the Pearl Jam formula: the rhythm section is foregrounded, the guitars are restrained, and the song does not allow itself to escalate into the kind of catharsis that 'Black' or 'Release' eventually deliver.

The song was the second single from Vitalogy, released in October 1995, and reached the top thirty on the Billboard Modern Rock chart. Its commercial reception was warmer than the album's lead single ('Spin the Black Circle') because 'Nothingman' was structurally accessible in a way that the band's mid-90s music had largely refused to be. The song's chart success therefore became, by the band's own account, a kind of accidental hit: the band had not designed the song for radio, but radio took it anyway.

The song's slow build into the closing minute's full release gave the slot the kind of patient melodic climb that the open-air venue's acoustics could carry. Vedder's vocal performance on this recording sat forward in the mix in a way that the studio version mirrors, and the bootleg captures the audience's sustained mid-show quiet that the song's verse demands. The slot's pacing function was to begin the show's first deliberate slowing of tempo.

immortality.text:
'Immortality' is the eleventh track on Vitalogy (1994), the album's penultimate song before the deliberately unlistenable hidden track 'Stupid Mop.' The music is Vedder's; the lyric is also Vedder's. The song was recorded during the Vitalogy sessions in early 1994 and was completed in the period immediately following the death of Kurt Cobain on April 5, 1994. This timing is part of why 'Immortality' became, against the band's own statements, one of the most-discussed songs of the Pearl Jam catalog: many fans and critics read the song as an elegy for Cobain.

Vedder has consistently denied this reading. He has said in multiple interviews (most directly in PJ20 and in a 1995 Rolling Stone conversation) that 'Immortality' was already written when Cobain died, that the song is not about any specific person, and that the resemblance between the song's preoccupations and Cobain's situation is the result of the two men working in the same culture under the same pressures rather than the result of one writing about the other. The denial is consistent across decades; the band has not changed its position on the question since 1995.

The lyric is, in Vedder's framing, about the cumulative weight of fame and the way that weight pushes some musicians into self-destruction without their consent. The song is therefore not about Cobain specifically but about the structural conditions that produced Cobain alongside many other casualties. This is a more interesting argument than the elegy reading, because the elegy reading treats Cobain as exceptional while Vedder's framing treats him as representative.

The arrangement is one of the most patient on Vitalogy. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into McCready's solo. The song is the longest on Vitalogy after 'Tremor Christ' and is structured for cumulative emotional weight rather than for cathartic release. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming is restrained throughout. McCready's solo at the song's climax is one of his most melodic on the album, closer to a Carlos Santana feel than to the Hendrix vocabulary he typically deploys.

byShow.pj-2011-11-06: On 6 November 2011 at Praça da Apoteose, 'Immortality' arrived in the show's twelfth slot as one of the most structurally ambitious Vitalogy tracks the band could deliver in mid-set position. The song's slow build into the closing minute's full release gave the slot the kind of patient emotional climb that the show's late-mid-set sequence demanded. The lyric (often read as a post-Cobain meditation on the costs of generational fame, though Vedder has repeatedly declined to confirm that reading) sat over the performance the way it has sat over every late-Vs.-era live reading of the song. The Rio placement reflected the tour's commitment to deploying Vitalogy material in structurally weighted positions.

indifference.text:
'Indifference' is the twelfth and final track on Vs. (1993), the album-closer that the band chose to follow 'Leash' with as a deliberate tonal contrast. The music is credited to all five members; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most direct pieces of writing in the early Pearl Jam catalog about the question of political engagement, and one of the few songs in the catalog where the lyric refuses to resolve its central question.

The lyric repeats a question across its verses: how much difference does it make. The narrator describes a series of acts of resistance (small refusals, small protests, small attempts to be heard) and asks whether any of them have changed anything. The song does not answer the question. It documents the asking and lets the listener observe both the resistance and the doubt about whether the resistance is doing what it is supposed to do. This is Vedder at his most philosophically honest: the song is not pretending that political engagement is obviously worth the cost, and it is not pretending that disengagement is acceptable either.

The arrangement is one of the most patient closes the band has ever recorded. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that does not vary; the chorus does not lift in any conventional sense. The song is structurally a meditation rather than a song. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming is the slowest on Vs., which suits the lyric's deliberation. McCready's guitar work on the recording is restrained throughout; he does not solo, which is unusual for a Pearl Jam album closer. The song fades out on a sustained chord rather than resolving, which is the song's argument made musical: there is no resolution to the question.

The song was never released as a single but has been one of the band's most reliable encore-closers across three decades. The song works best as the last song of a show, where its question can hang in the air after the audience has filed out, rather than being resolved by another song that follows. The band's preference for 'Indifference' as a closer has been consistent across tours; it is one of the songs that signals a show is now over in a permanent rather than temporary sense.

The song's lyric (a refusal to be ground down by the day's accumulated forces) sat over the encore's late position the way it has across the song's two-decade live history. The Rio placement reflected the band's reading of the night's emotional weight: the show had earned a slow resolution rather than a high-velocity discharge.

in hiding.text:
'In Hiding' is the eighth track on Yield (1998) and one of the most direct songs Vedder wrote about an episode of personal isolation he experienced during the late 1990s. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written after Vedder spent several days alone in his Seattle home, deliberately avoiding contact with the outside world following a period of cumulative emotional exhaustion that the band's celebrity had imposed. He has discussed this episode in multiple interviews, most prominently in PJ20 and in a 1998 Spin conversation, framing it as a deliberate experiment in voluntary disappearance rather than as a depressive episode.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most patient pieces of writing. The narrator describes the disappearance, the days of silence, the gradual accumulation of clarity that came from refusing the demands of social presence. The song does not editorialize about whether this withdrawal was healthy or unhealthy; it documents the experience and lets the listener observe both the relief and the eventual return. This is a Vedder preoccupation that recurs across the catalog (Off He Goes works similar territory) and that is one of the durable subjects of his late-90s writing.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most architectural pieces. The verse is built on a tight, mid-tempo riff that resolves through a chorus that opens into a wider harmonic move. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic, more in the Pete Townshend vein than the Hendrix one. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording (Yield was Cameron's first album with the band, after Jack Irons left during the No Code tour) is among the most controlled of his Pearl Jam tenure.

The song's narrator (deliberately retreating from a world that has become unmanageable, then re-emerging with a sense of recovered agency) sat well in slot 12's pacing function. The Vila Capanema bootleg captures the audience's sustained engagement through the closing build.

The bootleg captures the audience's sustained engagement through the closing build.

red mosquito.text:
'Red Mosquito' is the eighth track on No Code (1996), one of the more stylistically unusual songs on an album of stylistic experiments. The music is credited to Stone Gossard, Mike McCready, and Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written after Vedder spent several days bedridden with a serious illness in San Francisco in late 1995, during which he was forced to cancel a Neil Young concert appearance the band was supposed to support. The red mosquito of the title is the metaphor he assigned to the illness, a tiny aggressive thing that had grounded him.

The lyric is unusually surreal for Vedder. The narrator describes the experience of being sick from outside himself, observing his own body's collapse with the same detachment he typically reserves for third-person character songs. The image of the mosquito as a feverish hallucination is one of the more vivid pieces of figurative writing in the No Code catalog. Vedder discussed the song in a 1996 promotional interview around No Code's release as a song that came out fully formed in a single afternoon, after the illness had passed.

The arrangement is the most blues-inflected thing on No Code. The verse is built on a slide-guitar figure that Stone Gossard plays with an open-tuning approach he rarely deployed on Pearl Jam recordings. McCready's solo at the song's center is one of his most extended on the album. Jack Irons's drumming on the recording (his only full studio album with the band before anxiety would force his departure) provides the song with a loose, almost swampy feel that no other Pearl Jam track had achieved before.

byShow.pj-2011-11-09: On 9 November 2011 at Vila Capanema, 'Red Mosquito' arrived in the show's sixteenth slot as one of the No Code-era tracks the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour rotated into circulation when the show's mid-set sequence called for sustained groove-anchored rock. The song (originally written about Vedder's 1995 illness in San Francisco that forced Neil Young to take over vocals during a Mountain View show) carried its specific autobiographical layer into the Curitiba performance. The slot's pacing function was to maintain the show's mid-section tempo with a No Code deep-cut that the smaller venue could carry.

inside job.text:
'Inside Job' is the thirteenth and final track on Pearl Jam (2006), the self-titled Avocado album. The music is Mike McCready's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of only a handful in the band's catalog that McCready wrote primarily on his own; he has discussed in interviews from the 2006 promotional cycle that he wrote the music during a period of personal crisis and that the song represented his own statement about the work of recovery. McCready has been publicly open about his addiction recovery since the late 1990s, and 'Inside Job' is the song most directly tied to that recovery in his catalog.

The lyric, by Vedder, takes McCready's musical statement and makes it more universal. The narrator describes the work of repairing a damaged self as a job that no one else can do for the speaker; the recovery has to be done from the inside. The song is therefore a collaboration in the deepest sense: McCready provided the music as a personal statement, Vedder translated that statement into something that listeners outside McCready's specific situation could use. This kind of layered authorship is rare in the Pearl Jam catalog and is part of why 'Inside Job' has remained a critical favorite even though it was never a single.

The arrangement is one of the most expansive on Avocado. The song runs over seven minutes, which is the longest track on the album, and the closing instrumental section is McCready's most ambitious solo in the post-2000 Pearl Jam catalog. The arrangement builds slowly through the first four minutes before releasing into a sustained instrumental climb that does not resolve until the song fades out. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the build forward without breaking, which is one of his structural strengths as a Pearl Jam drummer.

comatose.text:
'Comatose' is the third track on Pearl Jam (2006). The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the shortest things on the Avocado album (under two and a half minutes) and one of the most aggressive. The verse is built on a thrash-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus releases the verse's tension into a sustained scream rather than a melodic lift. The song is therefore the album's most direct engagement with the punk-tempo vocabulary that the band had begun reincorporating after Riot Act.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about emotional shutdown. The narrator describes a state of internal numbness, the kind of dissociation that arrives during prolonged crisis when the system protects itself by going dark. The song does not editorialize about whether this state is healthy or unhealthy; it documents the experience and lets the music's velocity carry the emotional content. Vedder has discussed the song in 2006 promotional interviews as a state he had visited himself during the Riot Act period and that he was writing about retrospectively.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most economical pieces. The song is structured for sustained anger rather than for cathartic release; the music does not allow the listener relief, which suits the lyric's posture. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is among the most aggressive on Avocado. McCready's solo is short, fast, and harmonically destabilizing.

The ninety-second hardcore-adjacent track gave the encore a high-velocity opening that contrasted structurally with the slow material that had closed the main set. Cameron's drumming on the studio recording is some of the fastest the band has tracked, and the live arrangement preserved that velocity. The Morumbi placement, between 'Alive' and 'Black,' suggested the band wanted to use the encore's energy curve to reset the room before the longer-form material that 'Black' would deliver.

come back.text:
'Come Back' is the eleventh track on Pearl Jam (2006), one of the gentlest things on an otherwise aggressive album. The music is Mike McCready's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is a love letter to a partner who has left, written from the position of someone who has accepted the loss but cannot fully release the hope that the loss will reverse itself. The lyric is one of Vedder's most patient pieces of writing about romantic regret.

The arrangement is one of the most pared-down on Avocado. The verse is built on a slow, finger-picked acoustic guitar figure; the band enters under the second verse but stays restrained. McCready plays a single guitar layer that floats under the chorus rather than soloing. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed rather than sticked. The arrangement honors the lyric's intimacy by refusing to scale up to the kind of release that the album's other slow songs eventually deliver.

McCready has said in interviews from the Avocado promotional cycle that the music was the first thing he wrote for the album and that the song's gentleness is what set the tone for how the band approached the rest of the recording. The song was therefore a structural anchor for the album's emotional architecture, even though it appears late in the running order. The position-eleven slot suggests the band wanted listeners to encounter the song after they had absorbed the album's harder material; the gentleness lands harder when it follows the velocity of 'Severed Hand,' 'World Wide Suicide,' and 'Comatose.'

The Morumbi placement maintained the back-to-back slow sequence that 'Just Breathe' had begun, deepening the show's emotional weight before the encore energy began to build. The bootleg captures Vedder's most exposed vocal passage of the night.

of the earth.text:
'Of the Earth' is one of the few standalone live recordings in the Pearl Jam catalog to be released as an official single. The performance was recorded at the Forum in Los Angeles on October 6, 2009, during the Backspacer tour, and was issued as a free digital download for Ten Club fan-club members in late 2010. Stone Gossard wrote the music; Vedder wrote the lyric. The song was therefore not a studio composition prepared in advance for the audience; it was a song the band debuted live and then released without ever recording in a studio environment, which is a relatively rare publication path in the Pearl Jam catalog.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct ecological statements. The narrator describes humanity's belonging to the earth as a fact rather than as a metaphor, and the song's argument is that recognizing this fact requires a fundamental change in how the listener understands their place in the world. The song is therefore a companion piece to 'Do the Evolution,' which made the same argument from the inverse direction (showing what happens when humanity refuses to recognize its earthly belonging). Vedder discussed the song in 2011 promotional interviews around the PJ20 anniversary cycle as a song he had been wanting to write since the early 2000s and that finally arrived during the Backspacer-tour soundchecks.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most expansive pieces of writing for a live performance. The verse is built on a sustained chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a wider harmonic move. McCready's solo at the song's center is among his more melodic, more in the David Gilmour vein than the Hendrix one. Matt Cameron's drumming in the recorded version is restrained throughout, which is unusual for a Pearl Jam live recording.

byShow.pj-2011-11-06: On 6 November 2011 at Praça da Apoteose, 'Of the Earth' arrived in the show's twenty-second slot as one of the rarest songs the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour deployed: an unreleased track that has, across the band's touring history, been performed in fewer than a dozen shows total. The song (written during the late 2000s and never officially released on a studio album) was one of the deepest pulls the band could make, and the Rio placement reflected the tour's commitment to surfacing material that would not otherwise reach audiences. The bootleg from this night is one of the most-circulated documents of the song's brief live history.

arms aloft.text:
'Arms Aloft' is a Joe Strummer and the Mescaleros song from Streetcore (2003), the posthumous Joe Strummer album released after Strummer's death in December 2002. Pearl Jam began performing the song as a tribute to Strummer during the 2011 PJ20 anniversary cycle, twenty years after Pearl Jam had toured with The Clash adjacent to their early career and decades after Strummer had become one of Vedder's primary songwriting models. The Pearl Jam reading of the song honors Strummer by playing the song straight rather than reinterpreting it, which is the band's preferred approach to covering material by artists they consider foundational.

Vedder's relationship to Joe Strummer was direct rather than mediated. The two met during the 2002 Vote for Change preparations (Strummer would not live to see the actual tour), and Vedder spoke at the 2003 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction of The Clash with deep personal affection. Strummer's death in December 2002 was one of the personal losses that shaped the Riot Act period for Vedder, alongside the death of Layne Staley earlier that year. 'Save You' on Riot Act addresses Staley; the band's later cover of 'Arms Aloft' addresses Strummer.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Streetcore version's structure but adds a fuller rhythm section than the original. Jeff Ament's bass line is more active than the Mescaleros recording, and Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward. McCready's guitar tone is gritter than the Mescaleros version, which gives the cover a feel closer to early Clash than to late-period Strummer.

byShow.pj-2011-11-09: On 9 November 2011 at Vila Capanema, 'Arms Aloft' arrived in the show's second slot as the Joe Strummer cover the band had been folding into Pearl Jam Twenty Tour setlists as one of the tour's structural tributes. The 2003 Streetcore-era original (recorded by Strummer with The Mescaleros and released posthumously after Strummer's death in December 2002) gave the slot the kind of communal-anthem function that the song's chorus invites. Vedder's friendship with Strummer (which was documented in a 1990s interview where Strummer explicitly endorsed Pearl Jam as one of the few bands carrying the Clash-era political vocabulary forward) sat under the Curitiba performance, and the bootleg captures the audience's vocal participation through the title-line chorus.

dissident.text:
'Dissident' is the fifth track on Vs. (1993). The music is credited to Stone Gossard, Mike McCready, and Jeff Ament; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most narrative-driven pieces of writing in the early Pearl Jam catalog. The lyric tells a story: a woman shelters a political dissident on the run from authorities, falls into the kind of fear that prolonged sheltering produces, and eventually gives him up to the people pursuing him. The song does not name the country, the political situation, or the dissident's specific cause. The story is presented as a parable.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most morally honest pieces of writing. The narrator does not condemn the woman who eventually betrays the dissident. The song presents her decision as the kind of choice that becomes inevitable when fear and exhaustion accumulate beyond a person's capacity to hold the moral weight of resistance. This is a Vedder preoccupation that recurs across the catalog: he writes characters who fail morally and refuses to editorialize about the failures, leaving the audience to do the moral work the song deliberately declines to do.

The arrangement is one of the most architectural pieces on Vs. The verse is built on a tight, mid-tempo riff that resolves through a chorus that opens into a wider harmonic move. McCready's solo at the song's center is melodically expansive, more in the U2-via-Bono vein than in the band's typical Hendrix vocabulary. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording is among the most controlled of his Pearl Jam tenure, which suits the song's narrative patience.

byShow.pj-2011-11-09: On 9 November 2011 at Vila Capanema, 'Dissident' arrived in the show's ninth slot as one of the Vs.-era tracks the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour rotated into circulation. The song (Vedder's lyric about a woman shielding a political dissident at personal cost) carried its layered political weight into the Curitiba performance. The compressed under-four-minute structure suited the slot's pacing function: a propulsive Vs.-era piece that maintained the show's mid-set tempo after the audience-led 'Given to Fly' extension had built emotional commitment.

breath.text:
'Breath' is a Pearl Jam song from the Singles soundtrack (1992), released alongside 'State of Love and Trust' on the Cameron Crowe film about Seattle musicians. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was recorded during the band's earliest studio sessions in 1991, alongside the Ten material, but was held off the album for the Singles project. The song is therefore a contemporary of the entire Ten record and one of the rare Pearl Jam recordings from that period that did not make the cut for the band's debut.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct early pieces of writing about romantic devotion. The narrator addresses a partner with the kind of urgency that the early Pearl Jam catalog tended to reserve for grief and political anger; the song is therefore a small departure from the prevailing emotional tone of the Ten era. Vedder has not discussed the song's specific subject in interviews, which is consistent with how he treats the most clearly autobiographical lyrics in the catalog. The song's address is direct and the song's identity of addressee is held back.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most propulsive early pieces. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that climbs through the chorus into a wider harmonic move. McCready's solo at the song's center is brief and aggressive. The song's tempo and density make it closer to the harder Vs. material than to most of Ten, which is part of why it has been suggested that the song was held off the album for tonal reasons rather than for quality reasons.

byShow.pj-2011-11-09: On 9 November 2011 at Vila Capanema, 'Breath' arrived in the show's twenty-third slot as one of the Singles soundtrack tracks the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour rotated into circulation. The song (originally recorded for the 1992 Singles soundtrack alongside 'State of Love and Trust') carried its early-1990s Seattle-scene context into the Curitiba performance. The slot's pacing function was to maintain the show's late-set forward motion through a song whose live performance count was relatively low.

supersonic.text:
'Supersonic' is the eighth track on Backspacer (2009), a sub-three-minute punk-tempo burst that is one of the shortest things on the album and one of the fastest. The music is credited to Stone Gossard, Vedder, and producer Brendan O'Brien (a rare three-way co-credit that marks O'Brien's most explicit songwriting contribution to the Pearl Jam catalog). The lyric is Vedder's. The song was written in the Backspacer sessions in late 2008 and early 2009 during the same productive burst that produced 'Got Some' and 'The Fixer.'

The lyric is one of Vedder's most exuberant pieces of writing. The narrator describes a state of accelerated energy, the kind of forward momentum that arrives when the right combination of music, motion, and momentary clarity allows a person to feel fast in a way that they did not previously believe themselves capable of. The song does not editorialize about whether this state is sustainable; it documents the experience and lets the music's velocity carry the lyric.

The arrangement is the most unambiguously power-pop piece on Backspacer. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. The song is structured for sustained velocity rather than for cathartic release. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging. McCready's solo is six bars of melodic acceleration. Brendan O'Brien's contribution as co-writer is most audible in the song's structural compression: the song reaches its argument quickly and refuses to extend itself past necessity.

byShow.pj-2011-11-09: On 9 November 2011 at Vila Capanema, 'Supersonic' arrived in the show's twenty-fourth slot as one of the Backspacer-era propulsive tracks the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour deployed when the show's late-set energy curve called for renewed sustained forward motion. The compressed under-three-minute structure suited the slot's pacing function: a high-velocity reset before 'Black' delivered the show's primary emotional climax in slot 25.

footsteps.text:
'Footsteps' is the third and final installment of what Vedder later named the 'Mamasan' trilogy (with 'Alive' and 'Once'), and the only one of the three not included on Ten (1991). The song was recorded during the same 1991 sessions that produced the album but was held off the record and eventually released as the B-side to the 'Jeremy' single in 1992. It was eventually collected on Lost Dogs (2003), the rarities compilation. The music is Stone Gossard's (the song shares its harmonic DNA with 'Black,' both built on the same chord progression Stone had drafted as 'E Ballad'); the lyric is Vedder's.

The lyric completes the trilogy's narrative. Where 'Alive' depicts the moment of revelation (the narrator learning his stepfather is not his biological parent) and 'Once' depicts the violent transformation that revelation produces (the narrator becoming a serial killer), 'Footsteps' is the closing chapter: the same narrator, now captured and imprisoned on death row, addressing his mother one last time before his execution. The song is therefore a final letter from the trilogy's protagonist, and it documents the moment when the protagonist accepts his fate without forgiving the people whose actions produced him.

The arrangement is the most stripped of the three trilogy songs. The recording is acoustic and single-take, with Vedder accompanying himself on harmonica and minimal additional instrumentation. The choice to record 'Footsteps' acoustically while 'Alive' and 'Once' received full electric treatments is part of the trilogy's argument: the closing chapter is a confession, and confessions are made at low volume rather than with full bands behind them. Vedder has discussed this choice in PJ20 as a deliberate sequencing decision the band made early in the Ten sessions.

byShow.pj-2011-11-09: On 9 November 2011 at Vila Capanema, 'Footsteps' arrived in the show's thirtieth slot as the third installment of the Mamasan trilogy ('Alive' and 'Once' would close the trilogy structurally in slots 32 and 31 respectively). The song's specific narrative (the trilogy's closing first-person account of the serial killer narrator from a prison cell) is rarely performed live, and the Curitiba placement reflected the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour's commitment to surfacing the trilogy's full arc when possible. The bootleg captures one of the rarer 'Footsteps' live performances of the band's touring catalog.
byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Footsteps' arrived in the show's twentieth slot as the Mamasan trilogy's closing installment, the rare live appearance of the song originally written by Stone Gossard after Andrew Wood's 1990 death. The post-Paris night amplified the song's themes of violence and consequence in the prison-cell narrative the lyric documents.
byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome, 'Footsteps' arrived in the show's third slot as the Mamasan trilogy's closing installment. The rare deployment in the third slot (rather than late-encore as at Vila Capanema 2011) made the song an unusually early appearance for a track that the band typically reserves for emotional anchor positions.

leaving here.text:
'Leaving Here' is a Holland-Dozier-Holland song originally recorded by Eddie Holland in 1963 for Motown. The Who covered the song in 1965 during their early R&B-cover period (the recording was eventually released on the Odds and Sods compilation in 1974). Pearl Jam recorded their cover during the early 2000s and released it on the multi-artist tribute compilation Free the West Memphis 3 (2000), then collected it on Lost Dogs (2003). The cover is therefore part of a chain of covers: Pearl Jam covering The Who covering Eddie Holland.

The lyric is one of the more pointed pieces of early-60s Motown writing on the subject of male behavior. The narrator describes the women of the city collectively deciding to leave the men who have been mistreating them, framing the departure as a structural and unstoppable event rather than as a series of individual decisions. The song is therefore proto-feminist in a way that few 1963 popular songs were, and the choice to cover it during the early 2000s was a deliberate political gesture by the band.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Holland recording's structure but tilts the texture toward The Who's 1965 reading. McCready's guitar tone is gritter than the Motown original, and Matt Cameron's drumming has the Keith Moon-influenced controlled chaos that the Who recording established. The song is short (under three minutes) and structured for sustained velocity rather than for the soul groove the Motown original deployed.

The song's role in Pearl Jam's catalog (it appears on Lost Dogs, having been originally recorded for the 1996 Home Alive: The Art of Self Defense compilation) gave the slot a deep-cut historical layer. The Vila Capanema placement reflected the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour's commitment to surfacing rare covers in late-set positions.

setting forth.text:
'Setting Forth' is the third track on Eddie Vedder's solo soundtrack album for Sean Penn's 2007 film Into the Wild, the adaptation of Jon Krakauer's 1996 nonfiction book about Chris McCandless, the young man who walked into the Alaskan wilderness in 1992 and died there. Vedder wrote the song specifically for the film at Penn's invitation, and the entire soundtrack album functions as Vedder's first proper solo statement, recorded primarily by Vedder alone with minimal collaboration.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about departure. The narrator describes the act of leaving the ordinary world and beginning a journey whose destination is not yet known, which is the central narrative beat of the McCandless story. Vedder has discussed the song in promotional interviews from the 2007 release cycle as a song that came from his own decade-long preoccupation with the McCandless story; he had read Krakauer's book during the late 1990s and had been thinking about the questions it raised since.

The arrangement is one of Vedder's simplest. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure played at high tempo; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge. There is no solo. The song's brevity (under two minutes) and structural compression are deliberate: the song is meant to be the opening of a journey rather than the journey itself, and Vedder honored that structural position by refusing to extend the song past necessity.

The Into the Wild soundtrack received a Golden Globe nomination for Best Original Song (for 'Guaranteed,' the album's other Vedder-written track that received an awards push) and was widely treated as the most significant solo work Vedder had produced. 'Setting Forth' became one of the songs Vedder reliably plays at Pearl Jam shows during the encore acoustic moments, and his performances of it have become part of the canonical Pearl Jam encore vocabulary.

The song's role on a Pearl Jam set is unusual: it is one of the few Vedder-solo tracks the full band performs together, and the Morumbi placement reflected the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour's specific commitment to incorporating Vedder's solo work into the band's retrospective. The bootleg captures the closing wordless build, which the Brazilian audience carried at sustained volume.

The Curitiba placement followed the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour's specific commitment to incorporating Vedder's solo work into the band's retrospective. The closing wordless build was carried at sustained volume by the audience.

amongst the waves.text:
'Amongst the Waves' is the sixth track on Backspacer (2009), one of the warmest songs on an album of warm songs. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is the most explicit treatment in the Pearl Jam catalog of Vedder's lifelong relationship with surfing and with the ocean as a site of restoration, and it is therefore one of the few autobiographical tracks in the catalog whose autobiographical content the band has openly confirmed.

Vedder has been a serious surfer since the late 1980s, when he was working in San Diego and surfing the local breaks during the same period he was writing the demos that would become the 'Momma-Son' trilogy. The ocean is therefore one of the foundational sites of his songwriting practice, and Pearl Jam's catalog is full of oceanic imagery (Oceans on Ten, Long Road as a B-side, the entire Into the Wild soundtrack's wilderness preoccupation). 'Amongst the Waves' is the song that names this relationship directly rather than working through metaphor.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most genuinely happy pieces of writing. The narrator describes the experience of being in the water, riding the lift of a wave, encountering the kind of clarity that comes from physical engagement with the natural world. The song does not editorialize about whether this clarity is transferable to other domains of life; it documents the experience and lets the listener observe the joy. This is a Vedder mode that arrives only rarely in the catalog, and it is one of the durable curiosities of Backspacer that an album made during the optimism of the early Obama years gave him space to write this kind of unambiguous celebration.

The arrangement is one of the most pop-leaning on Backspacer. The verse is built on a clean four-bar progression that climbs into a chorus designed to be sung along to. McCready's solo at the song's center is one of his most melodic on the album, more in the Tom Petty vein than the Hendrix one. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed on the verses and sticked on the choruses, which is a textural shift that mirrors the lyric's movement from anticipation to release.

byShow.pj-2011-11-04: On 4 November 2011 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Amongst the Waves' arrived in the show's tenth slot as one of the Backspacer-era surfing-themed tracks the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour rotated into circulation. The song, written by Vedder during the Backspacer sessions in 2008, had carried a relatively low performance count by 2011, and the Morumbi placement reflected the night's commitment to surfacing less-played material from the band's most recent studio album. The slot's pacing function was to maintain the show's late-first-third emotional weight while introducing a song whose familiarity ran shallower than the surrounding material.
