gonna see my friend.text:
'Gonna See My Friend' is the opening track of Backspacer (2009), the song that announces the album's tonal break from the cumulative exhaustion of Riot Act and Pearl Jam (Avocado). The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written during the Backspacer sessions in late 2008 and was one of the first pieces of music the band recorded for the album. Its placement at track one is therefore a structural argument: the album begins with a song about leaving an old way of being behind.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about ending an addiction. The narrator describes the decision to walk away from a substance that has been controlling him, framing the decision as a visit to a friend rather than as a rupture. The song does not name the substance, but the lyric's specific imagery (the friend who knows what the narrator is doing, the route that has become familiar through repeated use) maps onto the recovery vocabulary that Vedder had been around for decades through his friendship with Mike McCready and his proximity to the Seattle music community's collective experience with addiction. Vedder has not confirmed a specific autobiographical reading in interviews, but he has confirmed the song's general subject in 2009 promotional material around Backspacer.

The arrangement is the most propulsive opener Pearl Jam had recorded since 'Go' opened Vs. in 1993. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging. McCready's solo at the song's center is short and aggressive, more in the Stooges vein than the Hendrix one. The song is under three minutes and ends without fading, which is the album's structural argument made musical: this period of the band's work would not allow itself to drift.

The song was one of the singles released ahead of Backspacer, issued in August 2009, and reached the top thirty on the Billboard Modern Rock chart. Its commercial reception was warm but not enormous, which is consistent with how the band's most directly autobiographical Vedder lyrics tend to be received: respected rather than embraced.

The 2009 track sat well in the slot's pacing function: a high-velocity reset after 'Given to Fly' had used its closing solo to lift the room. The compressed three-minute structure suited the night's faster-paced second-half-of-first-third pacing, and the Morumbi audience's energy through this slot was visible enough that the bootleg captures sustained crowd noise riding over the verse mix.

save it for later.text:
'Save It for Later' is an English Beat song from their 1982 album Special Beat Service, written by Dave Wakeling. The song was a moderate UK hit on its original release and grew into one of the more durable post-punk-into-pop crossover tracks of the early 80s. Pearl Jam began performing the song live in the mid-1990s and has continued to do so consistently for three decades, often in encores and frequently as a tag attached to 'Better Man.' The cover has become so associated with Pearl Jam in the band's American audience that a non-trivial number of younger fans first encounter the song through the Pearl Jam reading rather than through the English Beat original.

The lyric is one of the most quietly devastating pieces of writing in early-80s British pop. The narrator addresses a friend who is at a moment of decision in life, asking the friend to delay the decision rather than to make it badly under pressure. The song's emotional register is gentle counsel rather than urgent demand, which is unusual for a song built on the kind of energetic chord progression Wakeling deployed. Vedder has discussed the song in 2002 promotional interviews around Riot Act as a song he had loved since college and that he had been wanting to cover since the band first formed.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the English Beat structure but makes the song more direct. The original deploys a circular chord progression on twelve-string guitar with light percussion; the Pearl Jam reading adds a fuller rhythm section and lets McCready solo at the song's center, which the original did not allow. Vedder typically performs the song in a register slightly lower than Wakeling's original, which gives the cover a gravity the source recording did not have.

The song's status as a 'Better Man' tag has been a Pearl Jam concert convention since at least the 2000 tour. The two songs share a chord-progression DNA that allows the band to slide from one into the other without a noticeable transition, and the move has become one of the band's reliable mid-set surprises. Dave Wakeling himself has appeared with Pearl Jam on multiple occasions to perform the song, most prominently at the 2003 South Park Music Festival.

save it for later.text_pt:
'Save It for Later' é uma música do English Beat do álbum Special Beat Service (1982), escrita por Dave Wakeling. A canção foi um hit moderado no Reino Unido no lançamento original e cresceu pra virar uma das faixas mais duráveis de cruzamento entre pós-punk e pop do início dos anos 80. O Pearl Jam começou a tocar a música ao vivo em meados dos anos 1990 e continuou fazendo isso consistentemente por três décadas, frequentemente em bises e frequentemente como tag anexada a 'Better Man'. O cover virou tão associado ao Pearl Jam no público americano da banda que um número não trivial de fãs mais jovens encontra a música primeiro pela leitura do Pearl Jam em vez do original do English Beat.

A letra é uma das peças quietamente devastadoras de escrita do pop britânico do início dos anos 80. O narrador se dirige a um amigo que está em um momento de decisão na vida, pedindo ao amigo pra adiar a decisão em vez de tomá-la mal sob pressão. O registro emocional da canção é conselho gentil em vez de demanda urgente, o que é incomum pra uma música construída sobre o tipo de progressão de acordes energética que Wakeling empregou. Vedder discutiu a canção em entrevistas promocionais de 2002 em torno de Riot Act como uma música que ele amava desde a faculdade e que vinha querendo fazer cover desde que a banda se formou.

O arranjo do Pearl Jam preserva a estrutura do English Beat mas torna a música mais direta. O original emprega uma progressão de acordes circular em violão de doze cordas com percussão leve; a leitura do Pearl Jam adiciona uma cozinha rítmica mais cheia e deixa McCready solar no centro da música, o que o original não permitia. Vedder tipicamente toca a canção em um registro ligeiramente mais grave do que o original de Wakeling, o que dá ao cover uma gravidade que a gravação fonte não tinha.

O status da canção como tag de 'Better Man' tem sido convenção de concerto do Pearl Jam pelo menos desde a turnê de 2000. As duas músicas compartilham um DNA de progressão de acordes que permite à banda deslizar de uma pra outra sem transição perceptível, e o movimento virou uma das surpresas confiáveis de meio de set da banda. O próprio Dave Wakeling apareceu com o Pearl Jam em múltiplas ocasiões pra tocar a canção, mais proeminentemente no South Park Music Festival de 2003.

O original ska-rock de 1982 (escrito por Dave Wakeling e gravado pelo The Beat) deu ao slot um reset comprimido de vocabulário punk que a curva de energia de fim de set do show exigia. A colocação no Morumbi manteve a sequência conduzida por covers do bis que 'Last Kiss' tinha começado, e a função de andamento do slot era manter a energia do show na escalada propulsora pelas músicas finais.

byShow_pt.pj-2015-11-14: Em 14 de novembro de 2015 no Estádio do Morumbi, 'Save It for Later' chegou como a segunda metade do medley do slot 18 com 'Better Man'. O cover ska-rock de 1982 do English Beat deu à cauda do medley uma tag comprimida de vocabulário punk, e o público carregou a transição das harmonias sem palavras de 'Better Man' pra o tempo mais rápido do cover sem perda de volume.

O emprego duplo foi uma escolha estrutural incomum; a banda raramente repete músicas dentro de um único show. O cover ska-rock de 1982 do English Beat deu a ambos os slots um momento comprimido de vocabulário punk.

i wanna be your boyfriend.text:
'I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend' is a Ramones song from their self-titled 1976 debut album. The song was written by Tommy Ramone (Tom Erdelyi) and Dee Dee Ramone (Douglas Colvin), and it appears on the album as one of the gentler Ramones tracks, a deliberate counterpoint to the high-velocity punk material that surrounds it. The song is therefore one of the early Ramones recordings to demonstrate the band's range and their interest in classic 60s pop balladry as a lineage their music belonged to.

Pearl Jam began covering the song occasionally in the late 1990s and increased the frequency of performances after Joey Ramone's death in April 2001. The cover is part of the same tribute lineage that produced the band's regular performance of 'I Believe in Miracles' (the Brain Drain track) and that informed Vedder's 2002 induction speech for The Ramones at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Pearl Jam's relationship to the Ramones is therefore deep and ongoing, and 'I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend' is one of the songs through which that relationship gets renewed in concert.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Ramones original's tempo and chord progression but tilts the texture in a more layered direction. The original is built on a single guitar figure with minimal harmonic motion; the Pearl Jam version adds a McCready solo where the Ramones recording has none and lets Matt Cameron's drumming push the tempo forward at a pace slightly faster than the original. The song is short (under three minutes in both versions) and structured for sustained pop momentum rather than for cathartic release.

byShow.pj-2011-11-04: On 4 November 2011 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend' arrived in the show's twenty-eighth slot as the second Ramones-driven moment of the night, paired structurally with the band's broader Joey Ramone tribute work. The 1976 Ramones original (from the band's self-titled debut) gave the slot a sub-two-minute burst that the late-set energy curve demanded. The placement after 'Save It for Later' continued the cover-anchored encore sequence, and the bootleg captures the kind of fast, compressed punk-vocabulary delivery that the song's structure requires.
byShow.pj-2018-03-21: On 21 March 2018 at Maracanã, 'I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend' arrived as the middle tag of the twenty-eighth slot's three-way medley between 'Better Man' and 'Save It for Later'. The 1976 Ramones original gave the medley its compressed punk burst between two more anthemic communal moments.

baba oriley.text:
'Baba O'Riley' is the opening track of The Who's Who's Next (1971), one of the most consequential rock albums of the 1970s. The song was written by Pete Townshend, named for the spiritual teacher Meher Baba and the avant-garde composer Terry Riley (whose minimalist work influenced the song's iconic synthesizer pattern), and originally conceived as part of Townshend's abandoned Lifehouse rock-opera project. The song's opening organ pattern, generated by Townshend's experiments with synthesizer programming, is one of the most identifiable musical motifs in the rock canon.

Pearl Jam's relationship to The Who is foundational. Townshend has been one of Vedder's primary songwriting models since adolescence, and the band has performed Who material throughout its career. Vedder inducted The Who into the UK Music Hall of Fame in 2005 and has spoken at multiple subsequent Who-related events. The choice to cover 'Baba O'Riley' specifically is therefore a deliberate gesture of lineage: the song that opens The Who's most-loved album becomes, in Pearl Jam shows, one of the songs that closes Pearl Jam shows.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Townshend song structure but adapts the synthesizer pattern to electric guitar. McCready typically performs the opening organ figure on guitar with a clean tone, which gives the cover a slightly thinner texture than the original but allows the band to perform the song without keyboards onstage. Matt Cameron's drumming honors Keith Moon's original part without imitating it; Cameron is more economical than Moon was, which suits Pearl Jam's overall instrumental approach. The song's closing violin breakdown (in the original recording, performed by Dave Arbus) is omitted from the Pearl Jam reading, which lets the song end on the Townshend chord progression rather than on the original's coda.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'Baba O'Riley' arrived in the show's thirty-fourth slot as the Who cover. The 1971 Who original (from Who's Next, written by Pete Townshend) gave the late-set sequence its primary teenage-wasteland communal moment. The Brasília crowd carried the closing chorus at sustained volume.
byShow.pj-2018-03-24: On 24 March 2018 at Lollapalooza Brasil, 'Baba O'Riley' arrived in the show's twenty-fifth slot as the Who cover. The festival crowd carried the closing chorus at sustained volume.

blitzkrieg bop.text:
'Blitzkrieg Bop' is the opening track of the Ramones' self-titled 1976 debut album, and the most-anthologized Ramones song in popular culture. Written by Tommy Ramone with lyrics by Dee Dee Ramone, the song is structurally one of the simplest things on the album (three chords, two minutes, single-note vocal melody) and culturally one of the most consequential rock songs of the late 1970s. The 'Hey ho, let's go' chant has become so universal that the song now functions as something closer to a folk song than to a band-specific track in stadium and arena environments.

Pearl Jam began performing 'Blitzkrieg Bop' in the late 1990s and increased the frequency of the cover after Joey Ramone's death in April 2001. The song is part of the same tribute infrastructure that includes 'I Believe in Miracles' and 'I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend,' and the three Ramones covers together constitute Pearl Jam's most sustained ongoing tribute to a single band other than The Who. The choice of 'Blitzkrieg Bop' specifically is significant: the song the Ramones used to open their first album becomes, in Pearl Jam shows, one of the songs the band uses to mark moments of communal energy.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Ramones original's tempo and chord progression. The cover is brisk and direct in the way the original was, and the band does not extend the song past the original's two-minute length. Matt Cameron's drumming honors Tommy Ramone's original feel without imitating it, and McCready does not solo, which is unusual for a Pearl Jam cover and which honors the Ramones aesthetic of refusing the kind of guitar grandstanding that the late-70s mainstream rock vocabulary celebrated.

byShow.pj-2011-11-06: On 6 November 2011 at Praça da Apoteose, 'Blitzkrieg Bop' arrived in the show's tenth slot as the Ramones tribute the band had been folding into Pearl Jam Twenty Tour setlists, partly as the decade-long Joey Ramone memorial gesture and partly as part of the tour's broader retrospective framing. The 1976 Ramones original (from the band's self-titled debut) gave the slot a punk-vocabulary compression that the show's mid-set tempo curve called for. The 'Hey ho, let's go' chant landed at the kind of audience-led volume that the Sambadrome's open-air acoustics carried across the venue's wide pitch, and the bootleg captures the chant sustaining through the slot.
byShow.pj-2018-03-21: On 21 March 2018 at Maracanã, 'Blitzkrieg Bop' arrived in the show's twenty-second slot as the Ramones cover. The 1976 Ramones original's 'Hey ho, let's go' chant landed at the kind of audience-led volume that the open-air Maracanã carried.

mother.text:
'Mother' is a song from Pink Floyd's The Wall (1979), the conceptual double album that Roger Waters wrote and the band recorded under the production direction of Bob Ezrin. Within The Wall's narrative, 'Mother' is sung by the protagonist Pink as he addresses the maternal figure who has, in the album's argument, contributed to building the psychological wall that the album's title names. The song is therefore one of the most direct pieces of writing on The Wall about the way well-meaning protective behavior can become its own form of damage.

Pearl Jam began performing 'Mother' in the early 2010s, and the cover became part of the band's PJ20 anniversary cycle setlists. The choice is unusual; Pink Floyd is a band that Pearl Jam covers far more rarely than The Who, the Ramones, or Neil Young. The decision to incorporate 'Mother' into the band's live vocabulary during the PJ20 period was therefore a deliberate move to broaden the band's tribute lineage at the moment they were marking their own twentieth anniversary as a touring entity.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Pink Floyd song structure but tilts the texture in a more guitar-driven direction. The original is built around acoustic guitar and Roger Waters' vocal, with limited electric instrumentation; the Pearl Jam reading adds a fuller rhythm section and lets McCready play the closing solo with a more aggressive tone than David Gilmour deployed in the original recording. Vedder typically sings the song in a register lower than Waters' original, which gives the cover a different emotional weight than the source.

byShow.pj-2011-11-06: On 6 November 2011 at Praça da Apoteose, 'Mother' arrived in the show's twenty-fifth slot as the Pink Floyd cover the band had been folding into late-set sequences across the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour. The 1979 The Wall original (written by Roger Waters) gave the slot a slow, meditative weight that the show's late-set emotional architecture demanded. The Rio placement after 'Jeremy' continued the late-set sequence's emotional gravity, and the bootleg captures Vedder's vocal phrasing the song's lyric in a way that draws specific connections between the cover's subject and the band's own preoccupations with parental authority that 'Alive' had documented twenty years earlier.
byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'Mother' arrived in the show's twenty-first slot as the Pink Floyd cover (1979 The Wall, written by Roger Waters), continuing the show's Pink-Floyd-heavy thread that had begun with the 'Daughter / Another Brick' medley six slots earlier. The placement gave the late-set sequence emotional gravity. Vedder's vocal phrasing drew specific connections between Waters's anti-maternal-overprotection narrative and the band's own lineage of parental-authority preoccupations.

rockin in the free world.text:
'Rockin' in the Free World' is the closing track of Neil Young's Freedom (1989), and one of the most-performed protest songs of the late 20th century. Young wrote the song in early 1989 in response to a number of political situations he was watching that year, most prominently the late-Reagan-into-early-Bush moment in American politics and the contemporary news of the Iranian protests. The song's title is sarcastic; the lyric documents the failures of the freedoms it nominally celebrates, and the song's energetic chord progression carries the irony rather than dispelling it.

Pearl Jam's relationship to Neil Young is one of the most consequential band-to-band relationships in the post-1990 American rock catalog. The bands toured together in 1993 and again in 1995. Pearl Jam backed Young on the entire Mirror Ball album (1995), and the same sessions produced the 'I Got Id' and 'Long Road' Pearl Jam tracks that were issued separately as the Merkin Ball EP. Young inducted Pearl Jam into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2017. The two acts have therefore been entwined for thirty years, and 'Rockin' in the Free World' is the song through which that relationship gets renewed in concert most frequently.

The Pearl Jam arrangement of 'Rockin' in the Free World' preserves the Neil Young Freedom recording's structure but tilts the texture toward the band's own Vs.-era vocabulary. The verse is built on the original's tight chord progression; the chorus releases the verse's tension into a wider harmonic move that lets McCready solo at the song's center. The closing instrumental section frequently extends past the studio length, sometimes by several minutes, and on multiple historic occasions (the 1992 MTV Video Music Awards performance is the most famous) Young himself has joined the band onstage to trade guitar solos with McCready in extended jams.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Rockin' in the Free World' arrived in the show's thirty-fifth slot as the Neil Young cover the band uses to close shows with all the venue lights up, the audience-artist visual barrier dissolved. The 1989 Young original (from Freedom) gave the slot the kind of catharsis-encore function the song has served across the band's two decades of using it as a closer.

byShow.pj-2018-03-21: On 21 March 2018 at Maracanã, 'Rockin' in the Free World' arrived in the show's thirtieth slot, deploying the Neil Young cover with the venue lights up.

The Neil Young cover gave the cathartic-encore moment with the venue lights up. The song's specific weight in 2024 (the Trump era's continuation, with the song's 1989 lyric of American political failure retaining renewed legibility) carried into the Wrigley closing.
byShow.ev-2014-05-08: On 8 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Rockin' in the Free World' arrived in the show's twenty-eighth slot in solo-acoustic arrangement, an unusual deployment of the song that more typically closes PJ band shows with full-volume catharsis. The acoustic version preserved the Neil Young political vocabulary while transposing the energy into solo intimacy.

The Neil Young cover's deployment in 2021 carried specific weight: less than a year after Trump's January 6 capitol attack and during the Biden administration's first year, the song's anti-American-political-failure argument retained particular legibility.

rockin in the free world.text_pt:
'Rockin' in the Free World' é a faixa de fechamento de Freedom (1989) de Neil Young, e uma das músicas de protesto mais executadas do fim do século 20. Young escreveu a canção no início de 1989 em resposta a uma série de situações políticas que estava observando naquele ano, mais proeminentemente o momento do fim da era Reagan adentrando o início da era Bush na política americana e as notícias contemporâneas dos protestos iranianos. O título da canção é sarcástico; a letra documenta as falhas das liberdades que ela nominalmente celebra, e a progressão de acordes energética da canção carrega a ironia em vez de dissipá-la.

A relação do Pearl Jam com Neil Young é uma das mais consequentes relações banda-a-banda no catálogo de rock americano pós-1990. As bandas fizeram turnê juntas em 1993 e de novo em 1995. O Pearl Jam acompanhou Young no álbum Mirror Ball inteiro (1995), e as mesmas sessões produziram as faixas 'I Got Id' e 'Long Road' do Pearl Jam que foram lançadas separadamente como o EP Merkin Ball. Young induziu o Pearl Jam ao Rock and Roll Hall of Fame em 2017. Os dois atos têm portanto se entrelaçado por trinta anos, e 'Rockin' in the Free World' é a música pela qual essa relação se renova em concerto com mais frequência.

O arranjo do Pearl Jam de 'Rockin' in the Free World' preserva a estrutura da gravação de Young em Freedom mas inclina a textura pra o vocabulário próprio da era Vs. da banda. O verso é construído sobre a progressão de acordes densa do original; o refrão libera a tensão do verso em um movimento harmônico mais largo que deixa McCready solar no centro da música. A seção instrumental final frequentemente se estende além da duração de estúdio, às vezes por vários minutos, e em múltiplas ocasiões históricas (a apresentação no MTV Video Music Awards de 1992 é a mais famosa) o próprio Young se juntou à banda no palco pra trocar solos de guitarra com McCready em jams estendidas.

byShow_pt.pj-2015-11-20: Em 20 de novembro de 2015 no Mineirão, 'Rockin' in the Free World' chegou no slot 35 do show como o cover de Neil Young que a banda usa pra fechar shows com todas as luzes da casa acesas, a barreira visual público-artista dissolvida. O original de Young de 1989 (de Freedom) deu ao slot o tipo de função catarse-bis que a canção cumpriu ao longo das duas décadas em que a banda a usa como fechadora.
byShow_pt.pj-2015-11-22: Em 22 de novembro de 2015 no Maracanã, 'Rockin' in the Free World' chegou no slot 33 do show. O cover de Neil Young deu o último momento catártico de bis da perna brasileira, com as luzes da casa acesas e a barreira visual público-artista dissolvida.
byShow_pt.pj-2018-03-21: Em 21 de março de 2018 no Maracanã, 'Rockin' in the Free World' chegou no slot 30 do show, empregando o cover de Neil Young com as luzes da casa acesas.
byShow_pt.pj-2024-08-29: Em 29 de agosto de 2024 no Wrigley Field, 'Rockin' in the Free World' fechou o show no slot 26. O cover de Neil Young deu o momento catártico de bis com as luzes da casa acesas. O peso específico da canção em 2024 (a continuação da era Trump, com a letra de 1989 da canção sobre falha política americana retendo legibilidade renovada) passou pra o fechamento no Wrigley.

interstellar overdrive.text:
'Interstellar Overdrive' is the third track on Pink Floyd's debut album The Piper at the Gates of Dawn (1967). The song is credited collectively to the four members of the original Pink Floyd lineup (Syd Barrett, Roger Waters, Richard Wright, Nick Mason) and is one of the longest tracks on the record at over nine minutes. It is also one of the most foundational pieces of psychedelic rock instrumental writing from the late 1960s, structured as a sustained improvisation framed by a single recurring riff. The song became central to the early Pink Floyd live show before Syd Barrett's departure from the band in 1968.

Pearl Jam has covered the song on rare occasions across its career, typically deploying it as the kind of extended jam that requires a particular kind of show context to land. The cover is a deep cut even within Pearl Jam's tribute vocabulary; the band has never recorded a studio version, and the cover lives entirely in the bootleg ecosystem. The choice to perform 'Interstellar Overdrive' is therefore a deliberate gesture of lineage, signaling the band's interest in the British psychedelic tradition that runs from Pink Floyd through Hendrix into the Seattle scene's own experimental wing.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Pink Floyd structure but tilts the texture toward the band's own Vs. and Vitalogy guitar vocabulary. McCready typically extends the opening riff into a sustained jam that runs longer than the original recording's nine minutes. Matt Cameron's drumming honors Nick Mason's loose original feel, and Jeff Ament's bass line holds the song's harmonic center while McCready improvises above it. The song is therefore one of the few Pearl Jam concert performances where the instrumental content dominates and the vocal element is absent for several minutes.

Live, 'Interstellar Overdrive' is one of Pearl Jam's rarest covers. The song appears in a handful of setlists across decades, almost always at festivals or on tours where the band has decided to take a particular musical risk. Audiences who recognize the source treat the cover as a small gift; audiences who do not recognize the source receive a sustained guitar feature whose architecture is unusual for a Pearl Jam show but whose energy reads regardless of recognition.

byShow.pj-2013-03-31: On 31 March 2013 at Jockey Club, 'Interstellar Overdrive' arrived in the show's third slot as one of the rarest covers the Pearl Jam Twenty-era touring catalog has produced: the Pink Floyd instrumental from Piper at the Gates of Dawn (1967), originally written by Syd Barrett, Roger Waters, Nick Mason, and Richard Wright. The Pearl Jam version is functionally a band jam vehicle, with no vocal entry, and the Lollapalooza Brasil placement gave the slot an extended instrumental showcase that few Pearl Jam shows have featured. McCready's guitar work on this recording leans into the song's freeform structure, and the bootleg captures one of the longer instrumental improvisations the band performed on the 2013 South American leg.

The Porto Alegre placement gave the slot a ten-minute freeform section in the middle of an otherwise tight running order.

insignificance.text:
'Insignificance' is the seventh track on Binaural (2000), the album that marked Pearl Jam's most explicit experimental turn after the No Code period. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is also Vedder's. The song was written in the late 1990s and recorded during the Binaural sessions in Seattle in early 2000, in the period when the band was working with producer Tchad Blake. The Binaural sessions were the only Pearl Jam album not produced by Brendan O'Brien between 1993 and 2009. The song is therefore one of the few Vedder solo-music credits on a Pearl Jam album.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about the function of music during catastrophe. The narrator describes the experience of listening to music in a moment of large-scale political horror and finding that the music does not save anything, does not change anything, but does provide a small zone of meaning that the catastrophe cannot reach. Vedder discussed the song in 2000 promotional interviews around Binaural as a song he had been wanting to write for years and that finally arrived during the late-Clinton-era political moment that preceded the song's recording.

The arrangement is one of the most patient pieces on Binaural. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a McCready solo. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is among the most controlled of his Pearl Jam tenure. The song is structured for cumulative emotional weight rather than for cathartic release.

Live, 'Insignificance' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2000. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been warmed up enough to receive it. The song's specific argument about music during crisis became more legible to Pearl Jam audiences after September 11, 2001, when the band's relationship to its own catalog was reframed by the political weather of the Bush years. Subsequent performances of 'Insignificance' have therefore carried a layer of meaning the song did not have when it was first recorded.

byShow.pj-2013-03-31: On 31 March 2013 at Jockey Club, 'Insignificance' arrived in the show's twelfth slot as one of the Binaural-era deep cuts the band rotated into circulation across the Lightning Bolt-era touring catalog. The song's lyric (often read as a meditation on civilian life in wartime, written as the Iraq War context was beginning to dominate American discourse in 2000) carried its layered weight into the 2013 performance. The compressed under-four-minute structure suited the slot's pacing function: a propulsive Binaural-era piece that maintained the show's mid-set tempo.

lukin.text:
'Lukin' is the seventh track on No Code (1996), and one of the shortest songs Pearl Jam has ever recorded (under one minute). The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The title refers to Matt Lukin, the bassist of Mudhoney and one of the foundational figures of the Seattle scene that produced Pearl Jam. The song is named for him because Lukin's house, in Vedder's lived experience during the mid-1990s, was a refuge: when fame and obligation became unmanageable, Vedder would go to Lukin's place to escape, which is what the song's lyric documents.

Vedder has discussed the song in multiple interviews from the No Code promotional cycle and in PJ20. The story is consistent: Lukin's house was the place where Vedder could be a person rather than a public figure, where the conversation was about music or motorcycles or nothing in particular rather than about the band's commercial trajectory. The song is therefore a very short, very specific tribute to a friendship that protected Vedder during one of the most difficult periods of his career.

The arrangement matches the lyric's compression. The song is structured as a single punk-tempo burst with no chorus, no bridge, no solo. The band plays the verse riff at full volume for under a minute and ends without ceremony. This is one of only a few Pearl Jam recordings to refuse the basic verse-chorus structural conventions of rock songwriting, and the refusal is deliberate: the song is short because the experience it documents was a brief escape rather than a sustained refuge.

Live, 'Lukin' has been a regular setlist presence since 1996. The song works as a punk pivot in the middle of a set, where its brevity can disrupt the canonical Pearl Jam pacing without committing to an extended energy investment. Audiences who know the song wait for the burst; audiences who do not know the song often miss it entirely, since the song ends before recognition has time to settle.

The slot's pacing function was to maintain the high-velocity opening surge that 'Even Flow' had built. The Buenos Aires crowd's response sustained the volume across the song's brief runtime.

lukin.text_pt:
'Lukin' é a sétima faixa de No Code (1996), e uma das músicas mais curtas que o Pearl Jam já gravou (menos de um minuto). A música é de Stone Gossard; a letra é de Vedder. O título se refere a Matt Lukin, baixista do Mudhoney e uma das figuras fundadoras da cena de Seattle que produziu o Pearl Jam. A canção é nomeada por ele porque a casa de Lukin, na experiência vivida de Vedder em meados dos anos 1990, era um refúgio: quando fama e obrigação se tornavam inadministráveis, Vedder ia pra casa de Lukin pra escapar, que é o que a letra da canção documenta.

Vedder discutiu a canção em várias entrevistas do ciclo promocional de No Code e em PJ20. A história é consistente: a casa de Lukin era o lugar em que Vedder podia ser uma pessoa em vez de uma figura pública, em que a conversa era sobre música ou motos ou nada em particular em vez de sobre a trajetória comercial da banda. A canção é portanto um tributo muito curto e muito específico a uma amizade que protegeu Vedder durante um dos períodos mais difíceis da carreira dele.

O arranjo combina com a compressão da letra. A canção é estruturada como uma única rajada em andamento de punk sem refrão, sem ponte, sem solo. A banda toca o riff do verso em volume máximo por menos de um minuto e termina sem cerimônia. Essa é uma das poucas gravações do Pearl Jam que se recusam às convenções estruturais básicas verso-refrão da composição de rock, e a recusa é deliberada: a canção é curta porque a experiência que documenta foi um escape breve em vez de um refúgio sustentado.

Ao vivo, 'Lukin' é presença regular em setlist desde 1996. A canção funciona como pivô punk no meio de um set, em que sua brevidade pode interromper o andamento canônico do Pearl Jam sem se comprometer com um investimento estendido de energia. Públicos que conhecem a música esperam pela rajada; públicos que não conhecem a canção frequentemente a perdem inteiramente, já que a música acaba antes do reconhecimento ter tempo de se assentar.

A função de andamento do slot era manter a onda de abertura de alta velocidade que 'Even Flow' tinha construído. deep.text:
'Deep' is the tenth track on Ten (1991), one of the most aggressive things on a debut album that contains many aggressive things. The music is credited to Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most direct early Pearl Jam engagements with addiction as a social and personal subject, written and recorded in the immediate aftermath of Mother Love Bone vocalist Andrew Wood's overdose death in March 1990, and during a period when Seattle's musical community was watching multiple of its members struggle with heroin dependency.

The lyric is one of Vedder's bleakest pieces of writing on Ten. The narrator describes a series of figures whose addictions are destroying them, framed in third-person observation rather than in first-person confession. The song does not editorialize about whether the figures could be saved; it documents their decline and lets the music's slide-guitar texture carry the emotional weight. Vedder has discussed the song in interviews from the early 1990s as a song that came out of his observations of the Seattle scene during his first months in the city, when he was still new to the community and was watching the casualties accumulate without yet being able to name the people involved.

The arrangement is one of the most blues-inflected things on Ten. The verse is built on a slide-guitar figure that Stone Gossard plays with an unusual open tuning, and the chorus releases the verse's tension through a wah-wah-driven McCready solo that is among the most aggressive on the album. Dave Krusen's drumming on the recording is the slowest on Ten, which suits the song's weight. The song is therefore tonally one of the darker pieces on the record, even within the context of an album that is full of darkness.

Live, 'Deep' has been a rare setlist presence. The song's tempo and emotional density make it difficult to deploy in shows where the audience is expecting velocity, and the band has historically reserved the song for moments when its weight can land. Performances of 'Deep' often extend the closing instrumental section past the studio length, sometimes by several minutes, with McCready taking the song into territory that is closer to John Lee Hooker than to anything else in the Pearl Jam catalog.

byShow.pj-2013-04-03: On 3 April 2013 at Costanera Sur, 'Deep' arrived in the show's seventh slot as one of the rarer Ten-era deep cuts the Pearl Jam Lightning Bolt-era touring catalog has produced. The song (originally from the band's 1991 debut, written about a heroin addict moving through Seattle) carried its specific autobiographical layer into the 2013 performance. The compressed structure and the riff's tight verse-pattern landed at the slot's pacing function: Ten-era aggression deployed as a mid-set anchor.
byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Deep' arrived in the show's ninth slot as the Ten-era deep cut about a heroin addict moving through Seattle. The relatively rare live appearance gave the slot a deep-cut surprise, and the compressed structure landed at the slot's pacing function.

present tense.text:
'Present Tense' is the tenth track on No Code (1996), and one of the most patient pieces of writing in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Mike McCready's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is the longest track on No Code and is structured as a slow build from a meditative verse through a sustained instrumental climb that does not resolve into the kind of catharsis that Pearl Jam songs of comparable length usually deliver. The song's argument is its structure: the present tense is something the listener has to live in rather than something the music can deliver.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most explicit pieces of writing about the work of moving past trauma. The narrator describes the choice to live in the present rather than to remain captive to the past, framing the choice not as a single decision but as an ongoing practice that has to be renewed daily. The song is one of the few Pearl Jam tracks that openly draws from the vocabulary of recovery literature and meditation practice, and Vedder has acknowledged in interviews from the No Code period that the song was influenced by his own engagement with these traditions during the mid-1990s.

The arrangement is McCready's most ambitious No Code piece. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure; the band enters under the second verse but stays restrained through the bridge. The closing instrumental section runs for nearly two minutes, with McCready's solo extending the song's tempo without breaking it. Jack Irons's drumming on the recording (his only full Pearl Jam album) is brushed throughout, which gives the song the kind of textural softness that suits the lyric's posture.

Live, 'Present Tense' has been a setlist regular since 1996. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow build can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared by previous material. The audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in any Pearl Jam show; audiences carry the section without prompting, and Vedder typically steps back from the microphone during this part. The song is one of the catalog's quieter contracts between the band and its audience.

byShow.pj-2011-11-11: On 11 November 2011 at Estádio Beira-Rio, 'Present Tense' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as one of the No Code-era tracks the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour deployed when the show's mid-set sequence called for sustained meditative weight. The song's slow build into the closing minute's full release gave the slot the kind of patient emotional climb that the show needed at this point. The Beira-Rio bootleg captures the audience's sustained mid-show quiet through the song's verse, which the open-air venue's acoustics carried across the pitch.

The song's slow build into the closing minute's full release gave the slot the kind of patient emotional climb the show needed.
byShow.pj-2015-11-22: On 22 November 2015 at Maracanã, 'Present Tense' arrived in the show's second slot as one of the No Code-era tracks. sonic reducer.text:
'Sonic Reducer' is the opening track of the Dead Boys' debut album Young, Loud and Snotty (1977). The song was written by lead singer Stiv Bators, guitarist Cheetah Chrome (Eugene O'Connor), and drummer Johnny Blitz, and it is one of the foundational tracks of the Cleveland-into-New York punk scene that ran parallel to the early Ramones and Television. The Dead Boys would not survive long as a band (they broke up in 1979 after Stiv Bators's departure), but 'Sonic Reducer' has remained their most-covered song and one of the era-defining punk anthems of the late 1970s.

Pearl Jam has covered the song occasionally since the early 1990s. Vedder's relationship to Stiv Bators was direct rather than mediated; the two had crossed paths in the Los Angeles punk scene of the late 1980s, and Vedder has spoken about Bators's influence on his own vocal approach in multiple interviews from the early Pearl Jam period. Bators's death in 1990 (he was hit by a car in Paris and died of a head injury he had refused to allow doctors to treat) was one of the punk-scene losses that shaped Vedder's understanding of the music's stakes.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Dead Boys' tempo and chord progression. The cover is brisk and direct, and the band does not extend the song past the original's length. McCready's guitar tone is grittier than Cheetah Chrome's original, and Matt Cameron's drumming honors Johnny Blitz's original part without imitating it. The song is structured for sustained punk velocity rather than for cathartic release.

Live, 'Sonic Reducer' has been an irregular but treasured setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best as an encore or as a punk pivot in the late half of a set, where its velocity can carry a show home. The cover has been performed at Cleveland Pearl Jam shows with particular frequency, since Cleveland is the Dead Boys' home city and the song's local resonance is unusually durable there.

byShow.pj-2013-04-06: On 6 April 2013 at Parque O'Higgins, 'Sonic Reducer' arrived in the show's twenty-second slot as the Dead Boys cover the band had been folding into setlists since the late 90s. The 1977 Dead Boys original (from Young Loud and Snotty, written by Stiv Bators and Cheetah Chrome) gave the slot a punk-vocabulary explosion that the show's late-set energy curve required. Vedder frequently used the song as a vehicle for stage anarchy across the touring catalog, and the Lollapalooza Chile placement maintained that tradition.
byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Sonic Reducer' arrived in the show's thirty-third slot as the Dead Boys cover the band uses for late-set punk-vocabulary explosions.

low light.text:
'Low Light' is the ninth track on Yield (1998), and one of the most patient pieces of writing on the album. The music is Jeff Ament's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the few Pearl Jam ballads built around an Ament composition rather than a Stone Gossard or Mike McCready piece, and the arrangement reflects this: the bass line is foregrounded throughout the song, and the harmonic motion is more melodic than rhythmic.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about romantic devotion. The narrator describes the moment of finding a partner across difficult circumstances, framing the encounter as the kind of recognition that arrives once in a life and that has to be honored when it arrives. The song does not editorialize about how to honor it; it documents the recognition and lets the listener observe both the gratitude and the slight terror that accompanies any genuine connection.

The arrangement is built around a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure that Stone Gossard plays under Vedder's vocal, with Ament's bass line carrying the song's harmonic motion. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic, more in the David Gilmour vein than the Hendrix one. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed throughout, which gives the song the kind of textural softness that suits the lyric's posture.

Live, 'Low Light' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 1998. The song works best in the encore, where its stillness can mark a deliberate pause before the closing surge. The audience response to the song tends to be hushed during the verses and warm after, which is consistent with how Yield's quieter material has been received across decades.

byShow.pj-2011-11-11: On 11 November 2011 at Estádio Beira-Rio, 'Low Light' arrived in the show's sixth slot as one of the Yield-era ballads the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour rotated into circulation when the show's tempo curve called for slow, deliberately-paced material. The Ament-credited song (one of the few Pearl Jam tracks where Jeff Ament has primary lyric authorship) sat well in slot 6's pacing function: an emotional reset after the high-velocity opening had built audience energy. The bootleg captures Vedder's vocal sitting forward in the mix, the way the studio recording mirrors.
byShow.pj-2018-03-21: On 21 March 2018 at Maracanã, 'Low Light' arrived in the show's second slot as one of the Yield-era ballads. The Ament-credited song's gentle arrangement maintained the show's deliberate slow opening.

garden.text:
'Garden' is the ninth track on Ten (1991). The music is credited to Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written and recorded during the Ten sessions in early 1991, in the period when the United States was conducting Operation Desert Storm in Iraq and Kuwait. The lyric is one of the early Pearl Jam catalog's most direct engagements with American military intervention, framed through the central image of a 'garden' of stone, the rows of military headstones in national cemeteries that mark the cumulative cost of foreign wars.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most patient anti-war statements. The narrator does not denounce the soldiers who fight; the song's argument is structural rather than personal, focused on the systems that produce the cemeteries rather than on the people buried in them. This is a Vedder preoccupation that recurs across the catalog (it shapes 'Bu$hleaguer' a decade later, and 'Down' two years after that), and 'Garden' is the song where the argument first arrives in his writing.

The arrangement is one of the slower-building pieces on Ten. The verse is built on a chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a wider harmonic move; McCready's solo at the song's center extends past the studio length on most live performances. Dave Krusen's drumming is restrained throughout, which suits the lyric's posture of observation rather than confrontation.

Live, 'Garden' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 1991. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared. The song became more frequent in setlists during the Iraq War period (2003 onward), when the lyric's specific argument about American military intervention became current again. Performances of 'Garden' often extend the closing instrumental section past the studio length.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Garden' arrived in the show's twenty-ninth slot as the Ten-era track whose layered lyric (often read as a meditation on the impossibility of innocence in a violent world) carried its accumulated weight through twenty-four years of live history.
byShow.pj-2018-03-21: On 21 March 2018 at Maracanã, 'Garden' arrived in the show's sixteenth slot as the Ten-era track. The relatively rare live appearance gave the slot a deep-cut surprise.
byShow.pj-2024-08-31: On 31 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Garden' opened the show as the Ten-era track, an unusual opener choice for the band. The 1991 song's layered lyric (a meditation on the impossibility of innocence in a violent world) established the second Wrigley night's emotional architecture as deliberately weightier than night 1's slower opening sequence.

mind your manners.text:
'Mind Your Manners' is the second track on Lightning Bolt (2013) and the album's lead single. The music is Mike McCready's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is the band's most explicit return to punk-tempo writing in years, with a verse riff that runs at thrash velocity and a chorus that releases the verse's tension into a sustained scream. The song was released in July 2013 ahead of the album and was Pearl Jam's most commercially successful single of the 2010s in its first weeks of release.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct anti-religious-institution statements. The narrator addresses an unnamed authority figure (the song's argument is generalized rather than denominational) and refuses the moral authority that the figure has claimed. The song does not engage with theology; the argument is institutional, focused on the systems through which religious authority becomes a tool for controlling other people's lives rather than on whether the underlying belief is true or false. Vedder discussed the song in 2013 promotional interviews around Lightning Bolt as a song that came out of his observations of the late-Bush-into-early-Obama American political moment, when religious institutions had been particularly visible in shaping public policy.

The arrangement is one of McCready's most aggressive Lightning Bolt pieces. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging. The song was produced by Brendan O'Brien, who had returned to the band after the Backspacer cycle, and his preference for tight rhythm-section recording is audible throughout.

Live, 'Mind Your Manners' has been a setlist regular since 2013. The song works as a mid-set energy injection or as an early-set burst, where its velocity can establish or maintain the show's momentum. The audience response is consistent with how the band's punk-tempo tracks have been received throughout the catalog: physical recognition rather than singalong attention.

lightning bolt.text:
'Lightning Bolt' is the title track and fifth song on Lightning Bolt (2013). The music is credited to Stone Gossard and Mike McCready; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most directly autobiographical pieces of writing on the album, drawing from Vedder's experiences of finding moments of clarity that arrive without warning, the kind of insight that strikes like the lightning bolt the song's title names.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more optimistic pieces of writing from the 2010s. The narrator describes the experience of receiving sudden insight as a gift rather than as a disruption, framing the moment of clarity as something to be honored rather than questioned. The song does not editorialize about whether such moments are sustainable; it documents the experience and lets the music's tempo carry the energy.

The arrangement is one of the most sustained pieces of writing on Lightning Bolt. The verse is built on a chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a chorus that opens into a wider harmonic move. McCready's solo at the song's center is one of his most melodic on the album. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward at a pace that the band has rarely sustained on a recording.

Live, 'Lightning Bolt' has been a setlist regular since 2013. The song works best in the early-middle of a set, where its energy can establish the show's momentum without committing to a peak. The audience response is consistent with how the band's title tracks have been received throughout the catalog: warm recognition rather than explosive singalong attention.

The Porto Alegre crowd's vocal participation through the chorus sustained the volume the show's previous high-velocity sequence had built.

sirens.text:
'Sirens' is the sixth track on Lightning Bolt (2013) and the album's most-played live song after the title track. The music is Mike McCready's; the lyric is Vedder's. McCready has discussed the song in interviews from the 2013 promotional cycle as a song he wrote for his wife Ashley, framing the music as a gift she could carry beyond the moment of its composition. The song is therefore one of the few pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog with a documented dedication, and the arrangement reflects that personal stake.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about mortality within the context of love. The narrator describes the experience of holding a partner while remaining aware that the holding will not be permanent, framing the awareness not as a tragedy but as the source of the love's intensity. The song does not editorialize about how to live with this awareness; it documents the experience and lets the music's slow build carry the emotional weight. Vedder discussed the song in 2013 interviews as a song that took the McCready music in a more direct direction than the original instrumental had implied.

The arrangement is one of McCready's most patient Lightning Bolt pieces. The verse is built on a chord progression that does not vary through the bridge; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through a sustained instrumental climb. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is restrained throughout, which suits the song's posture. The closing solo extends past the studio length on most live performances.

Live, 'Sirens' has been a setlist regular since 2013. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been warmed up. The audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in any Pearl Jam show from the 2013 cycle onward.

McCready's lyric (a meditation on mortality from a long-married perspective) sat over the performance with the kind of emotional weight that the slow tempo demands. The Porto Alegre crowd's vocal participation through the chorus sustained the volume the song's structure invites.

The post-Paris weight gave the song's lyric its sharpest live reading: the 'one breath away from the rest of our lives' structure mapped exactly onto the previous evening's news.

all night.text:
'All Night' is one of the more aggressive Lost Dogs (2003) tracks, recorded during the Riot Act sessions in 2002 and held off the album for tonal reasons. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is a sub-three-minute punk-tempo burst that the band has used in setlists primarily as an early-set energy injection, and its reception by audiences who do not know the song from Lost Dogs tends to be physical recognition rather than singalong attention.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about extended physical and emotional engagement. The narrator describes the experience of being awake through the night with someone, framing the experience not as romantic in the conventional sense but as the kind of sustained presence that creates its own meaning. The song does not editorialize; it documents.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most economical pieces of mid-2000s writing. The verse is built on a tight, mid-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus releases the verse's tension into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. McCready's solo at the song's center is a controlled six-bar burst rather than an extended melodic statement. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging.

Live, 'All Night' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2003. The song works best in the early-middle of a set, where its velocity can keep momentum going without committing to a peak. Audiences who know the song from Lost Dogs sing along to the chorus; audiences who do not recognize it receive a Pearl Jam punk-tempo track at full volume, which lands regardless of recognition.

byShow.pj-2018-03-21: On 21 March 2018 at Maracanã, 'All Night' arrived in the show's fifth slot as one of the rarer Lost Dogs-era No Code outtakes, originally a 1996 outtake that finally surfaced on the 2003 Lost Dogs compilation. The compressed under-four-minute structure and all-five-members co-writer credit gave the slot a deep-cut surprise.

cant deny me.text:
'Can't Deny Me' is a non-album single Pearl Jam released in March 2018, the band's first new music since Lightning Bolt (2013) and the most explicitly anti-Trump statement in the catalog. The music is credited to Vedder; the lyric is also Vedder's. The song was distributed initially as a Ten Club fan-club exclusive and later made available on streaming platforms. The single's release was timed to coincide with the South American leg of the band's 2018 tour, and the song became one of the most-played songs in those setlists immediately on release.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct political statements. The narrator addresses an unnamed but unmistakable political figure (the song's references make the target legible: a then-current American president whose policies and rhetoric the song lists in compressed indictment) and refuses the moral authority that figure has claimed. The song does not engage with the underlying ideology; the argument is about the specific person and the immediate damage. Vedder discussed the song in 2018 promotional interviews as a song that came out of his cumulative frustration with the first year of the Trump administration and that he had been working on since the 2016 election results.

The arrangement is one of the most propulsive pieces Pearl Jam recorded in the 2010s. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward at a pace the band had not sustained on a single since the Vs. era. McCready's solo is short and aggressive.

Live, 'Can't Deny Me' became a setlist regular immediately on release in 2018. The song works best in the early-middle of a set, where its political velocity can establish a posture the rest of the show can build on. The song was eventually included on Gigaton (2020) as a track on the deluxe edition, which gave it a more permanent home in the catalog than its original single-only release had implied.

byShow.pj-2018-03-21: On 21 March 2018 at Maracanã, 'Can't Deny Me' arrived in the show's seventeenth slot as the band's first new song since Lightning Bolt 2013, released as a non-album single just two days before this show (March 19, 2018). The 2018 single's specific anti-Trump lyric ('You can't deny me') made the Rio show one of the song's earliest live performances. The Brazilian audience was hearing brand-new Pearl Jam material for the first time in five years.
byShow.pj-2018-03-24: On 24 March 2018 at Lollapalooza Brasil, 'Can't Deny Me' arrived in the show's seventh slot, the second live performance of the song in just three days (after the Maracanã premiere). The 2018 single's anti-Trump argument retained legibility in the festival context, and the Brazilian audience's response to the brand-new song was sustained.

sleeping by myself.text:
'Sleeping by Myself' originated as a track on Eddie Vedder's solo album Ukulele Songs (2011), which collected fifteen pieces of his songwriting around the ukulele as the central instrument. Pearl Jam recorded a band version of the song for Lightning Bolt (2013), which appears as the album's eleventh track. The Pearl Jam reading is therefore an arrangement of an existing Vedder solo composition rather than a new piece of writing, and the move is one of the few times in the catalog that Vedder has formally re-imported a solo song into the band's repertoire.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most quietly devastating pieces of writing about the end of a relationship. The narrator describes the experience of returning to an empty bed after a partner has left, framing the experience not as a tragedy but as the kind of small daily reckoning that constitutes the actual texture of grief. The song does not editorialize; it documents the moment and lets the listener observe both the loss and the slow accommodation to the loss.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Ukulele Songs version's melody and chord progression but adds a fuller rhythm section and lets the verse climb into a wider chorus than the solo version had allowed. Stone Gossard's guitar floats under the chorus rather than driving it, and McCready's solo at the song's center is melodic rather than aggressive. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed throughout, which preserves the original solo recording's intimate texture even within the band arrangement.

Live, 'Sleeping by Myself' has been a setlist regular since 2013. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its stillness can mark a deliberate pause before the closing surge. The audience response tends to be hushed during the verses and warm after, which is consistent with how Vedder's solo material has been received within Pearl Jam set contexts.

sleeping by myself.text_pt:
'Sleeping by Myself' originou-se como faixa do álbum solo de Eddie Vedder Ukulele Songs (2011), que coletou quinze peças da composição dele em torno do ukulele como instrumento central. O Pearl Jam gravou uma versão de banda da canção pra Lightning Bolt (2013), em que aparece como a décima primeira faixa do álbum. A leitura do Pearl Jam é portanto um arranjo de uma composição solo já existente de Vedder em vez de uma peça de escrita nova, e o movimento é uma das poucas vezes no catálogo em que Vedder formalmente reimportou uma música solo pra o repertório da banda.

A letra é uma das peças quietamente devastadoras de escrita de Vedder sobre o fim de uma relação. O narrador descreve a experiência de retornar a uma cama vazia depois que uma parceira foi embora, enquadrando a experiência não como tragédia mas como o tipo de pequeno acerto diário que constitui a textura de fato do luto. A canção não editorializa; documenta o momento e deixa o ouvinte observar tanto a perda quanto a acomodação lenta à perda.

O arranjo do Pearl Jam preserva a melodia e a progressão de acordes da versão de Ukulele Songs mas adiciona uma cozinha rítmica mais cheia e deixa o verso subir pra um refrão mais largo do que a versão solo havia permitido. A guitarra de Stone Gossard flutua sob o refrão em vez de conduzi-lo, e o solo de McCready no centro da música é melódico em vez de agressivo. A bateria de Matt Cameron é em vassourinhas durante toda a música, o que preserva a textura íntima da gravação solo original mesmo dentro do arranjo da banda.

Ao vivo, 'Sleeping by Myself' é regular em setlist desde 2013. A canção funciona melhor na segunda metade de um set, em que sua quietude pode marcar uma pausa deliberada antes da onda final. A resposta do público tende a ser silenciosa durante os versos e calorosa depois, o que é consistente com o jeito que o material solo de Vedder tem sido recebido dentro de contextos de set do Pearl Jam.

O vocabulário ukulele-dedilhado da canção deu ao slot uma passagem deliberadamente quieta.

wash.text:
'Wash' is one of the earliest Pearl Jam B-sides, recorded during the Ten sessions in 1991 and released in 1992 as the B-side to the 'Alive' single. The song was eventually collected on Lost Dogs (2003), which gathered the band's accumulated B-sides and outtakes into a single retrospective. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is therefore a contemporary of the entire Ten record and one of the rare Pearl Jam recordings from that era that did not make the cut for the band's debut.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most patient pieces of early-90s writing. The narrator addresses a partner with the kind of extended attention that the early Pearl Jam catalog tended to reserve for grief and political anger; the song is therefore a small departure from the prevailing emotional tone of the Ten era. Vedder has not discussed the song's specific subject in interviews, which is consistent with how he treats the most clearly autobiographical lyrics in the catalog.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most propulsive early pieces. The verse is built on a mid-tempo riff that climbs through the chorus into a wider harmonic move. McCready's solo at the song's center is melodic rather than aggressive, more in the Neil Young vein than the Hendrix one. Dave Krusen's drumming on the recording is among the most controlled of his Pearl Jam tenure.

Live, 'Wash' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since the early 1990s. The song's tempo and length make it ideal for early-set placement, where it can establish the show's emotional register without committing to a peak. Performances often extend the closing instrumental section past the studio length.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'Wash' arrived in the show's second slot as one of the rarer Ten-era B-sides the band rotates into circulation. The song's role on the Latin American Tour 2015 was structurally specific: deployed early to establish the show's deep-cut commitment. The compressed under-four-minute structure suited the slot's pacing function.
byShow.pj-2018-03-24: On 24 March 2018 at Autódromo de Interlagos (Lollapalooza Brasil 2018), 'Wash' opened the show as the rare Ten-era B-side. The choice to open a Lollapalooza headlining set with the 1991 Alive-single B-side reflected the 2018 tour's deep-cut commitment: Pearl Jam was treating festival headlining slots as an opportunity to surface material that a career-retrospective set would not include.

mountain song.text:
'Mountain Song' is the seventh track on Jane's Addiction's Nothing's Shocking (1988), the album that established the band as one of the foundational acts of the late-80s alternative rock scene. The song was written by lead singer Perry Farrell and bassist Eric Avery, and the song's bass line (built around an unusual descending figure) is one of the most identifiable instrumental motifs of late-80s American rock. The song is structurally slow and atmospheric in its opening verses before releasing into a sustained instrumental climb at its center.

Pearl Jam has covered the song occasionally since the late 1990s, and the cover has typically featured Perry Farrell himself as a guest vocalist when Farrell has been available. Vedder and Farrell have a longstanding professional relationship that dates back to the early 1990s through the Lollapalooza touring infrastructure (Farrell founded Lollapalooza in 1991), and the joint performances of 'Mountain Song' have become one of the more documented friendships in the post-grunge American rock scene.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Jane's Addiction structure but tilts the texture toward the band's own Vs.-era guitar vocabulary. Jeff Ament's bass line honors Eric Avery's original part, and Matt Cameron's drumming sustains the song's hypnotic feel without imitating Stephen Perkins's specific approach. McCready typically extends the closing instrumental section past the studio length, sometimes by several minutes.

Live, 'Mountain Song' has been an irregular but treasured setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best in the early-middle of a set, where its slow build can establish a tonal register that the rest of the show can build on. The cover's most documented performance is the Lollapalooza-era joint performance that has appeared in multiple Pearl Jam tour bootlegs.

byShow.pj-2018-03-24: On 24 March 2018 at Lollapalooza Brasil, 'Mountain Song' arrived in the show's ninth slot as the Jane's Addiction cover. The 1988 Jane's Addiction original (from Nothing's Shocking, written by Perry Farrell, Dave Navarro, Eric Avery, Stephen Perkins) sat over the festival context with the kind of cross-generational alt-rock recognition that Lollapalooza specifically invited; Lollapalooza had been Perry Farrell's invention in 1991, and playing his band's signature track at the Brazilian iteration of his festival was a structurally pointed gesture.

pulled up.text:
'Pulled Up' is the closing track of Talking Heads' debut album Talking Heads: 77 (1977), one of the foundational records of the New York post-punk scene that emerged from the CBGB ecosystem. The song was written by David Byrne and is one of the more direct pieces of writing on an album that otherwise specializes in obliqueness. The arrangement is built on a tight rhythm-section figure with Tina Weymouth's bass line carrying the song's harmonic motion and Chris Frantz's drumming holding a steady beat that contrasts the lyric's energetic tone.

Pearl Jam has covered the song occasionally since the early 2010s, and the cover is one of the rarer pieces of tribute material in the band's catalog. Talking Heads is not a band that Pearl Jam covers frequently; the choice to perform 'Pulled Up' specifically (rather than the more obvious Talking Heads anthems like 'Psycho Killer' or 'Once in a Lifetime') is therefore a deliberate gesture of lineage, signaling Pearl Jam's interest in the deeper Talking Heads catalog rather than only in the band's most-canonized material.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Talking Heads structure but tilts the texture toward the band's own guitar vocabulary. McCready's guitar tone is grittier than the original, and Matt Cameron's drumming honors Frantz's original feel without imitating it. The cover is brief and energetic, and the band does not extend the song past the original's length.

Live, 'Pulled Up' has been an irregular setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best as a punk-era pivot in encores or as a brief energy injection in the middle of a set. The cover's specific lineage (1977 New York post-punk) is probably not legible to most contemporary Pearl Jam audiences, which gives the cover a curiously private quality: those who recognize the song are receiving a deliberate signal, and those who do not are receiving a fast Pearl Jam track at full volume.

byShow.pj-2018-03-24: On 24 March 2018 at Lollapalooza Brasil, 'Pulled Up' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as the Talking Heads cover. The 1977 Talking Heads original (from Talking Heads: 77, written by David Byrne) gave the slot a New York post-punk vocabulary moment that the otherwise hard-rock-leaning setlist did not include elsewhere.

hold on.text:
'Hold On' is one of the more atmospheric Lost Dogs (2003) tracks, recorded during the Vitalogy sessions in 1994 and held off the album for tonal reasons. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the gentler pieces of writing from the mid-1990s Pearl Jam period, structured around a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure that the band rarely deployed on the harder Vs. and Vitalogy material.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more patient pieces of writing about extended struggle. The narrator addresses someone who is in a difficult moment of their life and offers the kind of counsel that recognizes the difficulty as temporary without minimizing the immediate pain. The song does not editorialize; it documents the offer of support and lets the listener observe both the gentleness and the helplessness that any such offer carries.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's quieter pieces from the Vitalogy era. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves without the kind of release that the album's harder tracks provided. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic. The song's tempo and texture are closer to Gossard's later No Code work than to anything that ended up on Vitalogy itself, which is part of why the song was held back.

Live, 'Hold On' has been an irregular but treasured setlist presence since 2003. The song works best in the encore, where its stillness can mark a deliberate pause before the closing surge. The audience response tends to be hushed during the verses and warm after.

byShow.pj-2018-03-24: On 24 March 2018 at Lollapalooza Brasil, 'Hold On' arrived in the show's seventeenth slot as the rare Lost Dogs-era track originally outtake from Vs. sessions. The Stone Gossard chromatic riff that defines the song carried its accumulated 25-year history of being held off official albums.

smile.text:
'Smile' is the fifth track on No Code (1996), and one of the most quietly devastating pieces of writing in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Jeff Ament's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written after Vedder received a postcard from Dennis Flemion of the Milwaukee band The Frogs, on which Flemion had written a brief note about wishing he were there to share a moment. The lyric is, in its most direct reading, Vedder's response to that postcard, expanded into a meditation on the small distances that separate friends.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most patient pieces of writing about long-distance friendship. The narrator addresses an absent friend, framing the absence not as a tragedy but as the kind of ordinary separation that constitutes most of any sustained relationship across decades. The song does not editorialize about how to bridge the distance; it documents the wish to be with the friend and lets the listener observe both the warmth of the wish and the impossibility of fulfilling it on demand.

The arrangement is one of Jeff Ament's most economical pieces of writing for a Pearl Jam song. The verse is built on a slow chord progression carried primarily by Ament's bass line; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that lets Vedder's harmonica enter under the second verse. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic. The song is structured for cumulative emotional weight rather than for cathartic release.

Live, 'Smile' has been a setlist regular since 1996. The song works best in the second half of a set or in the encore, where its stillness can mark a deliberate pause. The harmonica part has become one of Vedder's signature live instrumental moments, and the audience response tends to be hushed during the verses and warm after.

comfortably numb.text:
'Comfortably Numb' is the song from Pink Floyd's The Wall (1979) most often cited as the album's emotional peak, and one of the most-performed Pink Floyd songs in popular culture. The song was written by Roger Waters and David Gilmour (the only Wall track with a Gilmour co-writing credit), and the David Gilmour guitar solo at the song's center is one of the most-anthologized rock guitar performances of the late 1970s.

Pearl Jam has covered the song occasionally since the early 2000s, and the cover became more frequent in setlists during the 2010s as the band's relationship to the broader 70s rock canon became more explicit. Pink Floyd is not a band that Pearl Jam covers frequently (Mother is the only other Pink Floyd track that has appeared in any quantity), and the choice to perform 'Comfortably Numb' specifically is a deliberate gesture: the song is one of the most-known pieces of late-70s rock and the cover is therefore a contract with the audience rather than a deep cut.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Pink Floyd song structure but tilts the texture toward the band's own guitar vocabulary. McCready's solo at the song's center is the structural anchor of the cover, and his approach to the famous Gilmour solo is to honor it without imitating it. Vedder typically sings the song in a register lower than Roger Waters' original, which gives the cover a different emotional weight than the source. Matt Cameron's drumming honors Nick Mason's original part with the kind of restrained precision that the song's structure requires.

Live, 'Comfortably Numb' has been an irregular but treasured setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best in the encore, where its scale and length can carry a show home. The audience-led wordless vocal during the chorus has become one of the most reliable communal moments in any Pearl Jam show that includes the cover.

of the girl.text:
'Of the Girl' is the eighth track on Binaural (2000), one of the more harmonically unusual pieces of writing in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is built around a chord progression that draws from jazz vocabulary more than from the rock vocabulary the band typically deploys, and the result is one of the few Pearl Jam tracks that could plausibly be described as having a noir feel. The arrangement is sparse, with Stone Gossard's guitar carrying most of the harmonic motion and Matt Cameron's drumming keeping a restrained, almost shuffling tempo throughout.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more oblique pieces of writing about a romantic figure observed from outside. The narrator describes a woman whose interior life is mostly unknown to him, framing the unknowing not as a frustration but as the source of the woman's hold on his attention. The song does not editorialize about whether the unknowing is sustainable; it documents the observation and lets the music's noir texture carry the emotional content.

Vedder discussed the song in 2000 promotional interviews around Binaural as a song that came out of his interest in a particular kind of jazz-inflected songwriting that the band had not previously attempted. Stone Gossard's contribution was in adapting the jazz vocabulary into a structure the band could play live without making the song feel academically distant from rock conventions.

Live, 'Of the Girl' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2000. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow tempo can mark a tonal shift from the album's harder material. The audience response tends to be hushed during the verses and warm after, which is consistent with how Binaural's experimental tracks have been received throughout the catalog.

The slot extended the show's slow opening into a second Binaural-era track.
