dark matter.text:
'Dark Matter' is the title track of Pearl Jam's twelfth studio album, released in April 2024. The music is credited to the band collectively (Vedder, Gossard, McCready, Ament, Cameron) with co-credit to producer Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. Watt produced the entire Dark Matter album, marking the first time Pearl Jam had worked with a producer who was significantly younger than the band itself, and Watt's approach (he is known for leaning into rhythm-section punch and short, tight arrangements) shaped the entire record's sonic profile.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about cosmic-scale uncertainty as a metaphor for political and social uncertainty. The narrator uses the physics term 'dark matter' (the unknown substance that makes up most of the universe's mass) as a figure for the unseen forces that shape contemporary life, framing the unknowing not as a tragedy but as the structural condition the listener has to live inside. The song does not pretend to resolve the unknowing; it documents the condition and lets the music's velocity carry the energy.

The arrangement is one of the most propulsive pieces on the album. The verse is built on a tight rhythm-section figure that pushes the tempo forward; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through a McCready solo at the song's center. Andrew Watt's production fingerprint is most audible in the song's compression: the song reaches its argument quickly and refuses to extend itself past necessity, which is characteristic of Watt's work across his other production credits.

The song was the second single released from Dark Matter, issued in March 2024, and reached the top ten on the Billboard Mainstream Rock chart. Live, 'Dark Matter' has been a setlist regular since the Dark Matter World Tour began in 2024. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been warmed up.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Dark Matter' arrived in the show's fifteenth slot as the title track of the band's then-most-recent album (released April 2024, just over four months before the show). The song's full-band-credited composition and high-velocity riff gave the slot the kind of contemporary-anthem function that Lightning Bolt 2013's title track had served on previous tours.
byShow.pj-2024-08-31: On 31 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Dark Matter' arrived in the show's twelfth slot, deploying the title track for the second consecutive Wrigley night.

scared of fear.text:
'Scared of Fear' is the opening track of Dark Matter (2024), and the song that announces the album's tonal break from the contemplative Gigaton (2020). The music is credited collectively to the band with co-credit to producer Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was the first single released from the album, issued in February 2024, and was Pearl Jam's first new music to reach mainstream rock radio in over a decade.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about the emotional climate of the early 2020s. The narrator describes the experience of being scared not of any specific threat but of fear itself as an organizing principle of contemporary American life. The song does not engage with specific political situations; the argument is structural rather than topical, focused on the cumulative weight of living inside a culture organized around anxiety. Vedder discussed the song in 2024 promotional interviews around the Dark Matter release as a song that came out of his observations of the post-pandemic American mood.

The arrangement is one of the most aggressive pieces on Dark Matter. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward at a pace that the band had not sustained on a recording since the Vs. era. McCready's solo is short and harmonically destabilizing, which suits the lyric's posture.

Live, 'Scared of Fear' has been a setlist regular since the Dark Matter tour began. The song works as an opener or as an early-set energy injection, where its velocity can establish the show's posture. The audience response is consistent with how the band's most direct political tracks have been received: physical recognition rather than singalong attention.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Scared of Fear' arrived in the show's eighth slot as one of the Dark Matter-era tracks the 2024 tour was deploying as the band's first new material in eleven years (since Lightning Bolt 2013). The Ament-led song's compressed structure gave the slot a contemporary anchor.

waiting for stevie.text:
'Waiting for Stevie' is one of the more melodic tracks on Dark Matter (2024). The music is credited collectively to the band with co-credit to Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. The song's title references the singer-songwriter Stevie Wonder, whose late-career arc (a sustained pattern of taking long breaks between albums, with each album landing as an event rather than as a routine release) Vedder has discussed in interviews as a model the band has periodically considered for its own work.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing on Dark Matter. The narrator describes the experience of waiting for something good to arrive, framing the waiting not as an anxious state but as an honored anticipation. The song does not editorialize about whether the waiting will be rewarded; it documents the practice and lets the music's tempo carry the energy.

The arrangement is one of the album's more pop-leaning pieces. The verse is built on a clean chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a chorus designed to be sung along to. McCready's solo at the song's center is one of his most melodic on the album, more in the Tom Petty vein than the Hendrix one. Andrew Watt's production is audible in the song's hook-forward structure: the song's chorus is designed to be the part the listener remembers, and the verse exists primarily to set up the chorus.

Live, 'Waiting for Stevie' has been a setlist regular since the Dark Matter tour began. The song works in the early-middle of a set, where its warmth can land on an audience that has been warmed up by the album's harder opening tracks.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Waiting for Stevie' arrived in the show's ninth slot as another Dark Matter-era track, with Vedder's lyric a tribute to Stevie Wonder. The song's slow build into the closing chorus's anthemic release gave the slot a patient emotional climb.

wreckage.text:
'Wreckage' is the third track on Dark Matter (2024), and one of the most direct pieces of writing on the album about extended struggle and slow recovery. The music is credited collectively to the band with co-credit to Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was the third single released from Dark Matter and became one of the more critically discussed tracks on the album, partly because of the lyric's directness and partly because of the arrangement's unusual structural patience.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about looking back at a difficult period from a position of relative safety. The narrator describes the experience of surveying accumulated damage and finding the work of repair sustainable rather than overwhelming. The song does not pretend that recovery is easy; it documents the work and lets the listener observe both the difficulty and the slow accumulation of small repairs.

The arrangement is one of the album's most patient pieces. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a wider harmonic move; the chorus opens into a sustained vocal melody that lets the audience carry the section. McCready's solo at the song's center is one of his most melodic on the album. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is restrained throughout, which suits the lyric's posture of measured observation.

Live, 'Wreckage' has been a setlist regular since the Dark Matter tour began. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow build can land on an audience that has been warmed up. The audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in shows from the 2024 cycle.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Wreckage' arrived in the show's tenth slot as one of the Dark Matter-era ballads. The song's lyric (often read as a meditation on long-married endurance and mutual repair) gave the slot the kind of meditative weight the slow-tempo song demands.
byShow.pj-2024-08-31: On 31 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Wreckage' arrived in the show's ninth slot, the second consecutive Wrigley night to feature the Dark Matter ballad. The 2024 album's meditation on long-married endurance carried its emotional weight into the slot.

react respond.text:
'React, Respond' is the second track on Dark Matter (2024), one of the album's most aggressive immediate bursts. The music is credited collectively to the band with co-credit to producer Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is structurally close to the band's punk-tempo writing of the Vs. era, and its placement at track two is a sequencing argument: after the album's title-track-style opening with 'Scared of Fear,' 'React, Respond' pushes the pace further before the album allows itself any breathing room.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about the difference between automatic reaction and considered response. The narrator addresses the listener and frames the choice between reacting and responding as a moral one, suggesting that the patience required to respond rather than react is the skill that contemporary life most rewards. The song does not editorialize about what to react or respond to; the argument is structural rather than topical.

The arrangement is one of the album's most propulsive pieces. The verse is built on a tight rhythm-section figure that pushes the tempo forward; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. McCready's solo at the song's center is short and aggressive. Andrew Watt's production is audible in the song's compression: the song reaches its argument quickly and refuses to extend itself past necessity.

Live, 'React, Respond' has been a setlist regular since the Dark Matter tour began in 2024. The song works as an early-set energy injection, where its velocity can establish or maintain the show's posture. The audience response is consistent with how the band's punk-tempo Dark Matter material has been received: physical recognition rather than singalong attention.

byShow.pj-2024-08-31: On 31 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'React, Respond' arrived in the show's seventh slot as one of the Dark Matter-era propulsive tracks. The 2024 album's most explicitly punk-vocabulary song landed at the slot's pacing function: a high-velocity surge in the show's first third.

running.text:
'Running' is the eighth track on Dark Matter (2024), a sub-two-minute punk-tempo burst that is one of the shortest things on the album and one of the fastest. The music is credited collectively to the band with co-credit to Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. The song's brevity is part of its argument: Vedder has discussed the song in 2024 promotional interviews around Dark Matter as a deliberate exercise in compression, the band attempting to write a song that ends before the listener has time to settle into expectation.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about momentum as its own justification. The narrator describes the experience of moving forward at speed, framing the running not as escape from anything but as the kind of forward motion that becomes its own meaning. The song does not editorialize about whether the running has a destination; it documents the velocity and lets the music's tempo carry the energy.

The arrangement is the most punk-inflected piece on Dark Matter. The verse is built on a thrash-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus releases the verse's tension into a single sustained vocal phrase rather than into a melodic lift. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward at a pace that the band rarely sustains on a recording. McCready's solo is six bars of controlled acceleration, more in the Stooges vein than in the Hendrix vocabulary he typically deploys.

Live, 'Running' has been a setlist regular since the Dark Matter tour began. The song works as a mid-set energy burst, where its velocity can keep momentum going without committing to an extended energy investment. The audience response is consistent with how the band's shortest punk tracks tend to be received: the song ends before recognition has time to settle, and the audience reaction tends to arrive after the song is already over.

byShow.pj-2024-08-31: On 31 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Running' arrived in the show's eighth slot as another Dark Matter-era track. The compressed structure and the song's speed-of-thought lyric gave the slot continued forward motion.

upper hand.text:
'Upper Hand' is the ninth track on Dark Matter (2024), and one of the album's more harmonically expansive pieces. The music is credited collectively to the band with co-credit to Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the longest tracks on Dark Matter, and the arrangement is structured for slow build rather than for the punk-tempo compression that dominates the album's first half.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about asymmetric power. The narrator describes a relationship in which one party has accumulated unearned advantage over the other and frames the situation as the kind of structural condition that has to be recognized before it can be addressed. The song does not specify whether the relationship is romantic, political, or economic; the argument is generalized, designed to land on any listener who recognizes the pattern in their own life.

The arrangement is one of the album's most patient pieces. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a wider harmonic move; the chorus opens into a sustained vocal melody that lets the audience carry the section. McCready's solo at the song's center is one of his most expansive on the album. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is restrained throughout, which suits the lyric's posture of measured observation.

Live, 'Upper Hand' has been a setlist regular since the Dark Matter tour began. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been warmed up. The audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in shows from the 2024 cycle.

byShow.pj-2024-08-31: On 31 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Upper Hand' arrived in the show's fourteenth slot as one of the Dark Matter-era tracks the 2024 tour deployed regularly. The song's lyric (a meditation on power dynamics in long relationships) gave the slot the kind of interior weight the slow tempo demands.

wont tell.text:
'Won't Tell' is the seventh track on Dark Matter (2024). The music is credited collectively to the band with co-credit to Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the more interior pieces on Dark Matter, structured around a narrator who is keeping a secret and addresses the listener with the specific kind of restraint that secret-keeping requires.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more oblique pieces of writing on the album. The narrator describes the practice of withholding information that other people want, framing the withholding not as cruelty but as the kind of protective silence that some situations require. The song does not specify what is being withheld or why; the argument is about the practice of withholding rather than about any particular secret.

The arrangement is one of the album's more melodic pieces. The verse is built on a clean chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a chorus that opens into a wider harmonic move. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is brushed during the verses and sticked during the choruses, which is a textural shift that mirrors the lyric's movement from interior reflection to outward statement.

Live, 'Won't Tell' has been a setlist regular since the Dark Matter tour began. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its interior tone can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Won't Tell' arrived in the show's twenty-second slot as the rare Backspacer-era track. The relatively low performance count by 2024 made the slot a deep-cut surprise. The compressed structure suited the slot's pacing function: a brief Backspacer-era anchor in the late-set sequence.

setting sun.text:
'Setting Sun' is the closing track of Dark Matter (2024) and one of the most direct pieces of writing about mortality in the late Pearl Jam catalog. The music is credited collectively to the band with co-credit to Andrew Watt; the lyric is Vedder's. The song's placement at track eleven (the album's last) is a sequencing argument: after the album's accumulated material about fear, asymmetric power, and slow recovery, the closing position lets a contemplation of endings carry the album home.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentlest pieces of writing about the awareness of mortality. The narrator addresses the experience of watching a sunset and frames the daily ending as a rehearsal for the larger ending that all of life is moving toward. The song does not editorialize about how to live with this awareness; it documents the practice of watching and lets the listener observe both the gentleness of the framing and the seriousness of what is being framed. Vedder discussed the song in 2024 promotional interviews around Dark Matter as a song that came out of his own changing relationship to mortality as he reached his late fifties.

The arrangement is one of the most pared-down pieces on Dark Matter. The verse is built on a slow, finger-picked acoustic guitar figure; the band enters under the second verse but stays restrained through the bridge. McCready plays a single guitar layer that floats under the chorus rather than soloing. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed throughout. The arrangement honors the lyric's intimacy by refusing to scale up to a stadium-sized release.

Live, 'Setting Sun' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since the Dark Matter tour began. The song works best in the encore, where its stillness can mark the show's emotional pause before the closing surge. The audience response tends to be hushed during the verses and warm after, which is consistent with how the band's most patient slow material is received.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Setting Sun' arrived in the show's twenty-fourth slot as one of the Dark Matter-era tracks. The song's slow tempo and atmospheric arrangement gave the slot a meditative passage before the encore-territory anthems.
byShow.pj-2024-08-31: On 31 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Setting Sun' arrived in the show's twentieth slot as the Dark Matter-era ballad.

u.text:
'U' is one of the more obscure tracks in the Pearl Jam catalog, recorded during the Mirror Ball sessions in early 1995 (the Neil Young collaboration that produced the Mirror Ball album and the Merkin Ball EP) but ultimately not released on either project. The song was eventually collected on Lost Dogs (2003), which gathered the band's accumulated B-sides and outtakes. The music and lyric are credited to Vedder.

The song is short and atmospheric, structured around a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure with minimal additional instrumentation. The lyric is one of Vedder's most compressed pieces of writing, addressing an unnamed second-person figure with a sustained directness that the song's brevity makes more pointed rather than less. The 'U' of the title is the addressee; the song's argument is that the addressee is the entire subject, and any further specification would dilute the directness.

The arrangement reflects the Mirror Ball sessions' loose, semi-improvised aesthetic. Stone Gossard chose not to participate in the Pearl Jam-credited tracks during those sessions (his absence shaped 'I Got Id' and 'Long Road' as well), so 'U' features a band lineup that does not match the canonical Pearl Jam instrumental configuration. The recording's sparse texture is a feature rather than a limitation.

Live, 'U' has been a rare setlist presence. The song works best as a quiet moment in encores or as a Vedder-led acoustic interlude, where its brevity can mark a deliberate pause without committing to a full stylistic departure. The song's appearance in any setlist is therefore a deliberate gesture by the band rather than a routine choice.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'U' arrived in the show's fourteenth slot as the rare Lost Dogs Yield-era B-side. Vedder's twelve-minute-car-ride composition (the song was reportedly written during a single short drive in 1998) gave the slot a deep-cut surprise that fans of the Yield-Lost-Dogs era recognized immediately.

i wont back down.text:
'I Won't Back Down' is the second track on Tom Petty's first solo album Full Moon Fever (1989), and one of the most-covered songs in late-20th-century American rock. The song was co-written by Petty and Jeff Lynne (the Electric Light Orchestra leader who produced Full Moon Fever) and reached number twelve on the Billboard Hot 100 on its original release. The lyric is one of Petty's most direct statements of refusal, framed in compressed language that resists nuance in favor of stance.

Pearl Jam began performing the song with greater frequency after Tom Petty's death from cardiac arrest on October 2, 2017. Vedder's relationship to Petty was direct rather than mediated: the two had toured together (Pearl Jam opened for Petty in 2006) and Vedder had spoken about Petty's influence on his own songwriting in multiple interviews from the late 2000s onward. The cover is therefore part of an ongoing tribute, performed at most Pearl Jam shows since late 2017.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves Petty's original chord progression and tempo. The cover is brisk and direct in the way the original was, and the band does not extend the song past the original's length. McCready's solo at the song's center honors Mike Campbell's original part without imitating it. Vedder typically sings the song in a register close to Petty's original, which gives the cover a feel closer to a tribute than to a reinterpretation.

Live, 'I Won't Back Down' has been a setlist regular since 2017. The song works as an encore or as a mid-set communal moment, where its singalong chorus can land on an audience that has been warmed up. The audience-led wordless vocal during the chorus has become one of the more reliable communal moments in shows from the late 2010s and 2020s onward.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'I Won't Back Down' arrived in the show's twentieth slot as the Tom Petty cover. The 1989 Petty original (from Full Moon Fever) had become, since Petty's October 2017 death, one of the band's primary tribute vehicles. The song's seven-year tribute period by 2024 had cemented the cover as a regular late-set appearance, and the Wrigley placement gave the slot a Chicago-rock-history connection (Petty had played Wrigley's neighbor venue, the United Center, multiple times).
byShow.ev-2018-03-29: On 29 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'I Won't Back Down' arrived in the show's twenty-second slot as the Tom Petty cover. The Petty tribute (Petty had died October 2, 2017) was now in regular Vedder rotation; the SP placement continued the post-Petty-death tribute arc.

throw your arms around me.text:
'Throw Your Arms Around Me' is a song by the Australian band Hunters & Collectors, written by lead singer Mark Seymour and originally released in 1984. The song became one of the foundational pieces of Australian rock songwriting of the 1980s and has been widely covered across the English-speaking world since. Vedder began performing the song as a solo acoustic piece during Pearl Jam encores in the mid-1990s, and the cover has remained in the band's vocabulary across decades.

The lyric is one of the most direct love songs Mark Seymour wrote during the Hunters & Collectors period. The narrator addresses a partner directly and frames the act of physical embrace as the central event of a life, with everything else (work, ambition, time) arranged around the moments of holding. The song does not editorialize; it documents the centrality of the embrace and lets the listener observe both the simplicity of the framing and the depth of what is being framed.

The Pearl Jam arrangement is typically performed by Vedder solo on acoustic guitar, occasionally with band accompaniment in the song's later verses. The arrangement honors the Hunters & Collectors original's structure but preserves the song's intimate scale by refusing to extend it past necessity. Vedder typically sings the song in a register close to Seymour's original.

Live, 'Throw Your Arms Around Me' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog since the mid-1990s. The song works best as a Vedder-solo encore moment, where its quiet directness can mark a tonal pause before the show's closing surge. Audiences in Australia (where the original is well-known) and in countries where the cover has circulated through Pearl Jam bootlegs receive the song with similar attentiveness.

falling slowly.text:
'Falling Slowly' is the central song of the 2007 Irish independent film Once, written by Glen Hansard (of The Frames) and Marketa Irglova. The song won the Academy Award for Best Original Song at the 80th Academy Awards in February 2008, and Hansard and Irglova performed it during the ceremony. The song's structural simplicity (it builds slowly through a single chord progression that does not vary across the song's length) is part of its argument: the song refuses to release into the kind of cathartic peak that conventional pop ballads provide.

Vedder's relationship to Glen Hansard is one of the most documented friendships in the post-2000 acoustic-songwriter scene. The two have toured together, written together (Hansard contributed background vocals to 'Just Breathe' and other Backspacer tracks), and performed together at multiple charitable events. Vedder began performing 'Falling Slowly' as a solo acoustic piece during the late 2000s, and the cover became part of the band's encore vocabulary across the 2010s and 2020s.

The Pearl Jam arrangement is typically performed by Vedder solo on acoustic guitar, occasionally with Hansard himself when Hansard is available. The arrangement preserves the Once recording's structural patience and refuses to scale up the song's emotional content with band instrumentation. The cover's intimacy is the point.

Live, 'Falling Slowly' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best as a Vedder-solo encore moment, where its slow build can mark a deliberate emotional pause. Audiences who know the song from Once receive the cover with particular attentiveness; audiences who do not know the original receive a Vedder solo acoustic ballad whose quality lands regardless of recognition.

The song had become a Pearl Jam show staple after Vedder's friendship with Hansard developed during the Into the Wild soundtrack period; the Wrigley deployment continued the band's regular tribute to that friendship.

falling slowly.text_pt:
'Falling Slowly' é a canção central do filme independente irlandês Once (2007), escrita por Glen Hansard (do The Frames) e Marketa Irglova. A música ganhou o Oscar de Melhor Canção Original na 80ª cerimônia em fevereiro de 2008, e Hansard e Irglova a tocaram durante a cerimônia. A simplicidade estrutural da canção (ela constrói lentamente por uma única progressão de acordes que não varia ao longo da duração) é parte do argumento dela: a canção se recusa a liberar no tipo de pico catártico que baladas pop convencionais oferecem.

A relação de Vedder com Glen Hansard é uma das amizades mais documentadas na cena de compositores acústicos pós-2000. Os dois fizeram turnê juntos, escreveram juntos (Hansard contribuiu com vocais de fundo em 'Just Breathe' e em outras faixas de Backspacer) e tocaram juntos em múltiplos eventos beneficentes. Vedder começou a tocar 'Falling Slowly' como peça acústica solo no fim dos anos 2000, e o cover virou parte do vocabulário de bis da banda nos anos 2010 e 2020.

O arranjo do Pearl Jam é tipicamente executado por Vedder solo no violão, ocasionalmente com o próprio Hansard quando Hansard está disponível. O arranjo preserva a paciência estrutural da gravação de Once e se recusa a escalar o conteúdo emocional da canção com instrumentação de banda. A intimidade do cover é o ponto.

Ao vivo, 'Falling Slowly' tem sido presença regular mas não pesada em setlist no catálogo do Pearl Jam. A canção funciona melhor como momento de bis Vedder-solo, em que sua construção lenta pode marcar uma pausa emocional deliberada. Públicos que conhecem a música pelo Once recebem o cover com atenção particular; públicos que não conhecem o original recebem uma balada acústica solo de Vedder cuja qualidade aterrissa independentemente de reconhecimento.

A canção tinha virado standard em show do Pearl Jam depois que a amizade de Vedder com Hansard se desenvolveu durante o período da trilha de Into the Wild; o emprego no Wrigley deu sequência ao tributo regular da banda àquela amizade.

little wing.text:
'Little Wing' is a song by the Jimi Hendrix Experience from Axis: Bold as Love (1967), and one of the most-covered Hendrix compositions in the rock canon. The song is short (under two and a half minutes in the original recording) and structured around a chord progression that has become a kind of test piece for guitarists working in the Hendrix tradition. The studio recording's central guitar solo is one of the most-anthologized passages of Hendrix's playing.

Mike McCready's relationship to the Hendrix catalog is foundational. He has cited Hendrix as his primary influence in interviews across decades, and his playing on Pearl Jam recordings frequently quotes from Hendrix's vocabulary. 'Little Wing' has therefore become one of McCready's signature cover features, typically deployed as a tag attached to 'Yellow Ledbetter' at the close of Pearl Jam shows. The pairing is harmonically natural; both songs share a chord-progression DNA that allows McCready to slide from one into the other without a noticeable transition.

The Pearl Jam arrangement, when 'Little Wing' is deployed as a 'Yellow Ledbetter' tag, is typically a McCready-led instrumental excursion rather than a vocal performance of the Hendrix song. Vedder occasionally sings the opening verses, but the core of the cover is McCready honoring Hendrix's solo while keeping the band's rhythm-section foundation underneath. The pairing has become so associated with Pearl Jam encores that audiences in some markets explicitly listen for the 'Little Wing' tag as the signal that the show is over.

Live, 'Little Wing' has been a regular McCready-feature presence in Pearl Jam's catalog since the late 1990s. The cover almost never appears as a standalone piece; it is the closing element of the band's most-deployed encore-closer combination. The audience response is consistent with how Hendrix covers tend to be received in any country: with attentive recognition and the kind of physical stillness that demonstrates the audience knows what is happening.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Little Wing' arrived as the closing tag of the thirty-sixth slot's medley with 'Yellow Ledbetter'. The 1967 Hendrix original (from Axis: Bold as Love) is the most-quoted Hendrix piece in McCready's playing vocabulary; the explicit medley tag gave the show's final moment the Hendrix-tribute that 'Yellow Ledbetter's' DNA had been pointing toward all night. The Mineirão crowd held the closing passage as the stage lights dimmed.
byShow.pj-2024-08-31: On 31 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Little Wing' arrived as the closing tag of the twenty-fourth slot's medley with 'Yellow Ledbetter'. The 1967 Hendrix original gave the show's final moment its explicit Hendrix-tribute, closing the band's two-night Wrigley stand of summer 2024.

pendulum.text:
'Pendulum' is the seventh track on Lightning Bolt (2013), and one of the most atmospheric pieces of writing on the album. The music is credited to Stone Gossard, Mike McCready, and Jeff Ament; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is structured around a slow-rolling rhythm-section figure that creates the kind of hypnotic forward motion the song's title evokes, and the arrangement allows Vedder's vocal to float above the rhythm rather than driving against it.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more meditative pieces of writing about cyclical time. The narrator describes the experience of watching life's rhythms repeat, framing the repetition not as monotony but as the structural condition that gives any individual moment its weight. The song does not editorialize about whether the repetition can be escaped; it documents the cycles and lets the music's pendulum-like motion carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most unusual on Lightning Bolt. The verse is built on a chord progression that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through a sustained instrumental climb. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed throughout, which gives the song a textural softness unusual for the Lightning Bolt cycle.

Live, 'Pendulum' has been a setlist regular since 2013. The song works best as an opener or as an early-set tonal anchor, where its hypnotic feel can establish a register that the rest of the show can build on or depart from.

byShow.pj-2015-11-11: On 11 November 2015 at Arena do Grêmio in Porto Alegre, 'Pendulum' opened the show as one of the Lightning Bolt-era tracks the Latin American Tour 2015 was using to anchor opening sequences. The song's slow, atmospheric build (Cameron's mallet drumming, Gaspar's organ pad) gave the slot a deliberately subdued opening that contrasted with the typical high-velocity Pearl Jam show start. POA was the tour's first Brazilian date, and the choice to open with the most recent album's moodiest track signaled that this leg was going to lean heavier on Lightning Bolt material than on the catalog-wide retrospective the 2013 leg had performed. The Arena do Grêmio bootleg captures the audience settling into the song's slow climb.

long road.text:
'Long Road' is one of the two Pearl Jam tracks released as the Merkin Ball EP in late 1995, alongside 'I Got Id.' The recordings emerged from the Mirror Ball sessions with Neil Young in early 1995, and 'Long Road' is the song from those sessions that has remained most reliably in Pearl Jam's setlists across decades. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. Stone Gossard chose not to participate in the Pearl Jam-credited tracks during those sessions, so 'Long Road' features a band lineup that does not match the canonical Pearl Jam configuration; Mike McCready plays the rhythm guitar parts that Stone would normally have handled.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about endurance through grief. The narrator describes the experience of carrying a loss across a sustained period, framing the carrying as a road rather than as an event. The song does not editorialize about how to walk the road; it documents the walking and lets the music's tempo carry the meaning. Vedder discussed the song in subsequent interviews as a song that came out of his cumulative response to multiple losses in the Seattle music community during the early 1990s.

The arrangement is one of the most patient pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog from the period. The verse is built on a slow chord progression carried primarily by acoustic guitar; the band enters under the second verse but stays restrained through the bridge. McCready's solo at the song's center is melodic rather than aggressive. Jack Irons's drumming on the recording (this is one of his earliest Pearl Jam tracks before he became the band's full-time drummer for No Code) is brushed throughout.

Live, 'Long Road' has been a setlist regular since 1995. The song works best in the encore or as a tonal pause in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared. The song's performance at the September 21, 2001 'America: A Tribute to Heroes' telethon (in the wake of the September 11 attacks) is one of the most-cited Pearl Jam television performances and gave the song a permanent association with public mourning.

byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi in São Paulo, less than 24 hours after the Paris terror attacks of November 13, 'Long Road' opened the show as the kind of slow, meditative Merkin Ball-era track the band reaches for when a show needs to begin from emotional weight rather than physical energy. The Pearl Jam-Neil Young 1995 collaboration sat over the room with the specific weight the night required: Vedder wore a peace sign shirt, Ament wore an 'Unfuck the World' shirt, Cameron had drawn the Eiffel Tower on his bass drum. The Brazilian audience knew before Vedder sang a word that this would be the band's Paris-attacks show, and the slow opener gave the room space to settle into that shared knowledge.
byShow.ev-2014-05-08: On 8 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Long Road' arrived in the show's second slot as the 1995 Pearl Jam-Neil Young Merkin Ball collaboration in solo-acoustic arrangement. The song's slow build was preserved through Vedder's vocal intensity rather than band escalation.
byShow.ev-2018-03-28: On 28 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'Long Road' arrived in the show's fourth slot as the 1995 Merkin Ball Pearl Jam-Neil Young track.

love boat captain.text:
'Love Boat Captain' is the third track on Riot Act (2002), and one of the most direct pieces of writing in the Pearl Jam catalog about the Roskilde Festival tragedy. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written and recorded during the Riot Act sessions in early 2002, in the period when the band was still processing the deaths of nine fans during the band's set at the Roskilde Festival in Denmark on June 30, 2000. The song is the most explicit single text in the catalog addressing what the band experienced and what they decided to do about it.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most patient pieces of writing about institutional grief. The narrator addresses the listener directly and frames the work of recovering from collective tragedy as a practice that has to be sustained rather than completed. The song's central refrain (a counted invocation of the nine names of the people who died) was performed live by the band as a memorial element of the song before the studio recording was even released. The song therefore exists in two forms: the recorded version, which compresses the memorial element, and the live version, which extends it into the song's emotional center.

The arrangement is one of the most patient pieces on Riot Act. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through a sustained instrumental climb. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is brushed during the verses and sticked during the choruses, which is a textural shift that mirrors the lyric's movement from interior reflection to outward statement.

Live, 'Love Boat Captain' has been a setlist regular since 2002. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared. The Roskilde memorial element of the live performance has become one of the most documented communal moments in any Pearl Jam show.

byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Love Boat Captain' arrived in the show's third slot as the Riot Act-era track whose 2002 lyric (written in the immediate aftermath of Roskilde 2000, with the line 'lost nine friends we'll never know' explicitly memorializing the nine fans crushed at Roskilde) carried specific resonance on the post-Paris night. The song's structure, a slow build into the closing 'love is all you need' refrain, gave the Morumbi crowd the first sustained communal vocal moment of the night.
byShow.ev-2014-05-08: On 8 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Love Boat Captain' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as the Riot Act-era track. The song's Roskilde memorial layer (the 'lost nine friends' line) carried its 14-year-accumulated weight into the solo performance.

brain of j.text:
'Brain of J.' is the opening track of Yield (1998), one of the most propulsive album openers in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Mike McCready's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was the first thing the band recorded for Yield and is structured as a tight punk-tempo burst that announces the album's tonal break from the No Code experimental period.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more oblique pieces of writing. The 'J' of the title is generally understood to refer to John F. Kennedy and the lyric's central image (a missing brain) refers to the historical fact that Kennedy's brain was removed during his autopsy and subsequently disappeared from federal custody. The song is therefore a meditation on conspiracy, on the ways that institutional power produces the kind of unsolvable mysteries the conspiracies grow up around. Vedder discussed the song in 1998 promotional interviews around Yield as a song that came out of his interest in the cumulative effect of institutional mysteries on American political culture.

The arrangement is one of McCready's most aggressive Yield pieces. The verse is built on a punk-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves immediately back to the verse. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging. The song was produced by Brendan O'Brien, who has produced the majority of Pearl Jam's albums since Vs.

Live, 'Brain of J.' has been a setlist regular since 1998. The song works as an opener or as an early-set energy injection, where its velocity can establish or maintain the show's posture.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'Brain of J.' arrived in the show's seventh slot as the Yield-era opener (the actual track 1 of Yield 1998). The compressed under-three-minute structure and the chorus's high-velocity delivery suited the slot's pacing function.

tremor christ.text:
'Tremor Christ' is the fourth track on Vitalogy (1994), and one of the most harmonically unusual pieces of writing in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is credited to Vedder, Stone Gossard, and Jeff Ament; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is built around a chord progression that draws from non-standard rock vocabulary, with extended chords and unexpected harmonic shifts that the band rarely deployed elsewhere on Vitalogy.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most oblique pieces of writing on Vitalogy. The narrator addresses an unnamed figure (the 'tremor christ' of the title is the addressee, a figure who shakes with religious or quasi-religious conviction) and observes the figure with the kind of distance that the song's harmonic strangeness reinforces. The song does not editorialize about whether the figure's conviction is admirable or pitiable; it documents the observation and lets the music carry the ambiguity.

The arrangement is one of the most patient pieces on Vitalogy. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a McCready solo. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording (this is one of his last tracks with the band) is restrained throughout, which suits the song's posture of measured observation.

Live, 'Tremor Christ' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 1994. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its harmonic strangeness can land on an audience that has been warmed up enough to receive it. The audience response tends to be hushed during the verses and warm after.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'Tremor Christ' arrived in the show's eighth slot as the Vitalogy-era track whose structurally distinct chord progression and Vedder's low-register vocal delivery made it one of the more atmospheric pieces of the show. The Brasília placement reflected the tour's specific commitment to surfacing Vitalogy material.

getaway.text:
'Getaway' is the opening track of Lightning Bolt (2013), a brisk mid-tempo piece that announces the album's tonal break from the contemplative Backspacer (2009). The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was released as the album's third single in early 2014 and was Pearl Jam's most direct early-2010s engagement with the question of personal autonomy as a structural condition rather than as a moral choice.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about refusing other people's frameworks. The narrator describes the practice of holding to one's own beliefs in the face of social pressure, framing the holding not as defiance but as the kind of quiet maintenance that any individual life requires. The song does not specify what the beliefs are; the argument is structural, focused on the practice of holding rather than on the content of any particular position.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most economical Lightning Bolt pieces. The verse is built on a tight, mid-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a McCready solo. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging. The song was produced by Brendan O'Brien, who returned to the band for Lightning Bolt after the Backspacer cycle, and his preference for tight rhythm-section recording is audible throughout.

Live, 'Getaway' has been a setlist regular since 2013. The song works as an opener or as an early-set energy injection, where its tempo can establish or maintain the show's posture.

byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Getaway' arrived in the show's seventh slot as one of the Lightning Bolt-era tracks the Latin American Tour 2015 was deploying as mid-set anchors. The 2013 album track's compressed structure suited the slot's pacing function.

swallowed whole.text:
'Swallowed Whole' is the eighth track on Lightning Bolt (2013), and one of the more atmospheric pieces on the album. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most direct pieces of writing in the late Pearl Jam catalog about the experience of being absorbed by the natural world, particularly by the ocean (a Vedder preoccupation that runs from 'Oceans' on Ten through 'Amongst the Waves' on Backspacer and into much of his solo work).

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about ecological belonging. The narrator describes the experience of being so immersed in a natural environment that the boundary between self and environment becomes porous, framing the dissolution not as a loss of self but as an enlargement of self into the surrounding world. The song does not editorialize about whether this state is sustainable or transferable; it documents the experience and lets the music's flowing tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most patient pieces on Lightning Bolt. The verse is built on a slow chord progression carried by Stone Gossard's clean guitar; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that lets Vedder's vocal sustain across the full length of the section. McCready's solo at the song's center is melodic and restrained. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is brushed throughout.

Live, 'Swallowed Whole' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2013. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow tempo can mark a tonal shift before the closing surge.

byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Swallowed Whole' arrived in the show's fifteenth slot as one of the Lightning Bolt-era ballads the Latin American Tour 2015 had been rotating into circulation. The compressed structure suited the slot's pacing function.

i am mine.text:
'I Am Mine' is the second track on Riot Act (2002) and the album's lead single. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written in the immediate aftermath of the September 11, 2001 attacks and during the period when the band was preparing to return to touring after the Roskilde Festival tragedy of June 2000. The song is therefore written at the intersection of two of the most consequential events of the early Pearl Jam 2000s, and the lyric reflects the cumulative weight of that intersection.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct statements of personal autonomy. The narrator describes the work of holding to one's own identity in the face of cultural and political pressure to surrender it, framing the holding not as defiance but as a baseline requirement for any individual life. The song does not engage with specific political situations; the argument is generalized, designed to land on any listener whose context the song's emotional register fits. Vedder discussed the song in 2002 promotional interviews around Riot Act as a song that came out of the cumulative pressure of the post-9/11 American moment and that he wrote quickly once the lyric began to arrive.

The arrangement is one of the most propulsive pieces on Riot Act. The verse is built on a chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a wider harmonic move; the chorus opens into a sustained vocal melody that the audience can carry. McCready's solo at the song's center is one of his more melodic on the album. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward with controlled precision.

Live, 'I Am Mine' has been a setlist regular since 2002. The song works as an opener, as an early-set energy injection, or as a mid-set anchor; the band has used it in all three positions across tours.

byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'I Am Mine' arrived in the show's twenty-fourth slot as the Riot Act-era track whose 2002 lyric (written in the post-9/11 American political climate) carried renewed weight on the post-Paris night. The chorus's first-person assertion of self-ownership against external violence sat over the room with the kind of legibility that the band's original 2002 audience had not faced as directly.
byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'I Am Mine' arrived in the show's fourteenth slot as the Riot Act-era track whose post-9/11 lyric of self-ownership against external violence sustained its layered weight.
byShow.ev-2014-05-07: On 7 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'I Am Mine' arrived in the show's thirteenth slot as the Riot Act-era track in solo-acoustic arrangement.
byShow.ev-2014-05-11: On 11 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'I Am Mine' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as the Riot Act-era track.

its ok:
'It's OK' is a song by the Portland-based band Dead Moon, written by Dead Moon's frontman Fred Cole. The song appeared on the band's 1990 album Defiance and is one of the more characteristic pieces of Cole's late-career writing: a short, punk-tempo song with a single sustained refrain that became, in Dead Moon's live shows, a kind of anthem of resilience.

Pearl Jam's relationship to Dead Moon is direct. The bands shared the Pacific Northwest scene that produced both, and Vedder has spoken about Fred Cole's influence on his own approach to songwriting in multiple interviews from the late 1990s onward. Pearl Jam covered 'It's OK' as a tag attached to the closing instrumental section of 'Daughter' starting in the late 1990s, and the pairing has remained part of the band's live vocabulary across decades. The choice to use 'It's OK' as a 'Daughter' tag is harmonically natural; both songs share a chord-progression DNA that allows the band to slide from one into the other without a noticeable transition.

The Pearl Jam arrangement honors the Dead Moon original's tempo and chord progression. Vedder typically sings the song in a register close to Cole's original, and McCready's guitar tone is grittier than the Dead Moon recording's typical texture. The cover is brief (it usually adds less than a minute to the 'Daughter' performance) and structured for sustained energy rather than for cathartic release.

Live, 'It's OK' has been a regular tag for 'Daughter' in Pearl Jam shows for over two decades. The pairing has become so canonical that audiences in some markets explicitly listen for the 'It's OK' tag as the signal that the 'Daughter' performance is reaching its end. Fred Cole's death in 2017 gave the cover an additional layer of meaning as a tribute to his catalog.

all along the watchtower.text:
'All Along the Watchtower' is a song by Bob Dylan from his 1967 album John Wesley Harding, but the song is more widely known through Jimi Hendrix's cover on Electric Ladyland (1968), which transformed Dylan's sparse acoustic original into the electric rock anthem that has dominated the song's reception ever since. The Hendrix version is so canonical that Dylan himself has said in interviews that Hendrix's recording is now the version Dylan considers definitive, and Dylan has performed the song in arrangements closer to Hendrix's than to his own original since at least the 1970s.

Pearl Jam has covered the song occasionally across its career, typically deploying the Hendrix arrangement rather than the Dylan original. The choice to perform 'All Along the Watchtower' is a deliberate gesture of lineage that places the band in the Dylan-through-Hendrix songwriting tradition. The cover is therefore not just a tribute to Dylan or to Hendrix specifically but to the full chain of transformation that the song has undergone across decades.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Hendrix structure but tilts the texture toward the band's own guitar vocabulary. McCready's solo at the song's center honors Hendrix's iconic original solo without imitating it; his approach is to extend the Hendrix vocabulary into territory that Hendrix himself might have explored had he lived longer. Matt Cameron's drumming honors Mitch Mitchell's original part with the kind of restrained precision that the song's structure requires.

Live, 'All Along the Watchtower' has been an irregular but treasured setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best in the encore, where its scale and length can carry a show home. The audience response is consistent with how Hendrix covers tend to be received in any country: with attentive recognition and the kind of physical stillness that demonstrates the audience knows what is happening.

byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'All Along the Watchtower' closed the show in the thirty-third slot as the Bob Dylan original (popularized by the Hendrix 1968 cover) the band rotates into late-encore positions. The choice to deploy the Dylan/Hendrix anti-establishment classic as the show's true closer (after 'Yellow Ledbetter's' more ambiguous resolution) gave the post-Paris night a final political-vocabulary statement: the song's narrative of two riders approaching the city as the wind begins to howl carried the kind of apocalyptic weight that the news from Paris had foregrounded.

hard to imagine.text:
'Hard to Imagine' is one of the more obscure tracks in the Pearl Jam catalog, originally recorded during the Vs. sessions in 1993 and held off the album for tonal reasons. The song first appeared as a B-side to the 1996 'Lukin' single (a tour-only release that circulated in extremely limited quantity) and was eventually collected on Lost Dogs (2003), which gathered the band's accumulated B-sides and outtakes. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about anticipation and disappointment. The narrator describes the experience of holding onto an expectation through circumstances that should have erased it, framing the holding not as a failure of realism but as the kind of stubborn hope that constitutes most ongoing relationships. The song does not editorialize; it documents.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most patient pieces from the early 1990s. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure; the band enters under the second verse but stays restrained through the bridge. McCready's solo at the song's center is melodic and brief. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording is brushed throughout. The song's structural softness made it a natural exclusion from the harder Vs. album, but the same softness has given it durability across decades as a setlist alternative when the band wants to mark a tonal pause.

Live, 'Hard to Imagine' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since the late 1990s. The song works best in the encore or as a Vedder-led acoustic moment in the middle of a set, where its stillness can mark a deliberate pause.

byShow.pj-2015-11-11: On 11 November 2015 at Arena do Grêmio, 'Hard to Imagine' arrived in the show's twentieth slot as one of the rarest Pearl Jam Lost Dogs-era tracks the touring catalog has produced: originally recorded for Vs. and Vitalogy sessions, left off both, and finally released on the 1998 Chicago Cab soundtrack and 2003 Lost Dogs compilation. McCready has noted the song's title is 'frequently held up by fans' on signs at shows. The Porto Alegre placement delivered on years of accumulated audience requests.
byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome, 'Hard to Imagine' arrived in the show's twelfth slot as the rare Vs./Vitalogy outtake. McCready has noted the song's title is frequently held up by fans on signs at shows; the Amsterdam placement delivered on European audience requests.

fuckin up:
'Fuckin' Up' is the closing track of Neil Young and Crazy Horse's Ragged Glory (1990), and one of the most-played Crazy Horse-era Neil Young songs in concert. The song is structured around a sustained extended jam built on a single chord progression that does not vary across the song's length, with Young's guitar solo at the song's center extending past ten minutes in many live performances. The song became, in the early 1990s, one of Neil Young's signature anthems of self-reproach delivered at high volume.

Pearl Jam's relationship to Neil Young is foundational. The bands toured together in 1993 and 1995, Pearl Jam backed Young on the entire Mirror Ball album (1995), and Young inducted Pearl Jam into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2017. 'Fuckin' Up' has been a regular Pearl Jam cover since the mid-1990s, often performed as a tag attached to other Pearl Jam songs or as an extended encore feature when Young himself is not available to perform with the band.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Crazy Horse structure and tempo. McCready's solo at the song's center honors Young's original approach without imitating it; his vocabulary in the extended jam tends to extend Young's lines into territory that Young himself might have explored. Matt Cameron's drumming honors Crazy Horse drummer Ralph Molina's loose feel without imitating it.

Live, 'Fuckin' Up' has been an irregular but treasured setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best as an encore or as a tag attached to other songs in the late half of a set, where its sustained energy can carry a show home. The audience response is consistent with how Neil Young covers tend to be received in any country: with attentive recognition and the kind of physical engagement that demonstrates the audience knows what is happening.

imagine.text:
'Imagine' is the title track of John Lennon's 1971 solo album and one of the most-covered songs in popular music history. The song was written by Lennon and Yoko Ono and is structured around a slow piano figure that Lennon played himself on the original recording, with a vocal melody that has become one of the most familiar hooks in the late-20th-century catalog. The song's argument (a vision of a world without national, religious, or economic divisions) has remained legible across decades despite extended public debate about how literally to take Lennon's framing.

Pearl Jam has covered the song occasionally across its career, typically in moments when the cover's vision can carry specific weight. Vedder has performed the song solo on multiple occasions, most prominently at the September 21, 2001 'America: A Tribute to Heroes' telethon following the September 11 attacks. The cover became more frequent in Pearl Jam setlists during the late 2000s and 2010s as the band's relationship to its own role as a cultural institution became more sustained.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Lennon song structure. Vedder typically sings the song in a register close to Lennon's original, and the band's accompaniment is restrained, with a single piano or acoustic guitar carrying most of the harmonic motion and the rest of the band entering only in the song's later verses. The arrangement honors the original's intimacy by refusing to scale up to a stadium-sized release.

Live, 'Imagine' has been an irregular but treasured setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best in the encore or as a Vedder-solo moment in the middle of a set, where its stillness can mark a deliberate emotional pause. The audience-led wordless vocal during the chorus has become one of the more reliable communal moments in any Pearl Jam show that includes the cover.

byShow.pj-2015-11-14: On 14 November 2015 at Estádio do Morumbi, 'Imagine' arrived in the show's twenty-first slot as the night's most explicit response to the Paris attacks. The 1971 John Lennon original (Vedder had been folding the song into solo and band sets for over a decade as a pacifist gesture) sat over the Morumbi room with the specific weight the night required. During the performance, the Brazilian audience held up French flags on the venue screens, transforming the song into a transcontinental memorial for the Paris victims. The bootleg captures one of the most emotionally charged 'Imagine' renditions in the band's touring catalog.
byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Imagine' arrived in the show's twenty-first slot as the John Lennon cover. A week after the post-Paris Morumbi performance, the song's pacifist argument retained its specific weight on the BH date. The Mineirão crowd's vocal participation through the chorus sustained the volume the song's structure invites.
byShow.pj-2015-11-22: On 22 November 2015 at Maracanã, 'Imagine' arrived in the show's twenty-second slot as the John Lennon cover. Nine days after the post-Paris Morumbi performance, the song's pacifist argument retained legibility on the Rio date as the band closed the Brazilian leg.
byShow.ev-2018-03-28: On 28 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'Imagine' arrived in the show's twenty-third slot. The 2018 deployment continued Vedder's regular use of the Lennon cover as a pacifist intervention in the post-Trump-election American context.

let the records play.text:
'Let the Records Play' is the ninth track on Lightning Bolt (2013), and one of the more directly nostalgic pieces of writing on the album. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is a meditation on vinyl records as a physical and cultural object, written in the period when vinyl was experiencing its second commercial revival (the early 2010s) and when the question of how music gets consumed had become culturally legible again after a decade of mp3 dominance.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about music as a daily ritual. The narrator describes the experience of putting on a record at the end of a day and frames the practice not as nostalgia but as the kind of ongoing maintenance that any sustained relationship to music requires. The song's argument is structural rather than topical: vinyl is the example, but the ritual is the subject. This is a Vedder preoccupation that runs from 'Spin the Black Circle' on Vitalogy through this song two decades later.

The arrangement is one of Stone Gossard's most blues-inflected Lightning Bolt pieces. The verse is built on a slow chord progression carried by Gossard's slide-guitar figure; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that lets McCready solo at the song's center. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is brushed during the verses and sticked during the choruses, which is a textural shift that mirrors the lyric's movement from interior reflection to outward statement.

Live, 'Let the Records Play' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2013. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow blues feel can mark a tonal shift before the closing surge.

byShow.pj-2015-11-11: On 11 November 2015 at Arena do Grêmio, 'Let the Records Play' arrived in the show's sixteenth slot as another Lightning Bolt-era track, a Stone Gossard-led tribute to a vinyl-era listening culture. The compressed under-four-minute structure suited the slot's pacing function: a mid-set anchor in the show's Lightning Bolt-heavy second half.

my fathers son.text:
'My Father's Son' is the eleventh track on Lightning Bolt (2013), one of the darker pieces on the album. The music is Jeff Ament's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the more direct pieces of writing in the late Pearl Jam catalog about inherited damage, the patterns of behavior that pass from parent to child without anyone in the chain choosing to transmit them.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more interior pieces of writing about family. The narrator addresses an unnamed figure (the song's argument keeps the addressee deliberately ambiguous, allowing the listener to map the figure onto their own experience) and frames the inheritance of behavior patterns as a structural condition rather than as a moral failure on anyone's part. The song does not editorialize about how to break the inheritance; it documents the recognition that the inheritance exists and lets the music's tempo carry the emotional weight.

The arrangement is one of Jeff Ament's most propulsive Lightning Bolt pieces. The verse is built on a tight rhythm-section figure carried primarily by Ament's bass line; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a McCready solo. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging.

Live, 'My Father's Son' has been a setlist regular since 2013. The song works best in the early-middle of a set, where its weight can establish a tonal register without committing to a peak.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'My Father's Son' arrived in the show's thirteenth slot as one of the Lightning Bolt-era tracks the Latin American Tour 2015 was deploying as deep-cut anchors. The song's narrative (a son inheriting his father's psychological weight, in dialogue with the broader Vedder catalog of father-themed material from 'Alive' onward) carried its accumulated weight into the 2015 performance.

in my tree.text:
'In My Tree' is the fourth track on No Code (1996), and one of the more harmonically distinctive pieces of writing in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is credited to Mike McCready, Jeff Ament, and Jack Irons; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is structured around an extended polyrhythmic figure that Jack Irons developed during the No Code sessions, and the rhythmic complexity of the recording is one of the things that made the song stand out on an album of stylistic experiments.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more contemplative pieces of writing about retreating from cultural pressure. The narrator describes the practice of climbing into a tree to find perspective, framing the climb not as escapism but as the kind of structural distance that any sustained engagement with the world requires. The song does not editorialize about whether the perspective gained from the tree is transferable back to the ground; it documents the climb and lets the music's polyrhythmic feel carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most rhythmically unusual on No Code. The verse is built on a polyrhythmic figure that Jack Irons sustains throughout the song; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a McCready solo. The song's complexity made it difficult to translate to live performance with subsequent drummers, and the song appeared more rarely in setlists after Matt Cameron joined the band in 1998. Recent performances have restored the song to regular rotation.

Live, 'In My Tree' has been a regular but irregular setlist presence since 1996. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its rhythmic complexity can land on an audience that has been warmed up enough to follow the song's structural argument.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'In My Tree' arrived in the show's ninth slot as the No Code-era track distinguished by Jack Irons's polyrhythmic drumming pattern (though Cameron now plays the live arrangement). The song's lyric about retreat and self-protection sat over the show's mid-section weight with the kind of meditative pause the slot demanded.

rain.text:
'Rain' is a Beatles song originally released in 1966 as the B-side of the 'Paperback Writer' single. The song was written by John Lennon and Paul McCartney (with Lennon receiving primary credit) and is one of the foundational pieces of Beatles psychedelia, predating Revolver by a few months and pointing toward the experimental direction the band would take across the next two years. The song's central technical innovation, the backwards vocal track that closes the recording, was one of the first uses of tape reversal in mainstream pop and influenced an entire decade of subsequent psychedelic recording.

Pearl Jam has covered the song occasionally across its career. The choice is unusual; The Beatles is not a band that Pearl Jam covers frequently, and the choice to perform 'Rain' specifically (rather than the more obvious Beatles anthems) is a deliberate gesture of lineage that places the band in the Lennon-influenced songwriting tradition. The cover is therefore a tribute to a specific Lennon recording rather than to the Beatles catalog generally.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Beatles song structure but tilts the texture toward the band's own guitar vocabulary. McCready's guitar tone is grittier than Harrison's original, and Matt Cameron's drumming honors Ringo Starr's distinctive tom-heavy original part with restrained precision. The cover does not include the backwards vocal coda of the original.

Live, 'Rain' has been an irregular setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best as a mid-set tonal pivot, where its psychedelic feel can disrupt the canonical Pearl Jam pacing without committing to an extended energy investment.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'Rain' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as the Beatles cover the band had been folding into Latin American Tour 2015 setlists. The 1966 Beatles original (B-side of Paperback Writer, written by John Lennon) gave the slot a psychedelic-era pulse that the otherwise hard-rock-leaning setlist did not offer elsewhere.
byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão in Belo Horizonte, 'Rain' opened the show as the Beatles cover (1966 B-side of Paperback Writer, written by John Lennon). The unusual choice of opener established the show's commitment to deep-cut covers; BH was the fourth Brazilian date of the tour, and the band was visibly leaning into rare material for the late-leg shows.

redemption song.text:
'Redemption Song' is the closing track of Bob Marley and the Wailers' Uprising (1980), the last studio album Marley released before his death in May 1981. The song was performed by Marley alone on acoustic guitar, a stylistic departure from the rest of the Wailers catalog and one of the few times Marley recorded a song without his band's full instrumental presence. The lyric draws explicitly from a 1937 speech by the Jamaican Pan-African leader Marcus Garvey, framing the song's call for self-emancipation as part of a longer Black political tradition.

Pearl Jam has covered the song with some regularity since the early 2000s, and Vedder has frequently performed the song as a Vedder-solo acoustic moment in the encore. The choice to cover Marley specifically (rather than other late-70s acoustic singer-songwriters from the broader reggae or singer-songwriter traditions) is a deliberate gesture: Marley is one of the few figures in 20th-century popular music whose political lyrics achieved both mass commercial reach and sustained moral seriousness, and the cover honors that achievement.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Marley original's structure. Vedder typically performs the song solo on acoustic guitar, occasionally with band accompaniment in the song's later verses. The arrangement honors the original's intimate scale by refusing to expand the song into the kind of full-band reading that would dilute the lyric's directness. Vedder typically sings the song in a register close to Marley's original.

Live, 'Redemption Song' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best as a Vedder-solo encore moment, where its quiet directness can mark a deliberate emotional pause before the show's closing surge. Audiences in countries where Marley's catalog has deep cultural reach receive the cover with particular attentiveness.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'Redemption Song' arrived in the show's twentieth slot as the Bob Marley cover. The 1980 Marley original (from Uprising, the last album Marley released before his 1981 death) gave the slot a Caribbean-leaning acoustic moment that the otherwise hard-rock-leaning setlist did not include elsewhere. Vedder's performance preserved the original's solo-acoustic intimacy.

leash.text:
'Leash' is the eleventh track on Vs. (1993), and the song that immediately precedes 'Indifference' as the album's penultimate cut. The music is credited to Stone Gossard and Mike McCready; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is the spiritual sequel to 'Why Go' on Ten, addressing the same young woman whose involuntary psychiatric institutionalization the earlier song had documented. By the time of Vs., the woman had been released from the institution but was, by Vedder's account in interviews from the 1993 promotional cycle, still under significant parental control. 'Leash' is the song addressing that continued control directly.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct anthems of generational refusal. The narrator addresses an unspecified authority figure (parents, institutions, anyone exercising unearned control over a young person's life) and demands the release of the controlled. The song's central refrain is a sustained command to drop the leash, delivered at full volume and without the kind of nuance that the band's slower material typically requires. The song is therefore one of the few Pearl Jam tracks structured entirely around a single uncomplicated demand.

The arrangement is one of the most aggressive pieces on Vs. The verse is built on a tight, mid-tempo riff that climbs through the chorus into a wider harmonic move; the closing instrumental section extends past the studio length on most live performances. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording is among the most physical of his Pearl Jam tenure. McCready's solo at the song's center is short and aggressive.

Live, 'Leash' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 1993. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its anger can land on an audience that has been warmed up. The audience-led wordless vocal during the chorus has become one of the more reliable communal moments in shows that include the song.

byShow.pj-2015-11-17: On 17 November 2015 at Mané Garrincha, 'Leash' arrived in the show's twenty-sixth slot as the Vs.-era anti-authoritarian track. The song's chorus ('Drop the leash, drop the leash, get out of my fucking face') gave the slot the kind of compressed Vs.-era aggression the late-set sequence required.

crazy mary.text:
'Crazy Mary' is a song by the singer-songwriter Victoria Williams, originally released on her 1987 album Happy Come Home. The song became culturally legible to a much wider audience in 1993 when Pearl Jam covered it for the multi-artist tribute compilation Sweet Relief: A Benefit for Victoria Williams. Williams had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1992 and the Sweet Relief project was organized to fund her medical care; the album collected covers of Williams's songs by major rock acts of the early 1990s, and Pearl Jam's version of 'Crazy Mary' became the album's most-played track.

The lyric is one of Williams's most patient pieces of writing about a marginalized figure observed from outside. The narrator describes Mary, a woman who lives apart from her community and whose interior life remains opaque to the people around her, framing the observation with the kind of attentive empathy that Williams brought to most of her writing. The song does not editorialize about Mary's circumstances; it documents her existence and lets the listener observe both the gentleness of the framing and the seriousness of what the song is asking the listener to consider.

The Pearl Jam arrangement extended the Williams original significantly. The cover runs over six minutes (the original is under five) and the closing instrumental section, with McCready's solo extending past the studio length, has become one of the cover's defining features. Victoria Williams herself has joined Pearl Jam on stage for the song on multiple occasions, and the live performance with Williams present has become one of the documented inter-artist collaborations of Pearl Jam's career.

Live, 'Crazy Mary' has been a regular setlist presence since 1993. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow build can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared. The audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in shows that include the song.

byShow.pj-2011-11-11: On 11 November 2011 at Estádio Beira-Rio, 'Crazy Mary' arrived in the show's twenty-seventh slot as the Victoria Williams cover the band had been folding into setlists since the 1993 Sweet Relief: A Benefit For Victoria Williams compilation. The song's role in 2010s Pearl Jam shows is structurally distinct: it functions as a vehicle for extended improvisation by Boom Gaspar (keys) and Mike McCready (guitar), and the Beira-Rio bootleg captures one of the longer improvisation sections the song received on the 2011 Brazilian leg.
