The Brasília bootleg captures one of the longer improvisation sections the song received on the 2015 leg.

sometimes.text:
'Sometimes' is the opening track of No Code (1996), and one of the gentlest album openers in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is also Vedder's. The song is a deliberate departure from the band's previous album-opener strategy: where 'Once' opened Ten and 'Go' opened Vs., 'Sometimes' opens No Code with a hushed acoustic figure that does not allow the listener any expectation of immediate velocity. The choice was a sequencing argument that announced No Code's tonal break from the band's prior work.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more meditative pieces of writing about uncertainty. The narrator describes the practice of holding to a sense of self while acknowledging that the self is changing in ways the narrator does not yet understand. The song does not editorialize; it documents the practice of holding and lets the music's restraint carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most stripped pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog. The verse is built on a single chord progression that does not vary; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves without the kind of release the band's harder material typically delivers. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and brief. Jack Irons's drumming on the recording is brushed throughout.

Live, 'Sometimes' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 1996. The song works best as an opener (the band has used it in this position throughout the No Code touring cycle and beyond) or as a tonal pause in the middle of a set, where its quiet directness can mark a deliberate emotional shift.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Sometimes' arrived in the show's second slot as the No Code-era opener (the actual track 1 of No Code, 1996). The compressed under-three-minute structure with Vedder's hushed vocal delivery sat over the slow opening with the kind of interior weight the song's lyric demands.
byShow.ev-2014-05-06: On 6 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Sometimes' arrived in the show's seventh slot as the No Code-era opener, in solo-acoustic arrangement. The song's hushed intimate vocal delivery translated naturally to the solo format.
byShow.ev-2014-05-08: On 8 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Sometimes' arrived in the show's fourth slot as the No Code-era opener in solo-acoustic arrangement.
byShow.ev-2014-05-11: On 11 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Sometimes' arrived in the show's third slot as the No Code-era opener in solo arrangement.
byShow.ev-2018-03-28: On 28 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'Sometimes' arrived in the show's sixth slot.

pilate.text:
'Pilate' is the eleventh track on Yield (1998). The music is Jeff Ament's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the more obscure pieces of writing on Yield and one of the few Pearl Jam tracks named for a specific historical figure (Pontius Pilate, the Roman prefect of Judea who presided over the trial of Jesus). The choice of name signals the song's central preoccupation with the moral weight of executive decisions made under political pressure.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more oblique pieces of writing about complicity. The narrator does not directly identify with Pilate; the song's argument is structural, focused on the kind of position Pilate occupied (a person with the authority to refuse a request that all the available political pressure was urging the person to grant) and on what such positions reveal about the people who occupy them. The song does not editorialize about whether Pilate could have refused; it documents the position and lets the listener observe both the freedom and the trap that such positions contain.

The arrangement is one of Jeff Ament's most economical pieces of Yield writing. The verse is built on a slow chord progression carried primarily by Ament's bass line; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a brief McCready solo. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is restrained throughout, which suits the song's posture of measured observation.

Live, 'Pilate' has been a rare setlist presence since 1998. The song's specific subject matter and harmonic restraint make it difficult to deploy in shows where the audience is expecting more direct material, and the band has historically reserved the song for moments when its weight can land.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Pilate' arrived in the show's ninth slot as the Yield-era deep cut. The compressed under-four-minute structure suited the slot's pacing function: a Yield-era anchor in the show's mid-set.
byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome, 'Pilate' arrived in the show's eighth slot as the Yield-era deep cut.

infallible.text:
'Infallible' is the sixth track on Lightning Bolt (2013), one of the more directly political pieces of writing on the album. The music is credited to Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is a sustained address to a worldview that treats human institutions as capable of being permanently right, and the lyric's argument is that the worldview produces the conditions for its own catastrophic failure.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about the structural problems with certainty. The narrator addresses an unnamed but recognizable target (institutions that claim infallibility, people who refuse to acknowledge error, systems that punish the acknowledgment of mistakes) and frames the targets' refusal as the source of accumulated damage. The song does not specify which institutions are being addressed; the argument is generalized, designed to land on any listener who recognizes the pattern.

The arrangement is one of the most propulsive pieces on Lightning Bolt. The verse is built on a tight rhythm-section figure that pushes the tempo forward; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through a McCready solo. Matt Cameron's drumming pushes the tempo forward without flagging.

Live, 'Infallible' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2013. The song works best in the early-middle of a set, where its political velocity can establish a posture that the rest of the show can build on.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Infallible' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as one of the Lightning Bolt-era tracks the Latin American Tour 2015 was deploying as deep-cut anchors. The song's lyric (a meditation on certainty and its absence in political leadership) sat over the show's mid-section weight.

im open.text:
'I'm Open' is the twelfth track on No Code (1996) and one of the most stylistically unusual pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is credited to Jack Irons and Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is structured as spoken word over a slow ambient instrumental backing rather than as a sung track, which makes it one of the few Pearl Jam recordings to refuse the basic vocal conventions of rock songwriting.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about the practice of remaining open to experience. The narrator describes the difficulty of refusing the kind of protective closure that long exposure to disappointment encourages, framing openness as a discipline rather than as a default state. The song does not editorialize about how to maintain the discipline; it documents the work and lets the music's ambient backing carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most experimental on No Code. The instrumental backing is built around Jack Irons's percussive figure and a single sustained chord that does not resolve across the song's length. The recording's spoken-word vocal places the song closer to the spoken-word tradition of the early-90s alternative scene (Henry Rollins's spoken-word work is the most cited reference) than to anything Pearl Jam had attempted before or has attempted since.

Live, 'I'm Open' has been a rare setlist presence since 1996. The song's stylistic departure from the band's standard rock vocabulary makes it difficult to deploy in shows where the audience is expecting conventional Pearl Jam material, and the band has historically reserved the song for moments when its experimental feel can land.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'I'm Open' arrived in the show's thirteenth slot as one of the rarest No Code-era spoken-word pieces in the touring catalog. The track's Vedder-narrated meditation on receptivity gave the slot a structurally distinct interlude that the show's mid-section accommodated.

satans bed.text:
'Satan's Bed' is the seventh track on Vitalogy (1994), one of the more aggressive pieces of writing on the album. The music is credited to Stone Gossard, Jeff Ament, and Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the most direct pieces of writing in the early Pearl Jam catalog about refusing to be co-opted, framed in compressed punk-tempo language that resists nuance in favor of stance.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct refusals of the kind of cultural absorption the band was being subjected to during the Vitalogy period. The narrator addresses an unspecified force (industry, fame, fans who project unwanted expectations onto the artist) and refuses the absorption with the kind of compressed anger that the song's tempo reinforces. The song does not editorialize; it documents the refusal and lets the music's velocity carry the energy.

The arrangement is one of the most aggressive pieces on Vitalogy. The verse is built on a thrash-tempo riff that does not vary; the chorus releases the verse's tension into a sustained scream rather than a melodic lift. Dave Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording is among the most physical of his Pearl Jam tenure.

Live, 'Satan's Bed' has been a rare setlist presence since 1994. The song's tempo and emotional density make it difficult to deploy in shows where the audience is expecting slower material, and the band has historically reserved the song for moments when its anger can land. The song's appearance in any setlist is therefore a deliberate gesture by the band rather than a routine choice.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Satan's Bed' arrived in the show's fifteenth slot as the Vitalogy-era track whose 1994 lyric (an explicit refusal of celebrity-culture compromises) remained legible in 2015. The compressed structure suited the slot's pacing function.

oceans.text:
'Oceans' is the seventh track on Ten (1991), and one of the most stylistically distinctive pieces on the album. The music is credited to Stone Gossard, Jeff Ament, and Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is the only acoustic-driven moment on Ten and one of the few pieces of writing on the album that does not engage with trauma, institutional violence, or political grief. It is a love song, and the unusual position of being the album's only love song gives the recording a tonal weight that the song's brief duration would not otherwise carry.

The lyric is one of Vedder's earliest pieces of writing about Beth Liebling, his then-girlfriend (later wife from 1994 to 2000). The narrator addresses Liebling across geographic distance, framing the ocean between San Diego (where Vedder had been living) and Seattle (where the band was now based) not as a barrier but as the connective element of the relationship. Vedder's lifelong relationship to surfing is the implicit context for the song's central image; the ocean is something he literally lives in for parts of every year, and the lyric draws from that lived experience rather than from metaphor alone.

The arrangement is the most stripped piece on Ten. The verse is built on a single acoustic guitar figure that Stone Gossard plays under Vedder's vocal, with Jeff Ament's bass entering only in the song's later verses. Tim Palmer's mixing of the recording incorporated the now-famous fire-extinguisher percussion, one of the most-cited unconventional production choices in early-90s rock recording. The song's brevity (under three minutes) and structural restraint make it the album's deliberate moment of quiet.

Live, 'Oceans' has been a rare setlist presence since 1991. The song's stylistic departure from the rest of the Ten material makes it difficult to deploy in shows where the audience is expecting the album's harder catalog, and the band has historically reserved the song for moments when its quietness can land. The song's appearance in any setlist is therefore a deliberate gesture by the band rather than a routine choice.

byShow.pj-2011-11-11: On 11 November 2011 at Estádio Beira-Rio, 'Oceans' arrived in the show's nineteenth slot as one of the Ten-era ballads the Pearl Jam Twenty Tour had been pulling into circulation as part of the catalog-wide retrospective the tour was performing. The song (one of the gentlest tracks on the band's debut album, written about Vedder's relationship with surfing as a stabilizing presence in his early life) sat well in slot 19's pacing function: an emotional reset that deepened the show's mid-set weight. The Beira-Rio bootleg captures the kind of sustained quiet that the song's verse demands.
byShow.pj-2015-11-22: On 22 November 2015 at Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro, 'Oceans' opened the show as the slow Ten-era ballad. The Maracanã was the tour's last Brazilian date and one of the largest stadiums on the leg, and the choice to open with the gentlest track on the band's debut album (written about Vedder's relationship with surfing as a stabilizing presence) established the show's deliberate slow opening. The bootleg captures the Rio crowd settling into the song's atmospheric build.

who you are.text:
'Who You Are' is the third track on No Code (1996) and the album's lead single. The music is credited to Vedder and Jack Irons; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was the public announcement of No Code's tonal break from the band's prior work, structured around an Eastern-influenced rhythmic figure (Jack Irons's drum part draws from the tabla and frame-drum vocabulary that Irons had been studying) and a vocal melody that floats above the rhythm rather than driving against it.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more meditative pieces of writing about identity. The narrator addresses the listener and frames the work of becoming oneself as a practice rather than as a destination. The song's central refrain (a sustained address to who the listener is) carries the argument by repetition rather than by elaboration. Vedder discussed the song in 1996 promotional interviews around No Code as a song that came out of his interest in non-Western musical and meditative traditions during the mid-1990s.

The arrangement is the most stylistically unusual on No Code. The verse is built on Jack Irons's tabla-influenced drum figure with Stone Gossard's clean guitar floating above it; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through a McCready solo carried by an unusual guitar tone. The song was Pearl Jam's first single from a non-Brendan O'Brien-produced album (No Code was produced by Pearl Jam with Brendan O'Brien, but the song's production aesthetic is closer to the band's own preferences than to O'Brien's typical approach).

Live, 'Who You Are' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 1996. The song works best in the early-middle of a set, where its rhythmic distinctiveness can establish a tonal register without committing to a peak.

byShow.pj-2015-11-22: On 22 November 2015 at Maracanã, 'Who You Are' arrived in the show's tenth slot as the No Code-era opener (the actual track 1 of No Code, 1996). The song's distinctive Jack-Irons-influenced rhythm pattern (now executed by Cameron) gave the slot a structurally distinct mid-set anchor.

yellow moon.text:
'Yellow Moon' is the seventh track on Lightning Bolt (2013), one of the most patient pieces of writing on the album. The music is Jeff Ament's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the more atmospheric pieces in the late Pearl Jam catalog, structured around a slow chord progression that the band lets sustain across the song's length without releasing into the kind of cathartic climb the album's harder tracks deliver.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about transitions. The narrator describes the experience of standing at a moment of change, framing the change not as an event to fear but as the kind of natural transition that the cycles of the moon themselves model. The song does not editorialize about how to greet the change; it documents the moment and lets the music's slow tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of Jeff Ament's most economical Lightning Bolt pieces. The verse is built on a slow chord progression carried primarily by Ament's bass line; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that lets Vedder's vocal sustain across the full length of the section. McCready's solo at the song's center is restrained and melodic. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is brushed throughout.

Live, 'Yellow Moon' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2013. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow tempo can mark a tonal shift before the closing surge.

byShow.pj-2015-11-22: On 22 November 2015 at Maracanã, 'Yellow Moon' arrived in the show's nineteenth slot as one of the Lightning Bolt-era deep cuts. The song's Stone Gossard-led arrangement gave the slot a structurally distinct mid-set passage. The Maracanã placement made this one of the rarer slot-19 deployments of the song on the 2015 tour.

mankind.text:
'Mankind' is the eighth track on No Code (1996), and one of the most unusual pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog because it features Stone Gossard, rather than Eddie Vedder, as the lead vocalist. The music and lyric are credited to Stone Gossard, who has only rarely sung lead on Pearl Jam recordings (and almost never in the band's live shows). The song was Stone's most public lead-vocal contribution to a Pearl Jam album and is one of the few moments in the band's catalog where the vocal voice is not the voice the audience associates with Pearl Jam.

The lyric is one of Stone Gossard's more direct pieces of writing about how individual people can lose themselves in collective behavior. The narrator describes the practice of holding onto individual judgment within crowd dynamics, framing the holding as the kind of small daily resistance that any sustained ethical life requires. The song does not editorialize; it documents the practice and lets the music's pop-tempo arrangement carry the energy.

The arrangement is one of the most pop-leaning pieces on No Code. The verse is built on a bright chord progression that climbs through the chorus into a wider harmonic move; the song's tempo and vocal feel are closer to power-pop than to the band's typical rock vocabulary. Jack Irons's drumming on the recording sustains the song's bright feel throughout.

Live, 'Mankind' has been a rare setlist presence since 1996. The song's vocal arrangement (Stone Gossard would have to sing lead in any live performance, which is something he has been reluctant to do consistently) makes it difficult to deploy in regular rotation. Performances of the song are therefore a deliberate gesture by the band when Stone is willing to take the vocal spot.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Mankind' arrived in the show's twenty-sixth slot as the rare No Code-era Stone Gossard-led track (Gossard sings lead vocal on the studio version, and the band rotates the song into setlists when they want to feature Gossard's vocal). The Mineirão placement gave the slot the kind of structural surprise that deep-cut deployments invite.
byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome, 'Mankind' arrived in the show's tenth slot as the rare Stone Gossard-led vocal track.

bee girl.text:
'Bee Girl' is one of the more obscure tracks in the Pearl Jam catalog, originally released in 1994 as the B-side to the 'Daughter' single and eventually collected on Lost Dogs (2003). The music and lyric are credited to Vedder. The song is brief (under two and a half minutes) and acoustic-driven, structured as a conversational direct address rather than as a conventional sung lyric. The 'bee girl' of the title refers to the dancing girl in a bee costume from Blind Melon's 1992 'No Rain' music video, who became one of the most-discussed visual figures in early-90s alternative rock culture.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about how individual people get caught in cultural attention they did not seek. The narrator addresses the bee girl directly and frames her viral fame not as an opportunity but as the kind of sudden public attention that distorts the life of the person receiving it. Vedder had developed a particular sympathy for figures whose private lives had been disrupted by mainstream attention (the band's own experience with Time magazine and similar coverage informed this sympathy), and the song extends that sympathy to a young figure who had not chosen her own celebrity.

The arrangement is one of the most stripped pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog. The recording is essentially Vedder solo on acoustic guitar, with minimal additional instrumentation. The song's brevity and structural simplicity make it closer to a postcard than to a conventional song, which is part of why it was held off Vitalogy and released as a B-side rather than as an album track.

Live, 'Bee Girl' has been a rare setlist presence since 1994. The song works best as a Vedder-solo encore moment, where its brevity can mark a deliberate quiet pause. The song's appearance in any setlist is a deliberate gesture by the band rather than a routine choice.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Bee Girl' arrived in the show's nineteenth slot as one of the rarest tracks in the band's touring catalog: the live Rockline 1993 acoustic performance about Heather DeLoach (the bee-suited girl in Blind Melon's 'No Rain' video). The studio-acoustic delivery reduced to Vedder solo gave the slot a deeply intimate moment that the Mineirão crowd received with sustained mid-show quiet.

i want you so hard (bad boy news):
'I Want You So Hard (Boy's Bad News)' is the opening track of Eagles of Death Metal's third album Heart On (2008). The song was written by Jesse Hughes and Josh Homme, the two principals of the band, and is one of the more straightforward pieces of writing in the Eagles of Death Metal catalog (a project whose work otherwise tends toward tongue-in-cheek camp). The track is built around a sustained Hughes vocal that climbs across a tight, mid-tempo riff, and the song's structural simplicity is part of its appeal.

Pearl Jam began performing the song in the early 2010s, and the cover became a regular setlist presence during the Lightning Bolt touring cycle of 2013 to 2015. The choice to cover Eagles of Death Metal specifically reflects the friendships that connect the contemporary American hard-rock scene: Josh Homme has collaborated with Pearl Jam members on multiple occasions, and the cover is therefore part of an ongoing musical conversation rather than a tribute to a band Pearl Jam encountered only through recordings.

The Pearl Jam arrangement preserves the Eagles of Death Metal structure but tilts the texture toward the band's own guitar vocabulary. McCready's guitar tone is grittier than Hughes's original, and Matt Cameron's drumming honors Joey Castillo's original part with the kind of restrained precision that the song's structure requires. Vedder typically sings the song in a register close to Hughes's original.

Live, 'I Want You So Hard (Boy's Bad News)' has been an irregular but treasured setlist presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The song works best in the encore or as a punk-tempo pivot in the late half of a set, where its velocity can carry a show home.

eruption.text:
'Eruption' is the second track on Van Halen's self-titled debut album (1978), an instrumental guitar showcase performed by Eddie Van Halen alone. The recording is one minute and forty-two seconds long and is structured entirely around Van Halen's solo guitar performance, with no vocal element and no other band instrumentation. The track became one of the most influential pieces of guitar writing of the late 20th century, primarily for its display of the two-handed tapping technique that Van Halen would popularize through subsequent recordings and that would shape the entire generation of rock guitarists who came of age in the 1980s.

Mike McCready's relationship to the Van Halen catalog is as deep as his relationship to the Hendrix catalog, although McCready has spoken about Van Halen less frequently in interviews. McCready learned to play 'Eruption' as a teenager (this is something he has confirmed in multiple guitar-magazine interviews from the 1990s and 2000s) and the piece has remained part of his core technical vocabulary across decades. Pearl Jam's performances of 'Eruption' are therefore essentially McCready solo features, with the rest of the band stepping back to give him the space the original recording required.

The Pearl Jam arrangement is essentially McCready performing the original alone, with the rest of the band entering only at the song's close to provide a transition into whatever song follows. The cover is brief (it does not extend past the original's length) and structured as the kind of guitar feature that has become rare in mainstream rock since the 1990s.

Live, 'Eruption' has been a rare McCready-feature presence in Pearl Jam's catalog. The cover almost never appears as a standalone piece; it is typically deployed as an introductory segment to another song or as a mid-set transition. Eddie Van Halen's death in October 2020 gave subsequent performances of the cover an additional layer of meaning as a tribute.

byShow.pj-2015-11-20: On 20 November 2015 at Mineirão, 'Eruption' arrived in the show's twenty-eighth slot as the Van Halen instrumental cover, an extremely rare appearance that gave McCready a brief showcase of solo-guitar virtuosity in the Eddie Van Halen vocabulary. The 1978 Van Halen original (released the day after Eddie Van Halen turned 23) provided the slot a twentieth-century guitar-history reference point.

tuolumne.text:
'Tuolumne' is the opening track of Eddie Vedder's solo soundtrack album for Sean Penn's 2007 film Into the Wild. The piece is an instrumental performed by Vedder alone on acoustic guitar; there is no vocal element and no other instrumentation. The title refers to Tuolumne Meadows, a high-altitude alpine area in Yosemite National Park that the film's central figure Chris McCandless visits during his journey toward Alaska. The instrumental places the listener in that landscape before Vedder's vocal material begins to address McCandless's story directly.

The piece is brief (under two minutes) and is structured as a single rolling figure that does not vary across its length. The musical vocabulary draws openly from the John Fahey and Leo Kottke American Primitivism tradition of solo acoustic guitar composition, a tradition that Vedder had been studying privately for years before the Into the Wild commission gave him a public reason to deploy it. The piece is therefore one of the few pieces of writing in Vedder's catalog that engages explicitly with American instrumental traditions outside of rock.

Live, 'Tuolumne' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2008. The piece works best as an opener, where its meditative feel can settle a venue before the vocal material begins. Vedder typically performs the piece without speaking to the audience first, which gives the moment the kind of ceremonial weight that a deliberately wordless opening allows.

byShow.ev-2014-05-06: On 6 May 2014 at Citibank Hall in São Paulo, 'Tuolumne' opened the show as the Into the Wild instrumental. Vedder typically opens solo shows with the soundtrack's instrumental ukulele piece (named after the river running through Yosemite National Park where part of Christopher McCandless's story takes place); the Citibank opening followed that convention. The show was a late addition to the Brazilian leg (originally the run was May 7-9), with Glen Hansard opening, and the slow ukulele instrumental established the solo show's intimate seated-venue aesthetic.

The second night of the SP residency followed the same opening structural template as night 1 (May 6 was the late-added show).

long nights.text:
'Long Nights' is the seventh track on Eddie Vedder's Into the Wild soundtrack (2007), and one of the more melodically expansive pieces on the album. The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is also Vedder's. The song appears in the Into the Wild film during a sequence where Chris McCandless is reflecting on the people he has met during his journey, and the song's emotional register matches that reflective moment in the film's narrative.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about cumulative experience. The narrator describes the pattern of long nights spent thinking through the events of a recent stretch of life, framing the practice not as anxious but as the kind of ongoing accounting that any reflective life requires. The song does not editorialize about whether the accounting reaches conclusions; it documents the practice and lets the music's slow tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the more layered pieces on Into the Wild. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure that Vedder plays under his own vocal, with additional instrumentation entering only in the song's later verses. The recording features Glen Hansard (the Irish singer-songwriter Vedder had become friends with during the period) on background vocals, and Hansard's contribution gives the song a layered vocal feel that the rest of the soundtrack does not have.

Live, 'Long Nights' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2008. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow build can mark a tonal shift before the closing surge.

byShow.ev-2014-05-07: On 7 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Long Nights' arrived in the show's nineteenth slot as the Into the Wild duet (Vedder with Glen Hansard on the soundtrack). The 2014 performance was famously troubled: Vedder and Hansard attempted the song together twice and abandoned both attempts mid-song, with Vedder visibly frustrated by the harmonic alignment difficulties. The aborted performance became one of the most documented moments of the Brazilian solo tour.
byShow.ev-2014-05-08: On 8 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Long Nights' arrived in the show's sixteenth slot. After the previous night's failed Long Nights attempt with Hansard, the May 8 deployment carried specific weight: the 'redemption' attempt at the song that had broken down twice on May 7. Whether Hansard joined for this performance or Vedder performed the duet alone, the slot's deployment was deliberately re-attempting what had failed the previous night.

After the May 7 SP attempts that broke down twice, the Rio deployment was the song's redemption attempt of the Brazilian tour. Glen Hansard appeared on multiple tracks during the night, and the duet's structural difficulties from earlier in the tour were resolved by the Rio performance.

The May 12 deployment closed the tour's narrative around the song's structural challenges.

society.text:
'Society' is the eighth track on Eddie Vedder's Into the Wild soundtrack (2007), and one of the most-covered songs from the album. The original was written by Jerry Hannan, a singer-songwriter Vedder had known for years; Vedder's recording for Into the Wild was the first widely heard version of the song, and Hannan has subsequently received more sustained attention as a songwriter because of Vedder's adaptation.

The lyric is one of the most direct critiques of consumerist culture in the broader Vedder catalog. The narrator addresses an unnamed second person (the 'society' of the title is the addressee, framed as a personified social order) and refuses the order's demand to participate in its accumulating consumption. The song does not editorialize about whether refusal is sustainable; it documents the refusal and lets the music's slow build carry the meaning. The lyric maps onto the Into the Wild film's portrait of Chris McCandless's choice to abandon American consumer life, which is why the song became central to the film's emotional argument.

The arrangement is one of the more patient pieces on Into the Wild. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure; the band element (this is one of the few Into the Wild tracks with a full-band arrangement) enters under the second verse and stays restrained through the bridge. The closing instrumental section extends past the studio length on most live performances.

Live, 'Society' has been one of the most-played songs in Vedder's solo shows since 2007. The song works best in the second half of a set or in the encore, where its accumulated weight can land. Audiences in any country have received the song with the kind of attentiveness that the lyric's argument requires; the song's audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in any Vedder solo show.

byShow.ev-2014-05-06: On 6 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Society' arrived in the show's twenty-fifth slot as the Jerry Hannan cover (Hannan wrote the song; Vedder included it on Into the Wild). The song's anti-consumerist lyric carried the soundtrack's broader anti-civilization argument.

rise.text:
'Rise' is the third track on Eddie Vedder's Into the Wild soundtrack (2007), and one of the most propulsive pieces on the album. The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song appears in the Into the Wild film during a sequence where Chris McCandless is in motion across the American landscape, and the song's tempo and emotional register match that moment of forward momentum.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about the discipline of refusing despair. The narrator addresses the listener directly and frames the choice to keep moving as a daily practice rather than as a one-time decision. The song does not editorialize about how to maintain the practice; it documents the choice and lets the music's tempo carry the energy.

The arrangement is one of the brighter pieces on Into the Wild. The verse is built on a strummed mandolin figure that Vedder plays under his own vocal; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that lets the song's tempo climb. The mandolin tone gives the recording a distinctly American folk-revival feel that distinguishes it from the rest of the soundtrack's predominantly acoustic-guitar-driven material. The song is brief (under three minutes) and structured for sustained energy rather than for cathartic release.

Live, 'Rise' has been one of the most-played songs in Vedder's solo shows since 2007. The song works best as a mid-set energy injection, where its tempo can keep momentum going. Audiences across countries respond to the song with the kind of singalong attention that the chorus invites, and Vedder typically lets the audience carry sections of the song without prompting.

byShow.ev-2014-05-06: On 6 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Rise' arrived in the show's sixteenth slot as the Into the Wild track that the soundtrack's structure builds toward. The fingerpicked ukulele arrangement and the chorus's call to forward motion sat over the room with the kind of communal warmth the soundtrack's narrative invites.

no ceiling.text:
'No Ceiling' is the fifth track on Eddie Vedder's Into the Wild soundtrack (2007). The song is brief (under two minutes) and structured around a strummed acoustic figure that Vedder plays at high tempo throughout. The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song appears in the Into the Wild film during a sequence where Chris McCandless is experiencing a moment of genuine freedom, and the song's brevity and energy match that moment in the film's narrative.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most compressed pieces of writing about momentary liberation. The narrator describes the experience of being free of accumulated obligations and constraints, framing the freedom not as a destination but as the kind of brief moment that has to be honored when it arrives. The song does not editorialize about whether the freedom can be sustained; it documents the moment and lets the music's velocity carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most stripped pieces on Into the Wild. The recording is essentially Vedder solo on acoustic guitar, with minimal additional instrumentation. The song's brevity and structural simplicity make it closer to a sketch than to a fully developed song, which is part of its appeal: the song is short because the moment it documents is short.

Live, 'No Ceiling' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2007. The song works as a mid-set energy injection or as an encore, where its brevity can mark a deliberate moment of velocity. The song's tempo and length make it ideal for the kind of communal singalong that Vedder's solo audiences tend to deliver.

Vedder invited two fans onstage to join him for the song, continuing the fan-participation tradition that had defined his Brazilian solo touring since 2014. The Into the Wild track's compressed structure suited the brief audience-onstage moment.

far behind.text:
'Far Behind' is the fourth track on Eddie Vedder's Into the Wild soundtrack (2007). The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song appears in the Into the Wild film during a sequence where Chris McCandless is moving away from the people who love him, and the song's emotional register matches that moment of accumulating distance.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about leaving people behind. The narrator addresses the people the journey has put distance between, framing the distance not as betrayal but as the kind of structural condition that any sustained personal trajectory creates. The song does not editorialize about whether the leaving was right; it documents the leaving and lets the music's slow tempo carry the emotional weight.

The arrangement is one of the more pared-down pieces on Into the Wild. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure that Vedder plays under his own vocal, with minimal additional instrumentation. The recording features Glen Hansard on background vocals during the chorus. The song is brief (under three minutes) and structured for cumulative emotional weight rather than for cathartic release.

Live, 'Far Behind' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2008. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared.

far behind.text_pt:
'Far Behind' é a quarta faixa da trilha de Into the Wild de Eddie Vedder (2007). A música foi escrita por Vedder; a letra é de Vedder. A canção aparece no filme Into the Wild durante uma sequência em que Chris McCandless está se afastando das pessoas que o amam, e o registro emocional da canção combina com aquele momento de distância acumulada.

A letra é uma das peças mais gentis de escrita de Vedder sobre deixar pessoas pra trás. O narrador se dirige às pessoas entre as quais a jornada colocou distância, enquadrando a distância não como traição mas como o tipo de condição estrutural que qualquer trajetória pessoal sustentada cria. A canção não editorializa sobre se a partida foi certa; documenta a partida e deixa o tempo lento da música carregar o peso emocional.

O arranjo é uma das peças mais despojadas de Into the Wild. O verso é construído sobre uma figura de violão dedilhado que Vedder toca sob o próprio vocal, com instrumentação adicional mínima. A gravação traz Glen Hansard nos vocais de fundo durante o refrão. A canção é breve (menos de três minutos) e estruturada pra peso emocional cumulativo em vez de pra liberação catártica.

Ao vivo, 'Far Behind' é presença regular em setlist nos shows solo de Vedder desde 2008. A canção funciona melhor na segunda metade de um set, em que seu peso pode aterrissar em um público que foi emocionalmente preparado.

guaranteed.text:
'Guaranteed' is the closing track of Eddie Vedder's Into the Wild soundtrack (2007), and the song most directly associated with the film's emotional resolution. The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song appears in the Into the Wild film over the closing credits and won the Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song at the 65th Golden Globes ceremony in January 2008. Vedder accepted the award personally, which is one of the few major-awards ceremonies he has attended.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about the practice of refusing to let cumulative disappointment harden into cynicism. The narrator describes the work of remaining open to experience after years of accumulated reasons to close, framing the work not as easy but as the only available option for any sustained engagement with the world. The song does not editorialize about whether the work succeeds; it documents the practice and lets the music's quiet tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most pared-down pieces on Into the Wild. The recording is essentially Vedder solo on acoustic guitar, with minimal additional instrumentation. The song's brevity and structural simplicity place it closer to the singer-songwriter tradition of the early 1970s (the James Taylor and Cat Stevens early-career work is the most cited reference) than to anything in the Pearl Jam catalog.

Live, 'Guaranteed' has been one of the most-played songs in Vedder's solo shows since 2007. The song works best as an encore or as a Vedder-led acoustic moment in any setlist context. The song's deliberate intimacy makes the audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section one of the more durable communal moments in Vedder's solo touring catalog.

hard sun.text:
'Hard Sun' is the closing-rite song of Eddie Vedder's Into the Wild soundtrack (2007), and the most-played piece in his solo show vocabulary. The song is a cover of a 1989 track by the Canadian singer-songwriter Gordon Peterson, who recorded it under the name 'Indio' for his album Big Harvest. Peterson's original is little-known and out of print; Vedder's adaptation for Into the Wild has become the version most listeners know, and Peterson has spoken in subsequent interviews about how Vedder's adaptation extended the song's life beyond what the original recording's commercial reach had allowed.

The lyric is one of the more sustained anthems of weather-as-metaphor in late-20th-century American songwriting. The narrator addresses a sun that is unforgiving and frames the song's central question (whether the addressee will continue under the harshness or seek shelter elsewhere) without resolving it. Vedder's adaptation honored the structural ambiguity of Peterson's original; the cover does not editorialize about whether to stay under the hard sun.

The Pearl Jam-era arrangement preserves the Indio original's structure but tilts the texture toward a more sustained instrumental climb. The closing instrumental section frequently extends past the studio length, and the song became, in Vedder's solo tour vocabulary, the canonical encore-closer. Live performances often run over six minutes, with Vedder letting the band element (when present) extend the song's tempo without breaking it.

Live, 'Hard Sun' has been one of the most-played songs in Vedder's solo shows since 2007 and has appeared frequently in Pearl Jam shows as well. The song works best as an encore-closer, where its accumulated weight can carry the show home. The audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the most reliable communal moments in any Vedder solo show.

hard sun.text_pt:
'Hard Sun' é a canção rito de fechamento da trilha de Into the Wild de Eddie Vedder (2007), e a peça mais executada do vocabulário de show solo dele. A canção é cover de uma faixa de 1989 do compositor canadense Gordon Peterson, que a gravou sob o nome 'Indio' pra o álbum dele Big Harvest. O original de Peterson é pouco conhecido e fora de catálogo; a adaptação de Vedder pra Into the Wild virou a versão que a maioria dos ouvintes conhece, e Peterson falou em entrevistas posteriores sobre como a adaptação de Vedder estendeu a vida da canção além do que o alcance comercial da gravação original havia permitido.

A letra é um dos hinos mais sustentados de tempo-como-metáfora na composição americana do fim do século 20. O narrador se dirige a um sol que é implacável e enquadra a pergunta central da canção (se o destinatário continuará sob a dureza ou buscará abrigo em outro lugar) sem resolvê-la. A adaptação de Vedder honrou a ambiguidade estrutural do original de Peterson; o cover não editorializa sobre se ficar sob o sol duro.

O arranjo da era Pearl Jam preserva a estrutura do original do Indio mas inclina a textura pra uma escalada instrumental mais sustentada. A seção instrumental final frequentemente se estende além da duração de estúdio, e a canção virou, no vocabulário de turnê solo de Vedder, o fechador-de-bis canônico. Apresentações ao vivo frequentemente passam dos seis minutos, com Vedder deixando o elemento de banda (quando presente) estender o tempo da canção sem quebrá-lo.

Ao vivo, 'Hard Sun' é uma das músicas mais executadas em shows solo de Vedder desde 2007 e apareceu com frequência em shows do Pearl Jam também. A canção funciona melhor como fechadora de bis, em que seu peso acumulado pode levar o show pra casa. O vocal sem palavras liderado pelo público durante a seção final virou um dos momentos comunitários mais confiáveis em qualquer show solo de Vedder.

sleepless nights.text:
'Sleepless Nights' is a 1960 country-pop song written by the husband-and-wife team Felice and Boudleaux Bryant for the Everly Brothers, who first recorded it that year. The Bryants were two of the most prolific Nashville songwriters of the late 1950s and 1960s, and 'Sleepless Nights' is one of the more enduring pieces in their catalog. The song's structural simplicity (a single sustained lyric of romantic longing across a slow chord progression) is part of its durability.

Vedder began performing the song in his solo shows in the late 2000s and has continued to do so consistently. The cover is part of Vedder's broader engagement with mid-20th-century American songwriting traditions; he has spoken in interviews about the Everly Brothers as one of his foundational influences, alongside the Bryants' songwriting catalog. The choice to cover this specific Bryant composition (rather than the more famous 'Bye Bye Love' or 'All I Have to Do Is Dream') is a deliberate gesture toward the Bryants' less-anthologized work.

The Vedder arrangement preserves the Everly Brothers original's structure. Vedder typically performs the song solo on acoustic guitar, occasionally with band accompaniment in the song's later verses. The arrangement honors the song's brief duration (under three minutes in any version) and refuses to extend the cover past the original's length. Vedder typically sings the song in a register close to Don Everly's original.

Live, 'Sleepless Nights' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since the late 2000s. The song works best as a Vedder-led acoustic moment in the second half of a set, where its quiet directness can mark a deliberate emotional pause.

without you.text:
'Without You' is the seventh track on Eddie Vedder's Ukulele Songs (2011), and one of the songs most directly associated with the album's central concept. The album was constructed around the ukulele as the central instrument across fifteen pieces of original Vedder writing and selected covers. The choice of instrument was deliberate; Vedder had been carrying a ukulele on Pearl Jam tours for years before the album was conceived, and the small-scale instrument let him write material at a register the rock-band format could not accommodate.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about devotion. The narrator addresses an absent partner and frames the relationship as the central event of a life, with the partner's absence creating the kind of structural lack that the rest of life cannot fill. The song does not editorialize about whether the absence is permanent or temporary; it documents the lack and lets the music's small scale carry the emotional weight.

The arrangement is the most stripped Vedder had recorded up to 2011. The recording is essentially Vedder solo on ukulele, with no other instrumentation. The brevity (under three minutes) and structural simplicity match the album's broader argument: small instruments produce small songs, and small songs can carry emotional weight that large arrangements would only dilute.

Live, 'Without You' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2011. The song works best as a Vedder-on-ukulele moment in the middle of a set, where its quiet scale can mark a deliberate tonal shift. The song's audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in any Vedder solo show.

more than you know.text:
'More Than You Know' is the ninth track on Eddie Vedder's Ukulele Songs (2011), and one of the more melodic pieces on the album. The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is structured around a slow ukulele figure that Vedder plays at a deliberate tempo throughout, with no additional instrumentation entering across the song's length. The deliberate scale of the recording matches the album's broader concept of using a small instrument to address material that a full band would have over-dressed.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about cumulative knowledge in a long relationship. The narrator addresses a partner and acknowledges that the relationship has produced a kind of mutual recognition that exceeds what either party could have predicted at its start. The song does not editorialize about whether the recognition is sustainable; it documents the recognition and lets the ukulele's small voice carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most stripped pieces in the Vedder solo catalog. The recording is Vedder alone with the ukulele, and the song's brevity (under three minutes) and structural simplicity match the album's broader aesthetic. The choice to leave the song unaccompanied is part of its argument: small instruments produce small songs, and small songs can carry weight that large arrangements would dilute.

Live, 'More Than You Know' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2011. The song works as a quiet moment in the middle of a set, where its small scale can mark a deliberate tonal shift before the show's closing arc.

i wont hold on.text:
'I Won't Hold On' is the closing track of Eddie Vedder's Ukulele Songs (2011). The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song's placement at the album's close is a sequencing argument: after the album's accumulated material about devotion, distance, and mortality, the closing song lets a meditation on releasing attachment carry the album home.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about the practice of letting go. The narrator addresses someone or something the speaker has been holding onto for too long and frames the choice to release the hold not as failure but as the kind of mature discipline that any sustained life requires. The song does not editorialize about whether the release is easy; it documents the choice and lets the ukulele's restrained tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most pared-down pieces on Ukulele Songs. The recording is Vedder solo with the ukulele, and the song's structural simplicity matches the lyric's clarity. The song is brief and ends without the kind of cathartic release that the album's harder material would have demanded.

Live, 'I Won't Hold On' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2011. The song works best in the encore, where its closing-rite feel can mark the show's emotional pause before the final material.

goodbye.text:
'Goodbye' is the third track on Eddie Vedder's Ukulele Songs (2011). The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the more direct farewells in the broader Vedder solo catalog, structured around a single ukulele figure that does not vary across the song's length.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about ending a relationship. The narrator addresses a partner who is leaving and frames the leaving not as a rupture but as the kind of structural transition that some relationships eventually require. The song does not editorialize about whether the leaving was right or wrong; it documents the moment and lets the ukulele's small scale carry the emotional weight.

The arrangement is one of the most stripped pieces on Ukulele Songs. The recording is Vedder solo with the ukulele, and the song's brevity (under two minutes) makes it closer to a postcard than to a fully developed song. The choice to leave the recording unaccompanied is part of its argument: the song is short because the moment it documents is brief.

Live, 'Goodbye' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2011. The song works best as a quiet moment in the middle of a set or as a brief encore selection, where its small scale can mark a deliberate emotional pause.

light today.text:
'Light Today' is the twelfth track on Eddie Vedder's Ukulele Songs (2011), and one of the more atmospheric pieces on the album. The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is structured around a slow ukulele figure that Vedder plays at a deliberate tempo throughout, with the addition of background vocals from Cat Power (Chan Marshall) layered into the recording. Cat Power's contribution gives the song a vocal architecture that the rest of the album does not have.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more meditative pieces of writing about the discipline of finding clarity in dim circumstances. The narrator describes the practice of waiting through dark periods for the kind of light that arrives without warning, framing the waiting not as anxious anticipation but as a sustained attentiveness to small daily changes in conditions. The song does not editorialize about how long the waiting takes; it documents the practice and lets the music's restraint carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the more layered pieces on Ukulele Songs. Vedder's ukulele carries the harmonic motion, with Cat Power's vocal floating above the chord progression. The choice to bring Cat Power into the recording is part of the song's argument: the small ukulele sound benefits from a second voice, even though the album's broader concept tended to refuse external instrumentation.

Live, 'Light Today' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2011. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its slow tempo can mark a tonal shift before the closing surge.

youre true.text:
'You're True' is the fourth track on Eddie Vedder's Ukulele Songs (2011), and one of the more direct love songs in the broader Vedder solo catalog. The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is structured around a brisk ukulele figure that Vedder plays at higher tempo than most of the album's slower material, and the song's energy distinguishes it from the album's prevailing meditative register.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about confirmed devotion. The narrator addresses a partner and acknowledges, without qualification, the partner's authenticity within the relationship. The song does not editorialize about how the recognition was earned; it documents the recognition and lets the music's tempo carry the energy. The directness is unusual in the broader Vedder catalog, where romantic content tends to be obliquely framed rather than openly declared.

The arrangement is one of the brighter pieces on Ukulele Songs. The recording is Vedder solo with the ukulele, played at a faster tempo than most of the album's other tracks. The song's brevity and structural simplicity match the album's broader aesthetic, but the higher tempo gives it a distinctly different feel from the surrounding material.

Live, 'You're True' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2011. The song works as a mid-set energy injection in solo contexts, where its tempo can keep momentum going within a set that the rest of the album would have kept at slow.

broken heart.text:
'Broken Heart' is the fifth track on Eddie Vedder's Ukulele Songs (2011), one of the more direct pieces of writing on the album. The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is structured around a slow ukulele figure that does not vary across its length, which suits the lyric's central preoccupation with grief that does not resolve.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about loss. The narrator addresses the experience of carrying a grief that has not finished its work, framing the experience not as something to overcome but as the kind of structural condition that the rest of life has to accommodate. The song does not editorialize about how to carry the grief; it documents the carrying and lets the small ukulele scale honor the lyric's restraint.

The arrangement is one of the most stripped pieces on Ukulele Songs. The recording is Vedder solo with the ukulele, and the song's brevity matches the lyric's clarity. The song is short and ends without the kind of release that would have eased the lyric's argument; the choice to end without resolution is part of the song's meaning.

Live, 'Broken Heart' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2011. The song works as a quiet moment in the middle of a set, where its small scale can mark a deliberate emotional pause.

better days.text:
'Better Days' is the eighth track on Eddie Vedder's Ukulele Songs (2011). The song was written by Vedder; the lyric is Vedder's. The song appears in the closing credits of the 2007 film Eat Pray Love adaptation as well, although the Ukulele Songs version is the one most listeners encounter. The arrangement is structured around a strummed ukulele figure that Vedder plays at a brisk tempo, and the song's energy distinguishes it from the album's more meditative material.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more straightforwardly optimistic pieces of writing. The narrator addresses the listener and frames the anticipation of better times as a discipline rather than as a passive expectation. The song does not editorialize about whether better times actually arrive; it documents the practice of looking forward and lets the music's brisk tempo carry the energy.

The arrangement is one of the brighter pieces on Ukulele Songs. The recording is Vedder solo with the ukulele, played at a tempo that the album's slower material would not have allowed. The song's structural simplicity makes it ideal for the kind of singalong audience-led communal moment that Vedder's solo shows tend to produce.

Live, 'Better Days' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2011. The song works as a mid-set energy injection or as an encore, where its brisk tempo can keep momentum going. The audience-led wordless vocal during the chorus has become one of the more reliable communal moments in any Vedder solo show.

cant keep.text:
'Can't Keep' is the opening track of Riot Act (2002), and one of the more direct pieces of writing in the early-2000s Pearl Jam catalog. The music and lyric are both Vedder's. The song was written and recorded during the Riot Act sessions in early 2002, in the period when the band was processing the deaths of nine fans during the band's set at the Roskilde Festival in 2000. The song's tonal register reflects that processing without engaging with the specific events directly.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more contemplative pieces of writing about the inevitability of loss. The narrator describes the experience of holding onto people and circumstances that the structural conditions of life will not allow the holder to keep, framing the holding not as denial but as the kind of provisional arrangement that constitutes most ongoing relationships. The song does not editorialize about the unholding; it documents the awareness and lets the music's restrained tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the more pared-down opening tracks in the Pearl Jam catalog. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that does not vary; the band element enters in restrained layers across the song's length. McCready's guitar is restrained throughout. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed during the verses.

Live, 'Can't Keep' has been a regular setlist presence since 2002 and has appeared frequently in Vedder's solo shows as well, where the song's gentleness translates naturally to the solo acoustic context. The song works best as an opener or as a tonal pause in the early-middle of a set.

thumbing my way.text:
'Thumbing My Way' is the eighth track on Riot Act (2002). The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the more directly autobiographical pieces of writing on Riot Act, drawing from the imagery of hitchhiking that Vedder has used elsewhere in his catalog (Into the Wild's central narrative is structured around the same imagery, although the Into the Wild material would not be written for another five years).

The lyric is one of Vedder's more meditative pieces of writing about cumulative travel. The narrator describes the practice of moving from place to place across years and frames the practice not as escape from any specific situation but as the kind of ongoing motion that some lives require to maintain themselves. The song does not editorialize about whether the motion has a destination; it documents the practice and lets the music's restrained tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the more pared-down pieces on Riot Act. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure that Vedder plays under his own vocal, with restrained band accompaniment in the song's later verses. McCready's solo at the song's center is brief and melodic. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed throughout.

Live, 'Thumbing My Way' has been a regular setlist presence in Pearl Jam shows since 2002 and has appeared frequently in Vedder's solo shows as well. The song works best as a quiet moment in the second half of a set, where its slow tempo can mark a tonal shift before the closing material.

byShow.ev-2014-05-06: On 6 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Thumbing My Way' arrived in the show's twelfth slot as the Riot Act-era track. The song's slow build and Vedder's vocal intensity gave the slot an emotional center that the solo format amplified.

soon forget.text:
'Soon Forget' is the eleventh track on Binaural (2000), one of the most stylistically unusual pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog. The song is performed by Vedder solo on ukulele; there is no other instrumentation. This was the first appearance of the ukulele on a Pearl Jam recording, predating Vedder's Ukulele Songs solo album by over a decade. The song is therefore the seed of an entire stylistic direction Vedder would explore more fully in the 2010s.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more satirical pieces of writing about wealth as a substitute for meaning. The narrator describes a wealthy figure whose accumulated possessions have produced none of the satisfaction the figure expected and frames the figure's predicament not as personal failure but as the kind of structural disappointment that material accumulation tends to produce. The song does not editorialize about whether the figure can change course; it documents the disappointment and lets the small ukulele scale carry the satire.

The arrangement is one of the most pared-down pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog. Vedder plays the ukulele alone, and the band does not enter at any point during the song. The choice to record this material as a Pearl Jam album track rather than as a solo aside (which would have been more conventional in the catalog's logic of the time) was a deliberate stylistic gesture by the band, signaling that Pearl Jam's vocabulary was not limited to the rock-band format.

Live, 'Soon Forget' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2000. The song works best as a Vedder-on-ukulele moment in the middle of a set, where its small scale can mark a deliberate tonal shift. In Pearl Jam shows, the song typically appears as a quiet pause between heavier material; in Vedder's solo shows, the song is more naturally integrated into the surrounding material.

byShow.ev-2014-05-07: On 7 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Soon Forget' arrived in the show's eighth slot as the Binaural-era ukulele track (the song that introduced the ukulele to Pearl Jam's catalog in 2000, Vedder's first ukulele recording with the band). The Ukulele Songs material that defines Vedder's solo aesthetic traces directly to this 2000 origin point, and the SP placement gave the slot the kind of historical reference the audience appreciated.
byShow.ev-2014-05-12: On 12 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Soon Forget' arrived in the show's sixth slot as the Binaural-era ukulele-debut track.

speed of sound.text:
'Speed of Sound' is the ninth track on Pearl Jam's Backspacer (2009). The music is Vedder's; the lyric is also Vedder's. The song is one of the more pop-leaning pieces in the broader Pearl Jam catalog, structured around a brisk acoustic guitar figure with band accompaniment that stays restrained throughout.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentler pieces of writing about reflection and memory. The narrator describes the experience of how thoughts and memories travel faster than reasoning can keep up with, framing the speed not as confusion but as the kind of cognitive condition any reflective life produces. The song does not editorialize about how to manage the velocity; it documents the awareness and lets the music's tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the more pared-down pieces on Backspacer. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure; the band element enters in restrained layers across the song's length. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is brushed throughout, which suits the song's reflective register.

Live, 'Speed of Sound' has been a regular setlist presence since 2009 in both Pearl Jam shows and Vedder's solo performances. In solo contexts, the song's acoustic-driven structure translates naturally without the band; in Pearl Jam shows, the band stays restrained around Vedder's vocal in the same way the studio recording does. The song works best as a quiet moment in the second half of a set.

byShow.ev-2014-05-07: On 7 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Speed of Sound' arrived in the show's twelfth slot as the second of the night's three tour debuts. The solo-acoustic context for the song gave it the kind of intimate listening environment the song's quiet structure invites.
byShow.ev-2014-05-12: On 12 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Speed of Sound' arrived in the show's fourth slot. The song was one of the May 7 tour debuts; the May 12 appearance maintained the song's late-tour rotation.
byShow.ev-2018-03-29: On 29 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'Speed of Sound' arrived in the show's twenty-first slot.

future days.text:
'Future Days' is the closing track of Pearl Jam's Lightning Bolt (2013), and one of the most direct love songs in the late Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song's placement at track twelve (the album's last) is a sequencing argument: after the album's harder material about institutional refusal and personal struggle, the closing position lets a meditation on sustained partnership carry the album home.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentlest pieces of writing about long-term love. The narrator addresses a partner and frames the future tense of the song's title not as anxious anticipation but as a sustained promise of continued presence. The song does not editorialize about the conditions under which the promise can be kept; it documents the promise and lets the music's restrained tempo carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the most stripped pieces on Lightning Bolt. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure that Vedder plays under his own vocal, with the band element entering in restrained layers across the song's length. McCready's guitar lines are subtle and floating rather than soloing; Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed throughout. The arrangement honors the lyric's intimacy by refusing to scale up to a stadium-sized release.

Live, 'Future Days' has been a regular setlist presence in Pearl Jam shows and Vedder's solo performances since 2013. The song works best as an encore or as a Vedder-led acoustic moment in the middle of a set. The song's audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in any Pearl Jam show.

byShow.ev-2014-05-07: On 7 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Future Days' arrived in the show's twenty-third slot as the third of the night's three tour debuts. The Lightning Bolt 2013 closer (track 12, the album's emotional anchor) gave the slot the contemporary Vedder ballad vocabulary, and the song would go on to become a regular Vedder solo-set inclusion.

gone.text:
'Gone' is the ninth track on Pearl Jam (2006), the self-titled Avocado album. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song is one of the more directly autobiographical pieces of writing on the album, drawing from the imagery of leaving in a vehicle that has appeared elsewhere in the Vedder catalog.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more meditative pieces of writing about a particular kind of departure. The narrator describes the moment of getting into a car and driving away from a place the speaker has spent significant time, framing the departure not as escape from any specific situation but as the kind of structural transition that the rhythms of life occasionally require. The song does not editorialize about whether the departure was necessary; it documents the leaving and lets the music's slow build carry the meaning.

The arrangement is one of the more pared-down pieces on Avocado. The verse is built on a slow acoustic figure that climbs through the bridge into a wider harmonic move; the chorus opens into a sustained vocal melody that lets the audience carry the section. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is restrained throughout. The song was produced by Adam Kasper rather than by Brendan O'Brien, and Kasper's preference for raw rhythm-section recording is audible across the track.

Live, 'Gone' has been a regular but not heavy setlist presence since 2006 and has appeared in Vedder's solo shows as well, where the song's acoustic structure translates naturally without the band. The song works best as a tonal pause in the second half of a set.

byShow.ev-2014-05-12: On 12 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Gone' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as the Pearl Jam (2006) track. The song's lyric (a meditation on departure and freedom from social expectations) translated to the solo format.

around the bend.text:
'Around the Bend' is the closing track of No Code (1996), and one of the gentlest album closers in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song's placement at the album's close is a sequencing argument: after No Code's accumulated stylistic experiments, the closing position lets a quiet acoustic lullaby carry the album home.

The lyric is one of Vedder's gentlest pieces of writing about parental affection. The narrator addresses a child (Vedder did not have children at the time of the recording, but the song's direct address to a young person is unmistakable) and frames the future the speaker hopes for the child not as a list of achievements but as the kind of quiet daily pleasure that constitutes most of any well-lived life. The song does not editorialize; it documents the wish and lets the music's small scale carry the affection.

The arrangement is one of the most pared-down pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog. The recording is essentially Vedder solo on acoustic guitar, with minimal additional instrumentation. The song is brief (under three minutes) and structured for cumulative emotional weight rather than for cathartic release.

Live, 'Around the Bend' has been a rare setlist presence since 1996 in Pearl Jam shows and a more frequent presence in Vedder's solo performances, where the song's acoustic structure is the natural format. The song works best as a Vedder-led encore moment, where its quiet directness can mark the show's emotional pause before the closing material.

byShow.ev-2018-03-29: On 29 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'Around the Bend' arrived in the show's tenth slot as the rarest No Code-era track in the touring catalog (the song closes No Code 1996 but had been performed live fewer than a dozen times in two decades by 2018). The Brazilian audience was hearing one of the song's earliest documented solo-arrangement performances; the bootleg circulated immediately as one of the night's most celebrated moments.

light years.text:
'Light Years' is the fourth track on Pearl Jam's Binaural (2000), and one of the more direct elegies in the Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written and recorded during the Binaural sessions in early 2000, in the period after the deaths of multiple figures in the broader Seattle music community across the late 1990s. The lyric does not name a specific addressee, but the song's emotional register has been consistently understood by long-time listeners as a tribute to friends Vedder had lost across the decade.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more meditative pieces of writing about the durability of relationships across distance. The narrator addresses someone who has either physically died or has otherwise become unreachable and frames the relationship's continued meaning despite the unreachability as the kind of structural condition that grief eventually settles into. The song does not editorialize; it documents the awareness and lets the music's slow tempo carry the emotional weight.

The arrangement is one of the more layered pieces on Binaural. The verse is built on a chord progression that Stone Gossard plays at a measured tempo; the chorus opens into a wider harmonic move that resolves through the bridge into a McCready solo. Matt Cameron's drumming on the recording is restrained throughout. Producer Tchad Blake's approach to recording (he favored unusual mic placements that created a sense of physical space in the recording's stereo image) gives the song a textural feel that distinguishes it from the rest of the Pearl Jam catalog of the period.

Live, 'Light Years' has been a regular setlist presence since 2000 and has appeared in Vedder's solo shows as well. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared.
