4th of july.text:
'4th of July' is a 1987 composition by John Doe of the Los Angeles punk band X, the third track on side one of X's fifth studio album See How We Are. The song belongs to the late-period X catalog in which the band's earlier punk velocity gives way to a more direct singer-songwriter mode that reflected the broader American roots-music vocabulary the band had been exploring since the mid-1980s. Doe wrote the song as a meditation on a working-class couple's argument on the holiday rather than as a celebration of the holiday's official register.

The lyric is one of Doe's more direct pieces of writing about a domestic scene held together against the surrounding noise of the American holiday calendar. The narrator addresses a partner during the night of the 4th of July (the holiday's fireworks become the song's recurring sonic backdrop) and frames the small private exchange not as separate from the public celebration but as the kind of structural intimacy that any sustained relationship maintains under public conditions. The song does not editorialize about whether the celebration outside is meaningful; it documents the private exchange and lets the music's restrained tempo carry the meaning.

Vedder has performed the song as a cover in his solo shows for years. The cover is part of his broader engagement with the late-1970s and 1980s American punk and post-punk catalog, and a deliberate gesture toward the kind of working-class American songwriting that X helped popularize. The Vedder arrangement preserves the See How We Are original's structure: solo acoustic guitar at a tempo close to the X recording.

Live, '4th of July' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows. The song works best as a quiet moment in the second half of a set, where its restrained scale can mark a deliberate emotional pause.

byShow.ev-2014-05-11: On 11 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, '4th of July' arrived in the show's twenty-first slot as the Vedder solo Ukulele Songs track. The song's gentle ukulele arrangement and reflective lyric about American identity gave the slot a deep-Vedder-solo moment.

girl from the north country.text:
'Girl from the North Country' is a 1963 composition by Bob Dylan, the second track on side one of Dylan's second studio album The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan. The song is one of the gentler pieces on Freewheelin', set against the album's more directly political material; Dylan adapted the song's melody from the traditional English folk song 'Scarborough Fair' (which Paul Simon would popularize in a different adaptation a few years later). The song addresses a former romantic partner the narrator has left behind, framed as a request to a third party who is traveling north to relay regards to her.

The lyric is one of Dylan's gentler pieces of writing about cumulative romantic memory across distance. The narrator addresses an unnamed second person who is traveling toward the place where a former partner still lives and asks the traveler to check on her well-being, framing the request not as nostalgic but as the kind of structural carrying-forward of past affection that any reflective life produces. The song does not editorialize about whether the relationship was right or wrong; it documents the carrying-forward.

Vedder has performed the song as a cover in his solo shows for years. The cover is part of his broader engagement with the Dylan catalog. The Vedder arrangement preserves the Freewheelin' original's structure: solo acoustic guitar at a tempo close to the 1963 recording. Vedder's covers of Dylan tend to honor the originals without significant restructuring.

Live, 'Girl from the North Country' has been a regular but occasional setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows. The song works as a quiet moment in the middle of a set, where its small scale can mark a deliberate emotional pause.

byShow.ev-2014-05-12: On 12 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Girl From the North Country' arrived in the show's third slot as the Bob Dylan cover (1963, from The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, later re-recorded as a duet with Johnny Cash in 1969). Vedder's solo-acoustic version of the Dylan ballad gave the slot a deep-folk-vocabulary moment.

the ship song.text:
'The Ship Song' is a 1990 composition by Nick Cave, the third track on side one of Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds' sixth studio album The Good Son. The song belongs to the period in Cave's catalog when his earlier post-punk vocabulary gave way to a more sustained engagement with traditional songwriting; The Good Son was recorded after Cave's relocation to São Paulo, Brazil with his then-partner Viviane Carneiro, and the album's softer register reflects that period of Cave's life. The song is one of the most directly devotional pieces in the Cave catalog, structured as a piano-led ballad of romantic commitment.

The lyric is one of Cave's more direct pieces of writing about devotional intensity. The narrator addresses a partner and frames a sequence of nautical metaphors (the partner is asked to come aboard, to set sail, to go where the speaker is going) not as poetic decoration but as the kind of structural commitment that any sustained partnership requires. The song does not editorialize about whether the journey will succeed; it documents the invitation and lets the slow piano arrangement carry the weight.

Vedder has performed the song as a cover in his solo shows for years. The cover is part of his broader engagement with the Cave catalog (Vedder has spoken in interviews about Cave as one of the singular songwriters of the period and the two have appeared at various tribute events). The Vedder arrangement typically translates the Cave piano arrangement into a solo acoustic guitar format. Live, 'The Ship Song' has been a regular but occasional setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows. The song works best in the second half of a set.

byShow.ev-2018-03-30: On 30 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'The Ship Song' arrived in the show's third slot as the Nick Cave & the Bad Seeds cover (1990, from The Good Son). The Cave tribute gave the slot an Australian post-punk vocabulary moment that paired structurally with the Hunters & Collectors and Hansard tributes Vedder regularly featured.

here comes the sun.text:
'Here Comes the Sun' is a 1969 composition by George Harrison, the seventh track on side two of The Beatles' Abbey Road. The song was written by Harrison during a period when he had stepped away from a contentious Beatles business meeting and was sitting in Eric Clapton's garden in Surrey, England in early spring 1969. The song's emotional register reflects that moment of stepping away: a meditation on the arrival of warmth after a long period of cold conditions. The song is one of the most widely beloved pieces of Beatles writing and is among the most-streamed Beatles tracks in the broader catalog.

The lyric is one of Harrison's gentlest pieces of writing about the structural relief of seasonal change. The narrator addresses the listener and frames the sun's arrival not as miraculous but as the kind of recurring relief that the natural cycle reliably provides. The song does not editorialize about what the cold conditions were that the warmth is finally relieving; the metaphor is left for any listener to fill with their own circumstances.

Vedder has performed the song as a cover in his solo shows for years. The cover is part of his broader engagement with the Harrison catalog. The Vedder arrangement preserves the Abbey Road original's structure: solo acoustic guitar at a tempo close to the studio recording, with band accompaniment when available. The audience-led wordless vocal during the closing section has become one of the more reliable communal moments in any Vedder solo show.

Live, 'Here Comes the Sun' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows. The song works best as an encore or as a Vedder-led acoustic moment late in a set, where its blessing register can mark the show's emotional pause.

byShow.ev-2018-03-30: On 30 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'Here Comes the Sun' arrived in the show's tenth slot as the Beatles cover (1969, from Abbey Road, written by George Harrison). The Harrison tribute gave the slot a brighter mid-set moment after the show's slow opening sequence.

song of good hope.text:
'Song of Good Hope' is a 2012 composition by Glen Hansard, the eighth track on Hansard's first solo studio album Rhythm and Repose. Hansard had spent the previous fifteen years as the principal songwriter of the Irish rock band The Frames and as one half of the duo The Swell Season; Rhythm and Repose was his first record under his own name. The song belongs to the gentler stretch of his solo catalog, structured around a slow acoustic figure and a direct lyric of well-wishing for a friend in difficulty.

The lyric is one of Hansard's more direct pieces of writing about offering practical encouragement to someone in a hard period. The narrator addresses an unnamed second person who is currently struggling and offers a sequence of specific encouragements (the practice of taking small steps, the discipline of accepting help when help is offered, the structural reality that hard periods do eventually end), framing the encouragements not as platitudes but as the kind of patient practical advice that long friendship produces. The song does not editorialize about what the addressee is struggling with; it documents the encouragement.

Vedder has been close to Hansard since the late 2000s; Hansard appears as a featured vocalist on Vedder's Into the Wild soundtrack (2007) and the two have appeared together at various tribute events and benefit concerts. Vedder's covers of 'Song of Good Hope' are part of that sustained mutual engagement and a deliberate honoring of Hansard's writing. The Vedder arrangement preserves the Hansard original's structure: solo acoustic guitar at a tempo close to the Rhythm and Repose recording.

Live, 'Song of Good Hope' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows. The song works best as a quiet moment in the second half of a set or as an encore, where its blessing register can mark the show's emotional pause.

byShow.ev-2018-03-30: On 30 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'Song of Good Hope' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as the Glen Hansard cover (2015, from Didn't He Ramble). Hansard's friendship with Vedder had now produced over a decade of tributed material; the slot continued the regular Hansard-cover thread.

river cross.text:
'River Cross' is the closing track of Pearl Jam's eleventh studio album Gigaton (2020). The song is one of the more meditative pieces in the late Pearl Jam catalog. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was recorded during the Gigaton sessions in late 2019 and early 2020, in the period before the broader COVID-19 pandemic disruption; the song's eventual release in March 2020 (as the final track on an album that arrived as the world was entering an extended period of disruption) gave it an unintended additional resonance.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about the discipline of refusing despair under accumulated negative conditions. The narrator addresses the listener and frames the work of crossing through hard periods (the river of the title is read most directly as any structural condition that has to be traversed) not as easy but as the only available option for any sustained engagement with the world. The song's central refrain ('Won't hold us down') is one of the more direct pieces of resistance language in the broader late-period Vedder catalog.

The arrangement is one of the more layered pieces on Gigaton. The verse is built on a slow chord progression that Vedder plays under his own vocal at a measured tempo; the band element climbs through restrained dynamic shifts rather than through cathartic release. Matt Cameron's drumming is brushed throughout the verses. The closing instrumental section extends past the studio length on most live performances.

Live, 'River Cross' has been a regular setlist presence in Pearl Jam shows since 2020 and has appeared in Vedder's solo shows as well, where the song's acoustic-driven structure translates naturally without the band. The song works best as an encore or as a tonal pause late in a set, where its slow build can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared.

byShow.ev-2018-03-28: On 28 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'River Cross' arrived in the show's second slot. The song would later become the closing track of Pearl Jam's Gigaton (2020); the 2018 solo deployment was a pre-album preview of material that Vedder had been developing in the studio with the band.

long way:
'Long Way' is the second track on Eddie Vedder's third solo studio album Earthling (2022) and was the album's first single. The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. Earthling was produced by Andrew Watt, the producer Vedder had worked with on the Lightning Bolt-era and post-2020 Pearl Jam material; the album's broader sound reflects Watt's preference for a layered rock-band production that distinguished it from Vedder's earlier solo material (Into the Wild and Ukulele Songs both kept their arrangements deliberately small).

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about the practice of forgiving oneself for past mistakes. The narrator addresses an unnamed second person (read most directly as the speaker's own past self) and frames the act of accepting cumulative error not as evasion of responsibility but as the kind of structural reckoning that any sustained life eventually requires. The song does not editorialize about what specific mistakes the speaker is reckoning with; it documents the practice and lets the brisk rock arrangement carry the energy.

The arrangement is one of the brighter pieces on Earthling. The recording features full-band production with multiple guest musicians (Watt's network of collaborators contributed across the record). The song's tempo and structural simplicity make it ideal for the kind of audience-led singalong that Vedder's solo shows tend to produce. The song's closing chorus has frequently appeared as an audience-carried section in live performance.

Live, 'Long Way' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2022. The song works as a mid-set energy injection or as an encore opener.
brother the cloud:
'Brother the Cloud' is the sixth track on Eddie Vedder's third solo studio album Earthling (2022). The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written and recorded during the Earthling sessions in 2021 and is one of the more directly personal pieces of writing on the album. Vedder has spoken in interviews about the song as a meditation on the death of his older brother Christopher Mueller, who died unexpectedly in 2016; the song's eventual recording for Earthling came in the years after that loss had had time to settle into the kind of structural condition that sustained writing requires.

The lyric is one of Vedder's most direct pieces of writing about a specific bereavement. The narrator addresses the absent brother (the 'cloud' of the title is read most directly as the form in which the brother now exists in the speaker's continuing experience) and offers a sequence of rememberings, framing the address not as sustained grief but as the kind of ongoing relationship that any deeply important loss eventually settles into. The song does not editorialize about the death itself; it documents the continuing relationship.

The arrangement is one of the more layered pieces on Earthling. The verse is built on a chord progression that climbs through the bridge into a wider harmonic move; the chorus opens into a sustained vocal melody. The recording features full-band production. The song's emotional directness makes it one of the more weight-carrying pieces on the album.

Live, 'Brother the Cloud' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2022. The song works best in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared.
invincible:
'Invincible' is the opening track of Eddie Vedder's third solo studio album Earthling (2022). The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song serves as the album's structural opener and sets the tonal register for the rest of the record: a brisk rock arrangement at higher tempo than most of Vedder's previous solo material, with full-band production rather than the deliberately stripped arrangements of Into the Wild or Ukulele Songs. The song was produced by Andrew Watt.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about the practice of resisting cumulative discouragement. The narrator addresses an unnamed second person (read most directly as either the listener or as the speaker addressing his own past self) and frames the work of remaining structurally upright under pressure not as easy but as the only available option for any sustained engagement with the world. The song's central refrain functions as a piece of self-encouragement that the audience can carry without needing to know the specific circumstances the speaker is responding to.

The arrangement is one of the brighter pieces on Earthling. The recording features full-band production with multiple guest musicians; the tempo is sustained throughout, and the song refuses any quiet middle section that would have softened the album's opening argument. The song's structural simplicity makes it ideal for the kind of audience-led singalong that Vedder's solo shows tend to produce.

Live, 'Invincible' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2022. The song works best as a set opener or as a mid-set energy injection, where its brisk tempo can keep momentum going.
the haves:
'The Haves' is the fourth track on Eddie Vedder's third solo studio album Earthling (2022). The music is Vedder's; the lyric is Vedder's. The song was written and recorded during the Earthling sessions in 2021 with Andrew Watt's production. The song is one of the more meditative pieces on the album, structured around a slower tempo that distinguishes it from the album's brisker opening material.

The lyric is one of Vedder's more direct pieces of writing about cumulative gratitude across a sustained life. The narrator addresses the listener and frames the practice of recognizing what one has (the 'haves' of the title is read most directly as the goods of long partnership, settled friendships, and accumulated meaning, rather than as material wealth) not as complacent but as the kind of structural acknowledgment that any reflective life eventually requires. The song does not editorialize about the political register of the phrase 'the haves' (which carries class-political weight in standard American usage); the song's rerouting of the phrase is part of its argument.

The arrangement is one of the more pared-down pieces on Earthling. The verse is built on a finger-picked acoustic guitar figure that Vedder plays under his own vocal, with restrained band accompaniment in the song's later verses. The song's slow tempo and structural simplicity match the lyric's clarity; the song refuses any cathartic release that would have eased the lyric's meditation.

Live, 'The Haves' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since 2022. The song works best as a quiet moment in the second half of a set, where its small scale can mark a deliberate emotional pause.

good woman.text:
'Good Woman' is a 2003 composition by Chan Marshall, the songwriter who records and performs under the name Cat Power. The song appears as the opening track of her sixth studio album You Are Free, the record that brought Marshall's writing to a substantially wider audience after years of cult standing. The song features Eddie Vedder on background vocals on the studio recording (Vedder and Marshall had been friends since the late 1990s, and Vedder appears as a featured vocalist on multiple tracks across You Are Free).

The lyric is one of Marshall's most direct pieces of writing about the difficulty of choosing to leave a relationship that the speaker still cares about. The narrator addresses a partner and frames the leaving not as escape from a bad situation but as the kind of structural recognition that some relationships, however genuinely loving, are not the kind that can sustain either party's broader life. The song does not editorialize about the partner's quality; the partner is, by the song's own framing, a 'good' person whom the speaker still loves. The song's central argument is that genuine affection is not always enough.

The arrangement is one of the more layered pieces on You Are Free. The verse is built on a chord progression that Marshall plays at a slow tempo; Vedder's background vocal enters in the song's later verses and gives the recording a duet-like vocal architecture. The recording's emotional weight comes from the restraint of both vocalists rather than from any cathartic release.

Live, 'Good Woman' has been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's solo shows since the mid-2000s. The cover honors both Marshall's authorship and the duet history of the original recording. Vedder typically performs the song on acoustic guitar at a tempo close to the You Are Free recording. The song works best as a quiet moment in the second half of a set, where its weight can land on an audience that has been emotionally prepared.

byShow.ev-2014-05-06: On 6 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Good Woman' arrived in the show's eleventh slot as the Cat Power cover (2006 The Greatest, written by Chan Marshall). Vedder's tribute to Marshall's songwriting gave the slot a contemporary cover that the Brazilian audience received quietly.
byShow.ev-2014-05-11: On 11 May 2014 at Citibank Hall, 'Good Woman' arrived in the show's fifth slot as the Cat Power cover.
byShow.ev-2018-03-29: On 29 March 2018 at Citibank Hall, 'Good Woman' arrived in the show's fifth slot as the Cat Power cover.

waving palms.text:
'Waving Palms' is an instrumental piece that appeared in Eddie Vedder's solo shows in São Paulo in March 2018 (the Espaço das Américas residency). The piece is brief and structured around a sustained chord progression that Vedder plays on piano or ukulele, depending on the night; there is no vocal element and no formal lyric. The piece operates as the kind of meditative interlude that Vedder occasionally inserts into his solo sets between heavier vocal material, a practice he has used since the Into the Wild touring period.

The piece's title (which Vedder announced from the stage rather than printing on any released setlist) refers to the silhouettes of palm trees moving in evening wind, an image that Vedder has used in spoken introductions to other pieces across his solo touring catalog. The piece does not have a recorded studio version; it exists only as a live setlist appearance and is not included on any of Vedder's three studio solo albums (Into the Wild, Ukulele Songs, Earthling). The piece is therefore part of the broader category of Vedder solo material that exists primarily as a live-touring object rather than as a recorded artifact.

The arrangement is among the most stripped pieces in Vedder's solo touring vocabulary. The recording context is solo Vedder with a single instrument, and the piece's brevity (under three minutes in any documented performance) places it closer to a meditative cue than to a fully developed song. The piece's appearances have been concentrated in the 2018 São Paulo run; it has not been a regular setlist presence in Vedder's broader solo touring.

Live, 'Waving Palms' has worked best as a deliberate tonal pause in the middle of a set, where its small instrumental scale could mark a transition between heavier vocal material. The piece's specific association with the São Paulo 2018 shows gives it a regional setlist meaning that distinguishes it from Vedder's broader catalog of touring material.

byShow.ev-2018-03-28: On 28 March 2018 at Citibank Hall in São Paulo, 'Waving Palms' opened the show. The March 28 date was the first of three SP solo shows that followed Pearl Jam's Lollapalooza headlining set on March 24.
byShow.ev-2018-03-30: On 30 March 2018 at Citibank Hall in São Paulo, 'Waving Palms' opened the show. The third and final SP solo night of the 2018 residency.

another brick in the wall part 2.text:
'Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2' is a 1979 composition by Roger Waters, the eighteenth track on Pink Floyd's eleventh studio album The Wall. The Wall is a concept album about a fictional rock star (the 'Pink' of the album's narrative) whose isolation hardens into a metaphorical wall between himself and the surrounding world; 'Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2' is one of three songs on the album that share the 'Another Brick in the Wall' title, marking three structural points in the protagonist's accumulating alienation. Part 2 is the most widely known of the three and was the only Pink Floyd single ever to reach number one on the Billboard Hot 100.

The lyric is one of Waters's most direct pieces of writing about the structural cruelty of authoritarian schooling. The narrator (the protagonist Pink, in childhood) addresses the surrounding educational system that has reduced students to interchangeable units of compliance, framing the rejection of that system not as adolescent rebellion but as the kind of structural refusal that any person whose individuality has been suppressed eventually mounts. The song's central refrain ('We don't need no education / We don't need no thought control') is the most widely quoted single line in the broader Pink Floyd catalog. The recording famously features a children's choir from Islington Green School in north London, whose contributions were arranged by producer Bob Ezrin without the school's full knowledge of what the song's content would be; the children's contribution gives the song's argument an additional weight of irony, since the children themselves were producing the recording while the schools they attended were being criticized in the lyric.

The arrangement is one of the most disco-inflected pieces in the Pink Floyd catalog (Ezrin pushed the band toward a danceable rhythm against the band's initial resistance). David Gilmour's guitar solo at the song's center is one of the most widely studied solos in the rock-guitar canon. The song's structural simplicity made it usable as a singalong piece for live audiences across the four decades since its release.

In the Pearl Jam catalog, the song has appeared since 2015 as a tag attached to the closing section of 'Daughter', where the band uses Pink Floyd's chorus refrain as an extension of the broader argument 'Daughter' makes about institutional cruelty toward children. The pairing is structurally apt: 'Daughter' is itself a song about a child being abused by an authority figure who refuses to recognize her as a person, and the Pink Floyd chorus acts as a coda that connects the specific story of 'Daughter' to the broader institutional critique that Waters had made decades earlier.

byShow.pj-2024-08-29: On 29 August 2024 at Wrigley Field, 'Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2' arrived as the tag of the eleventh slot's medley with 'Daughter'. The 1979 Pink Floyd original (written by Roger Waters) gave the medley its anti-authoritarian classroom vocabulary moment, with the Wrigley crowd carrying the chorus at sustained volume.

superblood wolfmoon.text: 'Superblood Wolfmoon' is the second track on Gigaton (2020), the band's eleventh studio album and first since Lightning Bolt 2013. The high-velocity riff (Mike McCready and Stone Gossard sharing credit on the music) and Vedder's lyric (a meditation on a friend's death, often read as a tribute to Chris Cornell) made the song one of the album's most direct rock pieces.

byShow.pj-2021-10-02: On 2 October 2021 at Doheny State Beach (Ohana Encore Festival) in Dana Point, California, 'Superblood Wolfmoon' opened the show as the second-track-of-Gigaton-as-show-opener. The Ohana Encore Festival was the second iteration of Vedder's Dana Point festival (founded 2016, paused 2020, returned as 'Ohana Encore' in 2021 after the original Ohana didn't run that year), and the choice to open with the Gigaton-era track signaled the show's commitment to recent material.

dance of the clairvoyants.text: 'Dance of the Clairvoyants' is the lead single from Gigaton (2020), released January 22, 2020, and a structurally distinct piece in the Pearl Jam catalog: the song's Talking Heads-influenced arrangement (Vedder has cited David Byrne explicitly as the reference point) and Matt Cameron's co-writing credit on the music made it a deliberate departure from the band's typical hard-rock vocabulary. The 2020 single's mid-pandemic release (six weeks before global lockdowns began) gave its lyric of cosmic uncertainty an unintended timely resonance.

byShow.pj-2021-10-02: On 2 October 2021 at Doheny State Beach, 'Dance of the Clairvoyants' arrived in the show's sixth slot. The Talking Heads-influenced Gigaton single's pandemic-era release (January 2020, six weeks before global lockdowns) gave the 2021 deployment a post-pandemic-emergence quality the audience could read.

quick escape.text: 'Quick Escape' is the third track on Gigaton (2020). The song's narrator describes a near-future in which the rich have escaped Earth's climate collapse to live on Mars, leaving the rest behind; the lyric explicitly addresses the Bezos-Musk billionaire-space-escape vocabulary that had emerged in the late 2010s American discourse. McCready's Led Zeppelin-influenced riff (he has cited 'Kashmir' as the structural reference point) gave the song the kind of doomy mid-tempo weight the lyric demands.

byShow.pj-2021-10-02: On 2 October 2021 at Doheny State Beach, 'Quick Escape' arrived in the show's seventh slot. The Gigaton track's billionaire-space-escape lyric carried specific 2021 weight: Bezos's first Blue Origin spaceflight had occurred just over two months before this show (July 20, 2021), making the song's lyric unexpectedly literal.

seven oclock.text: 'Seven O'Clock' is the fourth track on Gigaton (2020). The song's slow build and Vedder's lyric (containing the line 'Sitting Bull and Tatanka, much more than a buffalo' as one of the song's most-quoted moments) gave the album its structural emotional anchor. The seven-minute runtime made it Gigaton's longest track.

byShow.pj-2021-10-02: On 2 October 2021 at Doheny State Beach, 'Seven O'Clock' arrived in the show's tenth slot. The Gigaton ballad's seven-minute slow build gave the slot the kind of patient emotional climb the song's structure invites.

take the long way.text: 'Take the Long Way' is the seventh track on Gigaton (2020), and unusual in the Pearl Jam catalog for being the only Matt Cameron-led vocal on the album (Cameron typically drums for Pearl Jam but had been the lead vocalist of his other band Soundgarden during their 1989-1997 and 2010-2017 active periods). The song's hardcore-tempo riff and Cameron's full-throated vocal gave Gigaton its most aggressive moment.

byShow.pj-2021-10-02: On 2 October 2021 at Doheny State Beach, 'Take the Long Way' arrived in the show's thirteenth slot. The Cameron-led Gigaton track gave the slot the album's most Soundgarden-vocabulary moment, with Cameron singing lead in a Pearl Jam show context.

again today.text: 'Again Today' is a song by Brad, the side project led by Stone Gossard with Shawn Smith on lead vocal. Brad's discography (Shame 1993, Interiors 1997, Welcome to Discovery Park 2002, and others) sat in parallel to Gossard's Pearl Jam work; 'Again Today' (from Interiors) was the song Pearl Jam most often covered as a tribute to the side project after Shawn Smith's death in April 2019. Smith's death made every subsequent 'Again Today' performance a memorial gesture.

byShow.pj-2021-10-02: On 2 October 2021 at Doheny State Beach, 'Again Today' arrived in the show's eighteenth slot as the Brad cover, performed as a tribute to Brad lead vocalist Shawn Smith who had died on April 5, 2019. The two-and-a-half-year tribute period made the deployment an established memorial gesture; Stone Gossard's continued involvement with the song through both Pearl Jam and Brad gave the slot a side-project-tribute weight.

wasted reprise.text: 'Wasted Reprise' is the brief reprise track from Pearl Jam (2006), the band's eponymous album also known among fans as 'Avocado' for its cover art. The reprise (under one minute) served on the album as an interlude between 'Marker in the Sand' and 'Life Wasted', and the live performance of the song typically pairs with 'Life Wasted' the same way the album does.

byShow.pj-2021-10-02: On 2 October 2021 at Doheny State Beach, 'Wasted Reprise' arrived in the show's twenty-first slot, opening the encore. The under-one-minute reprise served as the album-tracklisting structural lead-in to 'Life Wasted' that follows in slot 22.

life wasted.text: 'Life Wasted' is the third track on Pearl Jam (2006). The song's high-velocity riff and Vedder's lyric (the chorus 'I have faced it / a life wasted') is widely read as a meditation on grief and survival in the post-Roskilde, post-9/11 American context. Cameron's drumming drives the song at full velocity throughout.

byShow.pj-2021-10-02: On 2 October 2021 at Doheny State Beach, 'Life Wasted' arrived in the show's twenty-second slot, paired with the preceding 'Wasted Reprise' the same way the Pearl Jam (2006) album tracklisting pairs them. Cameron's drumming drove the song at full velocity.

nothing as it seems.text: 'Nothing as It Seems' is the second track on Binaural (2000) and one of the most structurally distinct pieces in the Pearl Jam catalog: Jeff Ament wrote the music as a slow, atmospheric piece centered on his fretless bass, with Vedder's lyric carrying a meditation on perception and reality. The song has been a steady but not heavy live presence; its slow tempo and structural ambiguity make it the kind of track the band deploys when they want to open or anchor a show with deliberate atmospheric weight.

byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome in Amsterdam, 'Nothing as It Seems' opened the show. The unusual choice of opener (the song typically lives mid-set rather than as a show opener) established the show's deliberately atmospheric opening structure. The Ament-led fretless-bass piece gave the indoor Dutch venue an unusual quiet beginning.

alright.text: 'Alright' is a Vedder solo composition from his Earthling-era recordings (released as a non-album single during Vedder's 2020-2022 work). The song's optimistic chorus and fingerpicked acoustic structure made it a natural fit for both solo and band shows during the period.

byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome, 'Alright' arrived in the show's fourth slot as the Vedder solo-era composition deployed in band arrangement. The compressed structure suited the slot's pacing function: a brief contemporary anchor in the show's slow opening sequence.

black diamond.text: 'Black Diamond' is the closing track of KISS's 1974 self-titled debut album, written by Paul Stanley. The song is one of the band's most-covered classic-rock pieces, and Pearl Jam's rare KISS cover has been deployed at fewer than a dozen shows in three decades. The McCready-led arrangement preserves the original's hard-rock vocabulary.

byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome, 'Black Diamond' arrived in the show's fourteenth slot as one of the rarest covers in the band's three-decade touring catalog: the KISS 1974 track from the debut album. The McCready-led arrangement preserved the Paul Stanley hard-rock vocabulary, and the Amsterdam placement gave Dutch audience one of the few documented Pearl Jam KISS-cover deployments.

purple rain.text: 'Purple Rain' is the title track of Prince's 1984 sixth studio album, the song's slow build into the closing extended-guitar solo making it one of the most-covered Prince songs in rock-history. Pearl Jam's cover has been deployed only on rare occasions, typically when the band wants to mark a specific moment with the song's accumulated 1984-onward emotional weight (Prince's death on April 21, 2016, made every subsequent live cover a memorial gesture).

byShow.pj-2022-07-25: On 25 July 2022 at Ziggo Dome, 'Purple Rain' arrived in the show's eighteenth slot as the Prince cover. The 1984 Prince classic's deployment in a 2022 Pearl Jam show was extremely rare; six years after Prince's April 2016 death, the cover served as both memorial gesture and the kind of cross-vocabulary tribute (rock band covering R&B-funk-rock fusion) that the band had occasionally deployed across its touring history. The Amsterdam crowd sustained the closing extended-guitar passage.
